### Fixed (governance audit chain records the TRUE verdict, not a pre-gate `allow`)

- **The tamper-evident governance audit chain now records the real outcome of a governed decision — a refused action chains `refuse`, not `allow` (or nothing)** (refs [#2634](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2634); CB-24; CWE-778 insufficient logging). Root cause: `record_decision(actor, "allow", …)` fired BEFORE the gate that can refuse the action ran, so a REFUSED governed action was chained as ALLOWED (or, on one surface, not chained at all) — no surface could record a DENY, and the forensic chain lied about what happened. Five surfaces are fixed to record the verdict AT the gate, still BEFORE the downstream storage write so the #913 intent-capture guarantee holds on the allowed path: (1) **`set_namespace_standard`** (`src/mcp/tools/namespace.rs`) — the `record_decision("allow")` fired unconditionally before the #929/#2541 ownership gate; the gate now runs first and a refused bind chains `refuse`; (2) **`clear_namespace_standard`** (same file) — the refusing gate ran BEFORE the record, so a refused clear left NO forensic row at all (the opposite-ordering half of the class); refused clears now chain a `refuse` row; (3–5) **`pending_approve`** on all three surfaces — HTTP `approve_pending` (`src/handlers/governance.rs`), HTTP K10 `approval_decide` (`src/handlers/approvals.rs`), and MCP `handle_pending_approve` (`src/mcp/tools/pending.rs`) — recorded `allow` before `approve_with_approver_type` / the consensus + R40 signed-approval gates, so a #2643 self-approval / unregistered-approver / rejected-signature-quorum refusal was chained `allow`; each now records `allow` on approve / vote-accepted (emitted before the execution write) and `refuse` on any gate refusal, using the established `refuse` decision token the verify-audit-trail chain already understands. Operational errors (NotFound 404 / consensus 500) reach no governance verdict and record no verdict row. Design: a SINGLE row per governed decision carrying the true verdict — the intent-preservation requirement does NOT force a second row, because the `allow` verdict is recorded at the authorization point and before the durable execution write, so an execution failure still leaves the approver identity in the chain while a refused action never chains a false `allow`. Regression: `tests/governance_audit_verdict_2634.rs` (refused set/clear/approve → `refuse` and never `allow`; allowed → `allow`; both HTTP self-approval surfaces + the MCP surface pinned).

### Fixed (postgres HTTP set-standard no longer bypasses ownership via the visibility fold)

- **`set_namespace_standard_inner`'s postgres arm probes the bind-ownership row under a bypass-visibility context, so a #910 visibility denial can no longer skip authorization** (refs [#2709](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2709); CB-4; CWE-284). Pre-fix the postgres arm gated the ownership check as `if let Ok(resolved_mem) = app.store.get(&ctx, &standard_id)`; `PostgresStore::get` under the tenant-scoped request `ctx` (`bypass_visibility=false`) FOLDS a `scope=private` visibility denial into `Err(NotFound)`, so whenever `body.id` named another agent's non-shared memory the `if let Ok` arm was SKIPPED, NO authorization ran, and `set_namespace_standard` bound the row via an unfiltered SQL id lookup. Net: `POST /api/v1/namespaces/<alice-ns>/standard {"id":"<alice's private id>"}` with `X-Agent-Id: bob` returned 201 and replaced alice-ns's governance standard with alice's private memory — a silent authz bypass on the postgres HTTP leg only (the #2706 "always enforces ownership" claim was false there). The sqlite twin was correct because it probes with storage-level `db::get`, which does not fold visibility. The postgres arm now fetches the ownership-probe row under a `CallerContext::for_admin(AI_HTTP_INTERNAL)` context (the #2447 fold-avoiding precedent) and `match`es on the result: a resolved row runs `authorize_namespace_standard_bind` against the REQUEST principal (`ctx.effective_principal()`), a genuine `NotFound` skips authz + proceeds exactly as the sqlite `Ok(None)` branch does (first-write / non-existent id), and any other store error is surfaced. The probe row is used ONLY for the ownership gate and is never returned to the caller, so the #2537/#2707 read-path withholding is unchanged. Regression: `tests/ns_standard_set_ownership_2709_pg.rs` (sal-postgres: bob binding alice's private memory is refused 403 and never becomes the standard; owner bind + first-write auto-seed still succeed).
### Fixed (postgres federation funnel confines links/signals/action_transitions)

- **The postgres `/sync/push` funnel now namespace-scope-authorizes the `links[]`, `signals[]`, and `action_transitions[]` subcollections, matching the sqlite twin** (refs [#2711](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2711); CB-7; CWE-284; two-audit-confirmed). #2683/#2684 gated these three lanes on the sqlite receive funnel (`federation_receive.rs`) but the postgres twin (`sync_push_via_store` in `federation_signing_check.rs`) applied them with NO namespace check — the memories (#2447) and deletions (#1934/#2488) lanes were confined, but the `apply_remote_link` / `apply_remote_signal` / action-transition CAS loops were not. So an enrolled peer scoped `allowed_namespaces:["public/*"]` could push, to a POSTGRES-backed receiver: a `related_to` link whose endpoints are `secure/ops` rows (relating/relocating a foreign-tenant row by id), a signal in `secure/ops`, or a state transition of a `secure/ops` action — all applied. Each lane now routes through the SAME shared `crate::federation::receive_auth` verdicts the sqlite funnel uses, so the two backends behave identically: **links** gate BOTH endpoints' STORED namespaces via `inbound_by_id_namespace_authorized` (a claimed-only gate lets a `public/*` peer relate a `secure/ops` row by id) using the SCALAR `MemoryStore::namespace_by_id` probe (never a full-row `get` — the #2488 decrypt-fail-closed lesson) and fail CLOSED on an unresolvable-or-missing endpoint under Layer 1; **signals** gate the signal's own claimed namespace via `inbound_write_namespace_authorized(LANE_SIGNALS)`; **action_transitions** gate the STORED action's namespace via `inbound_write_namespace_authorized(LANE_ACTION_TRANSITIONS)` (never the wire-claimed one). Refusals are counted (`skipped`), never silently dropped. All three gates short-circuit byte-identically under the zero-config posture (`!has_allowlist()`). Regression: `tests/federation_confine_ns_scope_2711_pg.rs` (live-PG `sal-postgres` twin proving each out-of-scope link/signal/transition is refused and leaves the store unchanged, the in-scope control lands, and zero-config replication is byte-identical).
### Fixed (load_family lifecycle + pre-LIMIT visibility cross-backend parity)

- **The sqlite `memory_load_family` / `memory_smart_load` read path now applies the `lifecycle_visible_clause` fail-closed allow-list and filters `scope=private` visibility BEFORE the SQL `LIMIT`, matching the postgres twin** (refs [#2600](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2600), [#2601](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2601), [#2544](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2544); CB-15; data-integrity + correctness on an always-on core-profile read path). Two cross-backend divergences on `src/mcp/tools/load_family.rs::handle_load_family`: **(#2600)** the sqlite query carried NO lifecycle predicate, so quarantined + tombstoned rows were readable through this always-on tool, bypassing the #1948 fail-closed lifecycle allow-list — while postgres (`PostgresStore::list`) filtered them. The query now threads `crate::models::lifecycle_visible_clause("")` (`lifecycle_state IS NULL OR lifecycle_state IN ('open','active','blocked','done','abandoned')`), so both backends hide system-only states. **(#2601)** the #1555 `scope=private` visibility post-filter (`is_visible_to_caller`, which carries the #1921 team/unit/org subtree carve-out that has no SQL twin) ran in Rust AFTER `LIMIT ?4`, so it silently UNDER-returned — dropping visible rows the caller should see whenever hidden rows sorted above the `k` boundary. The path now mirrors the postgres `load_family_handler` escalation: filter, and when the visible set is short of `k`, re-ask at the `LIST_MAX_LIMIT` (1000) window and re-filter, so both backends return the same rows up to `k`. **(#2544, folded in)** `mcp::lookup_namespace_standard` resolved the bound standard via a bare `db::get` with NO lifecycle/expiry predicate, so an expired / tombstoned / quarantined memory was served as the live governing namespace standard into every recall / session_start; it now gates the bound memory with the same fail-closed lifecycle allow-list (`LifecycleState::is_recall_visible`) + expiry guard (`storage::lifecycle::is_expired`), returning `StandardLookup::Absent` for a non-live standard. Regressions: `tests/memory_load_family.rs::{load_family_excludes_quarantined_and_tombstoned_rows_2600, load_family_visibility_applies_before_limit_no_under_return_2601}` and `src/mcp/mod.rs::tests::inject_namespace_standard_skips_non_live_standard_2544`.

### Fixed (federated DELETE push-DLQ now active on the default build)

- **The delete-lane federation push-DLQ landing pass is no longer `#[cfg(feature = "sal")]`** (refs [#2717](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2717); CB-13, #2498 class; data-loss). #2681 un-gated the STORE-lane DLQ on the default build but left the DELETE lane gated at four sites in `broadcast_delete_quorum` (`src/federation/sync.rs`), on a rationale (`the sink trait is a sal-only surface`) that #2681 itself invalidated by making `async-trait` non-optional. On the shipped default binary (`cargo install`, Homebrew-from-source, iOS/Android static libs built `--no-default-features`) a federated STORE miss landed in `federation_push_dlq` and replayed, but a federated DELETE miss was a `tracing::warn!`-only event and was then silently dropped — the higher-integrity erasure lane leaking the GDPR-erased content a down peer could later LWW-resurrect, while the quorum verdict and the depth gauge both read healthy. The four `cfg` guards are removed (`config.dlq_sink`, the sink trait and the `push_dlq` types are all in the default build post-#2681; only `PostgresDlqSink` is `sal-postgres`-gated) and the false comment corrected, so the delete lane lands a DLQ row and replays on every shipped artifact. Regression: `tests/federation_delete_dlq_default_build_2717.rs` (a DEFAULT-build, non-`sal` twin proving a row is enqueued for a non-acking peer and not for an acking one).

### Fixed (peer-attestation NotUnicode / empty env fails closed, not silent zero-config)

- **`PeerAttestationConfig::from_env` is now EXHAUSTIVE over `std::env::VarError`; a present-but-non-UTF-8 value fails closed (CONFIGURED-BROKEN), not silent zero-config** (refs [#2722](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2722); CB-20, #2504 class; CWE-636 fail-open). Pre-fix the `from_env` match used a catch-all `_` for the error, so `Err(VarError::NotUnicode(_))` — returned when `AI_MEMORY_FED_PEER_ATTESTATION` **is present** but not valid UTF-8 (on Linux env values are arbitrary bytes, so a mis-encoded Latin-1 `EnvironmentFile` with one non-ASCII byte lands here) — fell through alongside `NotPresent` to `env_present=false → has_allowlist()=false`: the pre-#2504 zero-config posture (federated-delete namespace confinement OFF, #1056 TOFU OFF, scope gates OFF, faith-based attribution ON) with **no WARN** — quieter than the parse-error case #2504 was written to fix. The `Err` arms are now matched by explicit `VarError` variant (`pat-exhaustive-enum`, a future variant is a compile error): `NotUnicode` routes into the SAME configured-broken branch as a JSON parse error (`env_present=true`, empty peer map, `has_allowlist()==true`, CONFIGURED-BROKEN WARN) so the destructive inbound lanes fail closed. Only genuine `NotPresent` yields zero-config. F-2: the present-but-empty / whitespace-only value (documented-intentional zero-config; realistic producer is an unexpanded `AI_MEMORY_FED_PEER_ATTESTATION="${FED_PEERS}"`) now emits a `Once`-deduped informational WARN (the per-request `from_env` in `federation_receive.rs` would otherwise spam it) while its zero-config disposition is unchanged.

### Fixed (postgres soft-loser recall penalty was dead code)

- **`PostgresStore::search_with_source_uri` now matches the G7 soft-loser marker's real JSON shape** (refs [#2436](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2436), CB-16). `conserve_contradiction` stamps `metadata.contradiction_soft_loser` as a JSON boolean `true` (`serde_json::Value::Bool`), so postgres' `->>` operator renders it as the TEXT `'true'`. The predicate compared `(m.metadata->>'contradiction_soft_loser') = '1'`, which is ALWAYS false — the multiplicative recall down-weight never applied on postgres, so an LLM-confirmed-contradicted loser kept outranking its fresh winner at full score (a cross-backend divergence: the sqlite twins `json_extract(...) = 1` worked, the postgres mirror did not). Predicate corrected to `= 'true'`; an absent marker still yields `NULL` → factor 1.0 (no penalty, no error). The false in-code comment claiming the penalty applied is corrected. Regression: `tests/pg_soft_loser_penalty_2436.rs` (always-run sqlite value-shape + penalty pins; `#[ignore]`+`sal-postgres` live-PG parity proof).

### Fixed (HTTP get-standard no longer serves private standard bodies)

- **`GET /api/v1/namespaces?namespace=` and path-form `…/{ns}/standard` gate the standard body through `visibility::is_visible_to_caller`** (refs [#2543](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2543); #959 residual; CWE-284). Pre-fix the sqlite arm passed `caller=None` into `handle_namespace_get_standard` and the postgres arm used `CallerContext::for_admin`, so any caller who could name a namespace received title + content + governance of a default-private standard (the last unfiltered read of that body after #2537 closed the injection path). Both arms now resolve `X-Agent-Id` and share the MCP honesty shape: count-only `standards_withheld`, no id/owner leak. Shared-scope and owner reads unchanged. CLI/MCP stdio `None` trust-all posture unchanged.

### Fixed (namespace set-standard no longer caller-opt-in / silent claim)

- **MCP/HTTP `set_namespace_standard` always enforces ownership; unowned rows are never silently claimed** (refs [#2541](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2541); CWE-284). Pre-fix omitting `agent_id` skipped the #929 gate (could rebind any owned memory), and the unowned arm rewrote `agent_id` + stamped `scope=shared` (irreversible confidentiality downgrade). Ownership is always checked; claim rewrite removed. Daemon principal is the explicit CLI/operator bypass.

### Fixed (clear_namespace_standard cannot disarm unresolvable governance)

- **Claimed callers can no longer clear a namespace standard when the bound memory is severed or dangling** (refs [#2545](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2545); CWE-284). Pre-fix the #1777 owner gate short-circuited when the standard was unresolvable, so any claimed agent could `DELETE` the last governance evidence and restore allow-on-silence. MCP/sqlite and PostgresStore refuse unresolvable clears with a re-point remedy; healthy #1777 contracts unchanged.

### Fixed (plaintext peer gate: loopback exactness is now suite-enforced)

- **Regression pins for `host_is_loopback` exactness** (refs [#2677](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2677); CWE-319 class). Behaviour was already correct after #2477; the suite only covered happy-path loopback. Spoof hosts (`127.0.0.1.evil.com`, `localhost.evil.com`, query-embedded loopback strings, `127.0.0.2`) are refused by unit + `FederationConfig::build` tests so a future `starts_with`/`contains` "tidy" cannot silently re-open cleartext federation. Decimal/hex IPv4 forms normalise to `127.0.0.1` in the URL parser and remain correctly exempt (pinned).

### Fixed (release/Docker binaries ship federation `sal` feature)

- **Dockerfile and `release.yml` build with `--features sal` and assert the compiled feature set** (refs [#2676](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2676) packaging residual). Pre-fix default cargo features were only `sqlite-bundled`, so GHCR/deb/tarball artifacts could omit the SAL/federation surface Gate3 measured with an asserted build. `scripts/assert-compiled-features.sh` now runs in the image build and on each release matrix binary (`sqlite-bundled` + `sal`). `sal-postgres` remains opt-in for PG-native deployments (plan-c / explicit build), not forced onto every multi-OS release target.

### Fixed (federated REJECT cannot veto foreign-namespace pendings)

- **`/sync/push` `pending_decisions[]` REJECT is namespace-confined** (refs [#2532](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2532); CWE-284). #2478 gated APPROVE but deliberately left REJECT ungated; an enrolled peer scoped to `public/*` could permanently set `status=rejected` on another tenant's queue. REJECT now uses the same local-row probe + shared `pending_namespaces_authorized` gate as APPROVE. Out-of-scope refuse leaves the row pending (still approvable by legitimate in-scope actors — the correct multi-tenant outcome). In-scope reject still converges. Zero-config unchanged.

### Fixed (federated `namespace_meta` exact-scope no longer sets descendant defaults)

- **`/sync/push` `namespace_meta[]` / `namespace_meta_clears[]` require tree-scope coverage of descendants** (refs [#2536](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2536); CWE-284). #2479 confines the row's own namespace (and parent), but `resolve_governance_policy` walks leaf-first and returns the first ancestor with a policy — so a peer enrolled for exact `["secure"]` could set the DEFAULT policy of every `secure/**` child outside its allowlist. Full pattern-vs-pattern subsumption is not in the #239 `glob_match` SSOT; the control requires the same shared `inbound_write_namespace_authorized` verdict against a **concrete deep descendant probe** (`namespace/__ai_memory_2536_desc/deep`). Exact-scope and single-level `prefix/*` fail; `prefix/**` and `**` succeed. Amendment E (`*` global) unchanged. Zero-config meshes unchanged.

### Fixed (federated `pendings[]` can no longer resurrect a decided governance row)

- **`/sync/push` `pendings[]` refuses to resurrect or clobber a locally-decided pending action** (refs [#2529](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2529); CWE-284). Pre-fix `upsert_pending_action` was `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` over **every** column including `status` / `decided_by` / `approvals`, so an enrolled peer could push `status: "pending"` for an id this node had already rejected and re-arm `execute_pending_action` (which only checks `status == "approved"`), defeating consensus quorum history.
  - Receive loop: refuse wire rows with `status != "pending"` (decisions converge via `pending_decisions[]`); refuse when the **local** row is already terminal.
  - Storage: on conflict, only refresh request body fields, and only while local `status = 'pending'`; decision columns are never wire-writable on conflict.
  - Fresh undecided pendings still apply (zero-config + enrolled).

### Fixed (a typo in `AI_MEMORY_FED_PEER_ATTESTATION` no longer wide-opens federated DELETE)

- **Malformed or empty-present peer-attestation config no longer degrades to zero-config faith replication** (refs [#2504](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2504); CWE-284). Pre-fix `from_env` treated parse error like env-absent: `has_allowlist() == false`, which turns **off** the federated-delete namespace gate and the #1056 TOFU 401 while the WARN claimed "default-deny". Read `/sync/since` and destructive DELETE took opposite postures from the same broken value.
  - **Unset vs present:** env absent/empty → genuine zero-config (`has_allowlist` false). Env set (valid JSON including `{}`, or unparseable) → configured posture (`has_allowlist` true); empty peer map fails closed (no peer enrolled).
  - **WARN** names CONFIGURED-BROKEN: confinement stays ON; federated DELETE is not wide-open.
  - **`PeerScope` is `deny_unknown_fields`** so a typo'd key (`allowed_namespace`) fails closed instead of silent enrolled-unscoped.
  - Zero-config meshes (#2491) unchanged when the env var is truly unset.

### Fixed (GDPR Art. 17: MCP / CLI erasure did not replicate while writes did)

- **MCP `memory_delete` / `memory_forget` and CLI `delete` / `forget` now queue the erasure into a durable outbox that the daemon's existing federation push-DLQ replay worker drains and fans out** (refs [#2446](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2446); GDPR Article 17; 9-lens 3x3 adversarial vote citing `4d3ea1c5`, **option B, 8 of 9 lenses**). `sync::broadcast_delete_quorum` had exactly ONE production caller — the HTTP `DELETE /api/v1/memories/{id}` handler. Every other erasure funnel was purely local, so an agent calling `memory_forget` over MCP erased locally, got `success`, and every federated replica kept the row, re-served it, and could later LWW-resurrect it. The STORE path meanwhile fanned out. **Anti-entropy catch-up cannot cover this**: it propagates writes by PULLING rows, and an erased row is exactly the thing it can no longer see — only an explicit tombstone push can carry an erasure.
  - **Why an outbox rather than an inline broadcast.** Inline is structurally blocked (`FederationConfig::build` is called in exactly one place, `daemon_runtime::bootstrap_serve`; `ai-memory mcp` and the CLI never construct or receive one) AND behaviourally wrong: a blocking quorum broadcast inside the single-threaded JSON-RPC stdio loop (the #965 audit) would stall EVERY subsequent tool call including `memory_store` — precisely the #2577 failure mode whose fix had to introduce a hard budget. The outbox keeps erasure LOCAL, network-free and always-succeeding while the daemon does the paced, resumable, retryable propagation.
  - **NO schema migration.** `federation_push_dlq` already exists on BOTH backends at v48 with a partial-unique index on `(memory_id, peer_id) WHERE replayed_at IS NULL`, a paced + resumable replay worker with quarantine, attempt budget, cause labels, a depth gauge and an operator-documented drain — that IS an outbox. The one gap is that an MCP / CLI process does not know the peer list, so the funnels insert ONE row under the reserved sentinel `peer_id` `__ai_memory_all_peers__` and the daemon (which owns the live peer set AND the federation identity) expands it into per-peer rows on the first drain tick. Everything downstream is the existing machinery, unchanged. The sentinel cannot collide with a real per-peer row for the same memory — the index is keyed on the PAIR — and the expansion re-verifies that against the LIVE peer set and refuses fail-closed rather than mis-fanning-out.
  - **The accumulation bound is structural, not a sweep.** A row is written only when the local database carries a drainability marker that `bootstrap_serve` stamps on every boot where — and only where — a federated, `--features sal`, SQLITE-backed `serve` will actually drain THIS database. Every other boot CLEARS it. So a single-node MCP deployment (the overwhelmingly common case) writes **zero** rows forever, and turning federation off self-heals on the next boot instead of leaving rows nothing will ever drain. The marker is a SIDECAR file beside the database (`<db>.federation-outbox`), never a row in `federation_push_dlq` — **all three indexes on that table are partial `WHERE replayed_at IS NULL`**, so an in-table marker (which must pre-set `replayed_at` to stay out of the pending queue) would be invisible to every one of them and each probe would degrade to a FULL TABLE SCAN, on every erasure and once on the boot path under the shared writer mutex; the #1535 atlas-corpus burst left ~75k rows in that table. The sidecar makes the probe ONE `stat`, independent of DLQ depth, and is also the more honest home: drainability describes THIS HOST's daemon topology, so a database copied or restored elsewhere correctly does not inherit it.
  - **The restore-after-delete race is CLOSED on this path, not merely documented.** A queued erasure that replayed after the id was legitimately restored locally would DESTROY the peer's copy of a row this node currently holds — unintentional data loss, the highest-order harm under the North Star. `db::restore_archived` restores by the archived row's id VERBATIM, so ids are reused and the race is reachable. Because the outbox has a drain delay the inline broadcast does not, the expansion can and does re-check liveness inside the SAME transaction and clears the sentinel WITHOUT fanning out, with a loud WARN naming the supersession. This does not contradict PR #2662's analysis of the same hazard on the inline broadcast path — that path has no queue delay to re-check in, and its residual is unchanged.
  - **Erasure never starts failing.** Every outbox call is best-effort and infallible to the caller: a previously-local, always-succeeding operation does not begin returning errors because federation is unhealthy or the DLQ table is unwritable. The local erasure is already committed by the time the outbox runs; the row is a PROPAGATION record, never the erasure itself.
  - **Deliberately NOT queued:** gc / size-gc eviction and archive purge. Those are LOCAL retention-policy decisions, and replicating one node's TTL sweep to its peers would be data-loss amplification, not erasure. `memory_forget` queues the FULL matched id set (resolved before the delete commits, on the same connection) rather than the #1602 preview list, which is capped at `DRY_RUN_PREVIEW_CAP` (50) and would have silently propagated only the first 50 erasures of a bulk forget.
  - **Postgres, stated plainly.** The WRITE side is sqlite-by-construction (MCP stdio is sqlite-only per CLAUDE.md #1675/n24, and the CLI erasure verbs open a local rusqlite connection), so no erasure sentinel reaches a postgres `federation_push_dlq` today; a postgres-backed `serve` drains the POSTGRES table and never the co-located sqlite file, which is exactly why it does NOT stamp the marker. The DRAIN side is nevertheless implemented and tested on BOTH backends against a live PG 18.4, because an invalid SQL string on an unreachable path ships undetected until the day it becomes reachable.
  - **Known residual, unchanged by this fix:** `memory_delete` writes no `forget_tombstone` (only `forget` does), and `forget_tombstones` themselves do not propagate — `db::memory_is_tombstoned` gates the RECEIVE funnel against a node's OWN tombstones and there are zero references to it under `src/federation/`. So a peer that never applied a delete holds no tombstone for that id and remains re-resurrectable by a third node until the queued erasure lands. Reported, not silently absorbed.

### Fixed (anti-entropy could stall permanently while reporting "in sync")

- **`/sync/since` now publishes a pull cursor derived from the rows it EXAMINED, not the rows it projected** (refs [#2441](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2441); LIVENESS + data-integrity).
  - **The defect.** The endpoint sends the page `LIMIT` to SQL, then runs the per-peer namespace allowlist and the `scope=private` visibility filter **in memory, after it**. Every cursor-shaped value it produced — the `latest_updated_at` diagnostic AND the server's own durable `db::sync_state_observe` clock entry — was derived from the POST-filter vector, and the puller (`daemon_runtime::sync_cycle_once`) derived its next `since` from `pulled.memories.last()`. A window composed entirely of out-of-scope rows therefore answered `count: 0`, `latest_updated_at: null`, **HTTP 200**. The puller got no new cursor, re-requested the identical window forever, and never advanced. The stall was recorded on BOTH sides, and every observable signal — status code, error rate, `scope_status` — read healthy. **Anti-entropy, the mechanism whose entire job is to converge diverged replicas, was the thing that could not converge.**
  - **The fix is two halves; either alone is inert.** Server: a new additive `next_since` wire field carries the honest cursor, and the same value now feeds `sync_state_observe`. Client: `sync_cycle_once` prefers `next_since` and falls back to the legacy `memories.last().updated_at` when the field is absent, so a mixed-version mesh keeps working exactly as before. `latest_updated_at` / `earliest_updated_at` keep their existing meaning (they describe the PROJECTED page) — no wire semantics are redefined.
  - **The new cursor is also tie-group-safe, which `memories.last()` never was.** The predicate is a strict `updated_at > since`, so advancing onto a timestamp several rows share SKIPS every sharer that fell beyond the `LIMIT` — silent row loss on the replica. When the page came back FULL it may have been cut mid-tie-group, so the cursor lands on the newest strictly-older timestamp examined and the trailing group is simply re-examined next round (idempotent: the receiver applies `insert_if_newer`). A FULL page that is ONE tie group holds the cursor and WARNs: stalling loudly is a DEGRADE, advancing would lose rows.
  - **Honest residual.** The postgres SAL adapter clamps its own `LIMIT` internally, so an operator who raises `AI_MEMORY_MAX_PAGE_SIZE` above that clamp can make a genuinely-cut page look short and re-open the tie hazard on that backend. That is the pre-#2441 behaviour of every puller, so it is not a regression — the new guard simply does not extend to it. Separately, both backends' catch-up SEND path skips rows whose at-rest envelope will not open (#2383, env #146), so a window composed entirely of undecryptable rows is invisible to this handler and still cannot advance the cursor; that is the same defect class one layer down and is not addressed here.
  - Pinned by `tests/federation_sync_since_watermark_2441.rs` (R-203 against parent `0b5662ba`: 5 of 7 fail there, including a loop-terminates liveness test that burns its whole round-trip budget without moving; the 2 that pass are guards against the naive `examined.last()` fix).
### Fixed (a federated deletion that failed to reach a peer was logged once and then vanished)

- **`broadcast_delete_quorum` now lands a `federation_push_dlq` row for every dispatched peer that does not ack, mirroring the #933 store-lane landing pass** (refs [#2498](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2498); DATA INTEGRITY — silent, permanent replica divergence). Pre-fix `enqueue_push_failure` had exactly ONE production caller — the bottom of `broadcast_store_quorum` — and the DELETE lane's per-peer failure arm did nothing but `tracing::warn!`. So a federated erasure that failed because the peer was DOWN, because its deadline elapsed, or because the receiver REFUSED it and reported `skipped > 0` inside an **HTTP 200** (already converted to a non-ack by #2341's `success_report_non_ack_reason`) was logged once and then lost. Nothing retried it: the replica kept a row the origin erased, permanently, and could later LWW-resurrect it into the mesh. On a GDPR-erasure or credential-rotation path that is a compliance failure that is invisible by construction, and under `QuorumPolicy::majority` a 3-node mesh still returns **200** to the caller while one node keeps the row forever.
  - The lane now collects `dispatched_peer_ids` before the fanout and records `explicit_failures` in the `Fail | Throttled` arm, then enqueues `dispatched ∖ acked` after the tracker is finalised — byte-identical bookkeeping to the store lane, including the **`deadline_exceeded`** bucket for a peer whose task never reported (invisible to the per-outcome arm, and only reachable via the subtraction). `#[cfg(feature = "sal")]`-gated because the sink trait is a sal-only surface; best-effort, so a sink error warns and continues and never propagates past a local erasure that already committed.
  - **No replay-side change was needed.** The enqueued `payload_json` is the verbatim delete body (`{sender_agent_id, memories: [], deletions: [id], dry_run: false}`), and `replay_once` passes `row.memory_id` as `expected_id`, which `post_once` uses only for the `ids` echo — a delete response carries no `ids`, so the ack path is unaffected. Verified by driving `replay_once` against a recovered peer and asserting the re-POSTed body.
  - **The `(memory_id, peer_id)` upsert collision, reasoned through rather than assumed.** Store-lane and delete-lane rows for the same memory+peer share one key with `DO UPDATE SET payload_json = excluded.payload_json`. **store-then-delete** is CORRECT: the delete is the newer intent for that key, replaying the superseded store body would resurrect a row the origin erased, and the peer converges to "absent" — which is the origin's state.
  - **KNOWN BOUNDED RESIDUAL — delete-then-restore.** A pending DELETE row that replays AFTER the same id was legitimately restored locally (`db::restore_archived` reuses the archived id verbatim) and re-replicated to that peer would destroy the restored replica row. It is reachable because nothing supersedes a pending row on a SUCCESSFUL push — the store/restore lanes enqueue only on FAILURE, and no "clear pending row for (memory_id, peer_id)" sink verb exists. Exposure is bounded (the replay drains the row on the first healthy peer tick, default 30 s; the origin's durable TEXT is untouched; the replica re-converges on the next anti-entropy catchup) and it is documented at the call site rather than papered over. Closing it needs a new `FederationDlqSink` verb — a public-trait change requiring its own 5-agent vote — and is deliberately out of scope. Do NOT "fix" it with a distinct upsert key for the delete lane: that leaves this case exactly as reachable AND regresses store-then-delete into a transient resurrection. The counterfactual it replaces — no delete DLQ at all — is the graver integrity failure.
  - The **#1821/G30 `forget_tombstones`** guard does not cover that residual: it is consulted on inbound WRITES (`db::insert_if_newer`) and at the `restores[]` receive chokepoint against the RECEIVER's own tombstones, and it never gates the inbound DELETE lane. In the residual's shape the peer never applied the delete, so it holds no tombstone for that id, and an operator-initiated `restore_archived` deliberately bypasses the tombstone gate as an authorized un-forget.
  - **`namespace_probe_unresolvable` is STILL DORMANT**, and this change does not wake it. The refused deletion now reaches the DLQ and is retried, but the specific cause LABEL stays unreachable: the receiver emits that token only as a `tracing` field (`federation_receive.rs:892,2168,2494,2600`; `federation_signing_check.rs:671`) and never in the HTTP 200 body, which carries only the `skipped` counter — so the sender's `last_error` is #2341's "peer 2xx but N item(s) skipped …" text and can never contain it. The remaining precondition is a receiver-side wire change echoing the cause in the 200 body. The stale in-code comment claiming the label was "dormant until the delete lane gains a DLQ enqueue (#2498)" is corrected in place to state the real precondition.
  - **Backend-blind by construction**, with evidence rather than assertion: the enqueue is `FederationDlqSink` trait dispatch, and `tests/federation_delete_dlq_2498.rs::pg_delete_lane_dlq_parity_2498` drives the SAME `broadcast_delete_quorum` code path through `PostgresDlqSink` and asserts the identical row (run against a live PG 18.4 scratch database; the shared tier stayed at schema v88 with zero residue).
  - **Scope survey (reported, not silently widened).** Of the thirteen `broadcast_*_quorum` lanes in `src/federation/sync.rs`, only `store` (#933) and now `delete` (#2498) have a DLQ landing pass. The other eleven — `archive`, `restore`, `link`, `consolidate`, `pending`, `pending_decision`, `action_transition`, `checkpoint_resolution`, `signal_create`, `namespace_meta`, `namespace_meta_clear` — plus `bulk_catchup_push` still lose a per-peer failure to a single warn line. Those are filed for follow-up, not fixed here.
### Security (the named-approver arm self-approved, and a misspelled scope published a row)

- **`ApproverType::Agent(required)` — the DESIGNATED-approver arm of the governance approve path — was a bare string compare, so the requester could approve their own action when the policy named them** (refs [#2538](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2538); CWE-863; 3x3 adversarial vote, 9 lenses, `4d3ea1c5` protocol, **7-2**). The `Human` arm three lines above carried BOTH a `SELF_APPROVAL_REFUSED` check (#1787/#1796/#1793) and an `is_registered_agent` check; the `Consensus` arm below carried the registered check (#216). The arm an operator selects *precisely to impose separation of duties* carried neither — it read `if approver_agent_id != required { reject } else { decide_pending_action(.., true, ..) }`. On the HTTP surface `approver_agent_id` derives from `X-Agent-Id`, a **claimed, not attested** principal, so a namespace whose designated approver was also the requester had its governance gate satisfied by the requester, and a policy naming an agent the operator never registered was satisfiable by anyone who could type that string.
  - **Both backends, and the trap that makes that non-obvious.** `approve_with_approver_type` is overridden by **`SqliteStore` only**; Postgres falls through to the trait default in `src/store/mod.rs`, which delegates to `MemoryStore::governance_approve_with_consensus` — a method `PostgresStore` implements with its own byte-for-byte duplicate of the same state machine. A fix in the sqlite override alone would never execute on Postgres. `tests/authz_named_approver_2538_pg.rs` therefore drives BOTH postgres entry points and asserts they agree; at the parent commit its failure message was literally `[trait-default approve_with_approver_type] expected self-approval rejection, got Approved`, which is the trap demonstrated rather than described.
  - **Disposition mirrors the `Human` arm exactly rather than inventing a third shape.** sqlite is surface-keyed through the hoisted `enforce_approver_identity_gate` (`ApproveSurface::Http` enforces unconditionally; `LocalOperator` enforces only under the `AI_MEMORY_AGENT_ID` opt-in); postgres enforces unconditionally, since its SAL is reachable only via the inherently multi-tenant HTTP daemon. In the single-operator MCP/CLI trust-all default the requester and the approver both resolve to the SAME durable `host:<hostname>` id (#1720 B1), and this arm admits exactly ONE approver, so an unconditional reject-self would leave the lone operator's own queued actions unapprovable with no adversary present. The vote weighed that against uniform enforcement and chose the surface-keyed shape 7-2; the unconditional variant's own advocates conceded the escape hatch (an un-approvable action is still `reject`-able — `reject_pending` is not approver-gated — and refusal is returned synchronously, never a silent expiry).
  - **Residual, stated rather than hidden:** under the opt-in, a policy whose designated approver IS the requester makes that action unapprovable by anyone. That is the intended reading of a separation-of-duties control — the action stays `pending` and rejectable, never wrongly approved — and the remedy is to re-point the policy (policy change is not itself a `GovernedAction`, so there is no deadlock-on-deadlock).
  - **Liveness is pinned, not assumed.** Both suites assert that a REGISTERED, non-requester designated approver still approves, that the pre-existing wrong-approver refusal fires FIRST and is byte-unchanged (so the new checks never leak whether some other id is registered), and that the sqlite `LocalOperator` opt-OFF path is byte-identical to before.
  - R-203 both backends: `storage::tests::agent_arm_refuses_self_approval_and_unregistered_2538` and `named_approver_cannot_self_approve_pg` / `unregistered_named_approver_refused_pg` each FAIL at parent `cc61a899` with `expected self-approval rejection, got Approved` / `expected unregistered rejection, got Approved`, and pass after. The postgres legs run against a live PG 18.4 + AGE 1.7.0 + pgvector 0.8.6 tier at schema v87 (**no schema change** — the #2445 guard is untouched).

- **An unrecognised `metadata.scope` token — including a one-character typo — made a row world-readable on every non-SQL read path** (refs [#2633](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2633); CWE-863 / FBL-14; same 3x3 vote, **8-1**). `src/visibility.rs` read `Some(None) => true`: "the scope key is present but is not a `MemoryScope` ⇒ **widest** posture". A row with NO scope key defaulted to owner-keyed private; a row with a MISSPELLED one (`"privat"`, `"sharedd"`, `"Private"` — the parse is case-sensitive) was public. One character apart, opposite postures. **On Postgres this predicate is the SOLE scope gate** — `PostgresStore` ships no SQL `visibility_clause` and filters `list` / `search` / `get_many` / kg in Rust through this function — so the widening was unmitigated there. The house rule is the opposite: `receive_auth::env_flag_default_on` keeps the secure default on an unrecognised token and `AI_MEMORY_INFERENCE_EGRESS` WARNs and fails closed to `deny` on a typo.
  - **The arm is now a CLOSED set.** The legitimate `#948`/`#978` federation shareable token stays broadly visible via `visibility::LEGACY_BROAD_SCOPES` (currently exactly `"shared"`); every other unrecognised token WARNs (`tracing` target `visibility.unknown_scope`, naming the row and the valid set) and falls through to the **absent-key default**.
  - **The disposition is `private_visible`, not a bare deny — deliberately.** The narrowest posture that closes the cross-tenant hole still lets the row's OWN owner (and an inbox target) read it, so a typo costs the writer reach, never access to their own data. Failing closed to `false` would make a misspelled row unreachable by the one principal who can repair it, which is data loss dressed as security. A dedicated test asserts a typo'd row is byte-indistinguishable from an absent scope key across five caller shapes — that equivalence IS the fix.
  - **`shared` is grandfathered, not migrated, and NOT reified as a sixth `MemoryScope` variant.** Both alternatives were on the ballot and both lost. Migration mutates durable rows and is irreversible across the federation boundary (peers keep emitting `shared`). The enum route is worse than it looks: `MemoryScope::from_str` is **not** visibility-private — `governance::refusal::required_scope_refusal` funnels through it and coerces an unparseable token to `Private`, so a parsing `Shared` variant flips every `scope:"shared"` write from SATISFYING a `required_scope = private` policy to being REFUSED by it. The rows carrying `scope:"shared"` are the `_standard:<ns>` governance-policy **placeholders** (`handlers::hook_subscribers` first-write + the #2541 ownership-restamp; `mcp::tools::namespace` set-standard restamp) — the policy CARRIER itself — so that route bricks `set_standard` in exactly the namespaces pinning a required scope, and would additionally make `"shared"` serde-reachable as a `CorePolicy::required_scope` value, widening a v1.0.0 public contract.
  - **Denying `shared` outright would have been a data-integrity defect strictly worse than the disclosure.** On Postgres the `set_standard` handler LOCATES the existing `_standard:<ns>` placeholder through `store.list(..)` — i.e. through this very predicate. Make it invisible and the lookup misses, the handler takes its first-write branch, and the namespace acquires a SECOND governance-standard row under a different owner: governance policy split-brain.
  - **Blast radius is confined by construction.** `MemoryScope`, `VALID_SCOPES`, `MemoryScope::COUNT`, `all()`, `all_strs()`, the "5 visibility scopes" docs narrative, `storage::is_visible`, the SQL `visibility_clause` and every SSOT pin are **untouched** — the fix lands in the one predicate that has the defect. `src/storage/mod.rs` is not touched by this half at all.
  - **Ingress validation, scoped so federation still converges.** The new `validate::validate_metadata_scope` refuses a typo'd INLINE `metadata.scope` (which `validate_scope` never saw — it only ever guarded the top-level `scope` PARAMETER) on the caller-origin funnels: `validate_create` (HTTP `POST /memories` + `/bulk`), `validate_update` (HTTP `PUT`), and the MCP update path, which validates inline rather than through the DTO validator. Accepted set = `VALID_SCOPES` ∪ `LEGACY_BROAD_SCOPES`, because the substrate itself writes `scope:"shared"` onto the governance placeholders. It is **deliberately NOT** wired into `validate_metadata` / `validate_memory`, which sit on the federation-receive, import, reflect and consolidate funnels: a refusal there would DIVERGE replicas (the #1821 secret-screen lesson — caller-origin refuses, federation/recovery degrades). An inbound peer row with a typo'd scope is stored verbatim and simply reads as private locally, and a regression test pins that.
  - **A SECOND reachable funnel was found and closed: the postgres `find_paths` path-traversal filter carried its own inline copy of the predicate, and that copy had drifted twice.** `<PostgresStore as MemoryStore>::find_paths` resolved each graph node's metadata and applied `if scope != MemoryScope::Private.as_str() { true } else { owner == caller }`, under a comment asserting parity with `is_visible_to_caller`. It had neither the #2633 narrowing (a typo'd token is `!= "private"`, so the node published the path) **nor the #1921 subtree restriction** (`team` / `unit` / `org` are also `!= "private"`, so they stayed world-readable on the postgres kg path long after every other read path was narrowed) — a cross-tenant disclosure in its own right, since `find_paths` returns memory ids and an id is the key to `GET /memories/{id}`. The stated reason for the copy — "we only have the metadata blob, not a full `Memory` struct" — is answered by selecting the two extra scalar columns the predicate needs (`SELECT id, namespace, metadata`) and calling the new field-level `visibility::is_visible_by_fields`, which `is_visible_to_caller` now also delegates to. There is again exactly ONE implementation of this predicate. The change is strictly NARROWING (fewer paths returned, never more) and is pinned by `tests/scope_find_paths_visibility_2633_pg.rs` against the live tier, including a liveness leg that passes in BOTH states so a predicate that simply returned `false` could not masquerade as a fix.
  - **`public` is NOT enumerated as a broadly-visible legacy alias, and that is a decision with evidence behind it.** Four in-repo fixtures seeded `scope: "public"`, and one of them (`tests/session_start_scope_private_1420.rs`) asserts the row is visible to a non-owner — so a naive read of the failure says "add `public` to the broad set". It is the wrong read: `validate::validate_scope` REFUSES `"public"` on every write surface, asserted by the pre-existing `validate::tests::test_invalid_scope`; NO production code writes it (the fixtures reach the DB through `db::insert` directly, bypassing the validator); and the live 8,724-row certified corpus contains zero `public` rows (only `collective` 7,861 and absent 863). Enumerating it would leave the substrate refusing to let an operator WRITE the token while publishing to everyone any row that carries it — the exact write/read incoherence this issue removes. `"shared"` is genuinely different and is grandfathered on that basis: five PRODUCTION sites still write it onto the `_standard:<ns>` governance placeholders, and it is the documented #948/#978 federation shape. `"personal"` was checked for the same reason and is likewise asserted INVALID by `test_invalid_scope`, so it is not a third alias. The coherence rule is now pinned by `broad_set_does_not_contradict_the_write_validator`, which forces any future widening to be a decision rather than a side effect.
  - **Correcting the #2633 scope statement.** `validate_scope`'s call sites only ever guarded the TOP-LEVEL `scope` parameter, so the read-path arm was not merely defence-in-depth: a caller writing `metadata.scope` INLINE was ungated on HTTP create, HTTP update and MCP update (the handler comment at `handlers/create.rs` says so outright — "inline metadata.scope still works; top-level is a shortcut"). `validate_create_gates_inline_scope` / `validate_update_gates_inline_scope` FAIL at the parent commit, which is the proof those funnels accepted a typo. MCP store was already gated (it resolves `params["scope"]` OR `metadata.scope` before validating) and the CLI exposes no inline-metadata surface.
  - **Three in-repo test fixtures depended on the defect** and are corrected, not masked: they stamped `scope: "public"` — a token that is not a `MemoryScope` and only ever passed the visibility gate because unrecognised meant world-readable — and now use `collective`, the real world-readable scope they always meant.
  - R-203: 5 of the 10 assertions in `tests/scope_unknown_token_2633.rs` FAIL at parent `cc61a899` (`typo_scope_is_not_world_readable`, `typo_scope_degrades_to_owner_keyed_private_not_to_nobody`, `typo_scope_matches_absent_key_posture_exactly`, `validate_create_gates_inline_scope`, `validate_update_gates_inline_scope`) and all 10 pass after.
### Added (Gate 3 packaging — binary feature self-report)

- **`ai-memory features` reports the cargo features compiled into this binary** (refs [#2676](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2676); Gate 3 packaging). Human form: `version:` + `features:` (sorted CSV). `--json` form: `{"version","features"}`. Provision / measure harnesses must assert the feature set (not merely `--version` success) — `scripts/assert-compiled-features.sh` is the pin. Pure compile-time table (`src/build_features.rs`); no DB, no network.

### Fixed (GA BLOCKER: `AI_MEMORY_STORE_URL=postgres://` was silently ignored — daemon wrote to the wrong store)

- **`serve` now REFUSES a `postgres://` store URL when the binary cannot open Postgres, instead of falling back to local SQLite and reporting healthy** (refs [#2679](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2679); DATA INTEGRITY / silent wrong-store write; the [#2444](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2444) false-success class). Reproduced against the published v0.10.0 release binary: `AI_MEMORY_STORE_URL=postgres://… ai-memory serve` created a real SQLite database + 1.1 MB WAL at `--db`, logged `database: <path>`, and said nothing about the discarded Postgres URL. Root cause: `resolve_store_url` is ungated (#1927 / #2444 hoist) but the only consumer that *acted* on it was `build_store_handle`, which is `#[cfg(feature = "sal")]`. Env and file channels therefore failed silent; argv `--store-url` already fails loud (clap, sal-gated). Fix: ungated `refuse_postgres_store_url_without_feature` at the top of `bootstrap_serve`, before `db::open`. Scope is **postgres:// only** — `sqlite://` and bare paths stay permissive so a legitimate local-file deployment is never a GA-day outage. With `sal-postgres` compiled in the guard is a pure no-op. Password redacted per #1579 A3. Pinned by unit test `issue_2679_postgres_store_url_fails_closed_without_feature` and binary test `tests/store_url_fail_closed_2679.rs` (refuse path creates neither the db file nor a WAL; legitimate no-URL serve still boots).

### Fixed (GA BLOCKER: shipped binary silently dropped federation push failures and reported healthy)

- **The default (sqlite-only) build now enqueues failed federation fanouts into `federation_push_dlq` and runs the replay worker** (refs [#2678](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2678); DATA INTEGRITY / silent write loss + false-success metrics; the [#2444](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2444) class). Pre-fix the DLQ trait, sink field, enqueue branch in `broadcast_store_quorum`, bootstrap wiring, and replay worker were all `#[cfg(feature = "sal")]` solely because `async-trait` was a SAL-only dep — while migrations created `federation_push_dlq` unconditionally, `ai_memory_federation_push_dlq_depth` registered with no `cfg` and pinned at 0 ("healthy"), and doctor had no DLQ section. Three affirmative all-clears over a sink that was compiled out. **Scoped fix:** make `async-trait` non-optional (+1 crate); un-gate `push_dlq` / `FederationConfig.dlq_sink` / the enqueue path / default-build `SqliteDlqSink` bootstrap + replay worker. Do **not** flip `default` features (would push 442 `cfg(feature="sal")` sites onto the shipped path). `PostgresDlqSink` stays `sal-postgres`-gated. Pinned by the existing `federation::push_dlq` unit suite (11 tests) which now compile and pass under the default feature set.



### Security (federation peer URLs accepted plaintext `http://` with no flag, cert, or acknowledgement)

- **A federation peer URL that is not `https://` is now REFUSED at boot, on BOTH peer-URL doors** (refs [#2477](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2477); CONTENT DISCLOSURE; 3x3 adversarial vote, 9 lenses, option D 6/9, citing the 5-agent vote `4d3ea1c5`).
  - **The defect.** `FederationConfig::build` formatted the raw operator `--quorum-peers` string straight into `PeerEndpoint::sync_push_url` with **no scheme validation whatsoever**; `src/federation/sync.rs` parsed the scheme only to populate a governance `NetworkRequest` action, never to require TLS. Federation replicates memory content that is **not** end-to-end encrypted (`src/encryption/mod.rs`; #1968 open), so `--quorum-peers http://peer:9077` shipped tenant memory in the clear to any on-path, DNS-position or BGP-position adversary. Meanwhile `docs/encryption.html` asserted unqualified that peer traffic "travels over mutual TLS … TLS 1.3 only (no fallback)".
  - **It was strictly weaker than a control already shipped.** #2448 built a **four-condition** opt-in ceremony for the *weaker* accept-ANY-server-cert case (`--insecure-skip-server-verify` **and** `--client-cert` **and** `--client-key` **and** an explicit falsy `AI_MEMORY_FED_REQUIRE_SERVER_VERIFY`, itself pinned by `asi-hard`). Plain `http://` needed **none** of them and disclosed strictly more. The mTLS control also cuts the other way: a peer pinning OUR client cert protects the PEER from an impostor client, not US from an impostor server.
  - **The guard is ONE validator called from BOTH doors.** `ai-memory sync-daemon --peers` (`cli::sync::build_sync_client`) is a fully independent peer-URL path that wired the #2448 ceremony but validated no scheme either — a fix scoped to `federation/peer.rs` alone would have been theatre. `tls::validate_peer_url_scheme` now gates both.
  - **Disposition.** `https://` always accepted. `http://` to a **literal** loopback host is always accepted with no hatch — the bytes never leave the kernel, dozens of this repo's own fixtures and every single-host dev mesh use `http://127.0.0.1:PORT`, and forcing a hatch-flip on all of them would train reflexive hatch use (a worse long-run posture). The loopback set is now the SSOT `tls::host_is_loopback`, shared with the inbound `tls_bind_guard` so the two cannot drift. A container-bridge hostname such as `http://alice:9077` is **not** loopback: it crosses an interceptable virtual NIC, and treating "feels local" as "is local" is the category error the control exists to prevent. Everything else — non-loopback `http://`, a foreign scheme, and a scheme-LESS `peer.example:9077` (previously accepted, then failing opaquely at request time) — is refused.
  - **Refusal is WHOLE-BOOT, never per-peer skip-and-continue.** `n = 1 + peer_urls.len()` feeds `QuorumPolicy::new`, so silently dropping a peer would change the quorum guarantee without saying so; and `PeerEndpoint.id` is a positional index (#2442), so a shrunken list also re-keys every queued DLQ row above the gap.
  - **`AI_MEMORY_FED_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_PEERS`** (env #154) is the staged-rollout hatch: permissive-knob grammar, default OFF, opened only by an explicit truthy token — unset, empty, `0`, or an unrecognised word all KEEP the refusal (the #131/FBL-14 rule: an unrecognised token must never silently widen a security control). **`asi-hard` pins it OFF** — the second permissive knob in that SSOT after `AI_MEMORY_ALLOW_SCHEMA_AHEAD`, and the second network access-control pin after `AI_MEMORY_FED_REQUIRE_SERVER_VERIFY` — so a hardened procurement deployment cannot re-open plaintext federation. Before this, `docs/deploy/asi-hard.env` verbatim still permitted it.
  - **The refusal message names the SECURE remedies first** (`https://`, `--quorum-ca-cert`, `AI_MEMORY_FED_PEER_FINGERPRINTS`) and the escape hatch LAST, pinned by an ordering assertion — a control whose message leads with "here is how to turn me off" is a control that gets turned off.
  - **Operator-visible break, flagged deliberately.** This repo's own `infra/plan-c` and `infra/lan-parity-test` compose fleets federate over non-loopback plaintext container hostnames; both now carry an explicit acknowledgement line rather than being left to fail on upgrade. Any external deployment with a non-loopback `http://` peer must move it to `https://` or set the hatch. `docs/encryption.html`'s unqualified mTLS claim is corrected in place so the shipped doc is true.
  - Pinned by `tests/federation_plaintext_peer_2477.rs` (R-203 against parent `0b5662ba`: 7 of 9 fail there; the 2 that pass are the loopback- and https-exemption guards, which exist to block an over-broad fix).
### Fixed (the federation DLQ routing key was a POSITIONAL peer index — decommissioning a peer misrouted queued writes to the wrong host and marked them delivered)

- **`PeerEndpoint.id` is now derived from peer IDENTITY (`peer-h1<32 hex>` = `SHA-256("ai-memory:peer-id:v1\0" || <normalised url>)`) instead of the `--quorum-peers` `.enumerate()` index** (refs [#2442](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2442); CROSS-TENANT DISCLOSURE + SILENT WRITE LOSS; 3x3 adversarial vote, 9 lenses, both sub-decisions). The id was treated as "just a Prometheus label" and was in fact the DURABLE routing key of `federation_push_dlq.peer_id` AND of the `sync_state` catch-up vector clock. Remove one peer from the flag list and every higher index shifts down: `push_dlq::replay_once`'s `config.peers.iter().find(|p| p.id == row.peer_id)` then SUCCEEDED against a different host, POSTed another tenant's full memory payload there, and stamped the row `replayed_at`. Both halves of the north star break at once — an unintended peer receives content it was never authorised to hold, and the intended peer never receives the write and diverges permanently, with no counter and no error. The same positional key also let a surviving peer INHERIT a decommissioned peer's catch-up watermark, which can skip rows outright.
  - **The id is a pure, total function of the normalised URL**, so adding, removing, or reordering peers never re-keys a survivor. The lookup can now only FAIL — it can no longer succeed against the wrong endpoint, which is the security property, not the id string.
  - **128 bits of digest, not 48, because this is a SECOND-PREIMAGE setting rather than a birthday one.** The fleet-size calculation (tens of peers) says 48 bits is ample, and it is wrong here: the hash input is OPERATOR-SUPPLIED, so an adversary who can get one URL into `--quorum-peers` picks it freely. The profitable target is a peer that has been REMOVED from the config but whose rows are still in `federation_push_dlq` — grind a URL whose id equals the departed peer's and `replay_once` hands you its queued payloads. That is ~2^48 SHA-256 evaluations, hours of commodity GPU time, and the boot-time collision guard CANNOT see it because the victim is not in the config to be compared against. At 128 bits the search is infeasible. The cost is zero: `PeerEndpoint.id` reaches **zero** Prometheus labels at v1.0.0 — every `with_label_values` call in the federation lane takes a closed-set token — so the `#304` label-space objection recorded in the pre-#2442 comment was **stale**, and is corrected in place rather than left to be re-derived as a false constraint.
  - **The derivation is a FROZEN WIRE FORMAT and says so.** The preimage is domain-separated and version-tagged (`ai-memory:peer-id:v1\0`), and the id prefix carries the version (`peer-h1`), because `normalize_peer_url` is deliberately SHARED with the `#341` duplicate-URL check and those two consumers have OPPOSING long-run requirements: the duplicate check SHOULD normalise more over time (IDNA, default-port stripping, percent-decoding) while the id must normalise identically forever or every persisted row is orphaned. `tests/federation_stable_peer_id_2442.rs::frozen_wire_format_golden_2442` is the tripwire that forces that to be a deliberate migration instead of a silent fleet-wide identity rotation with no failing test. The `h` in the prefix is load-bearing too: 32 hex nibbles are all-decimal-digits often enough to matter, so it is what makes a minted id structurally unable to impersonate the legacy `peer-<digits>` shape.
  - **Fail-closed collision guard.** `FederationConfig::build` refuses to start if two peers mint the same id, naming both URLs — a shared routing key would merge two peers' DLQ rows and misroute in a different direction. Mirrors the existing duplicate-URL boot refusal on the same loop. Extracted as a pure function so the branch is unit-testable rather than unreachable and untrusted.
  - **Legacy rows are SKIPPED, never auto-remapped — and what that costs is stated out loud.** Rows written by a pre-#2442 binary carry `peer-0`, `peer-1`, … Remapping `peer-N` -> `config.peers[N]` IS the defect, and a binary upgrade is precisely when operators edit peer lists, so guessing would re-commit it at the worst moment. Those rows are detected by the SHAPE of `peer_id`, skipped, and left in the table with their payload intact; after `MAX_REPLAY_ATTEMPTS` they quarantine and stop retrying automatically. **The loss is real and is not hidden:** until an operator re-keys them, those writes reach the peer only via its own `/sync/since` catch-up. The remediation is documented at `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md` §federation-push-DLQ, including the shell one-liner that computes a peer's stable id from its URL alone (no daemon needed) and the `attempt_count = 0` reset without which a re-key is a silent no-op against the take-exclusion.
  - **The attempt bump is not optional and the reason is liveness.** Pending rows drain `ORDER BY failed_at ASC`, and legacy rows are by construction the OLDEST, so a row that never burned its budget would sit at the head of every batch forever and STARVE live rows out of the replay window — a new silent-loss vector introduced by the fix. Bumping lets them converge to take-exclusion and hands the queue back. The annotation is applied EXACTLY ONCE and preserves the ORIGINAL enqueue reason verbatim, because `bump_dlq_attempt` overwrites `last_error` and the DLQ row IS the forensic record of why the write was undelivered.
  - **No new closed-set cause label**, on the convergent finding of three independent lenses. `classify_quarantine_cause` is an ORDERED SUBSTRING matcher over a string that peer-supplied text can reach, so an arm there would be attacker-steerable AND would override the row's real cause. The condition gets its own counter instead: `ai_memory_federation_push_dlq_legacy_positional_total`. The pre-existing 2-cause drift in the `federation_push_dlq_quarantined_by_cause` HELP string (`unenrolled_author_strict`, `namespace_probe_unresolvable`) is re-synced in the same commit.
  - **`sync_state` orphans self-heal and the runbook FORBIDS touching them.** A missing clock entry makes catch-up pull from the beginning, bounded to 500 rows/tick, oldest-first, idempotent via `insert_if_newer` — it converges on its own. But `sync_state_observe` is MONOTONIC with no API that walks a clock backwards, so an operator who mirrors the DLQ re-key onto `sync_state` and gets one row wrong permanently advances a cursor past rows that were never pulled, converting a benign orphan into irreversible write loss. The two have opposite correct answers; the runbook says so explicitly.
  - **Peer registration is logged at INFO, not debug.** The id is now opaque, so that line is the operator's id->url decoder for DLQ triage. It fires once per peer at boot.
  - **No schema migration.** `federation_push_dlq.peer_id` and `sync_state.peer_id` are bare `TEXT`; the resolution is a whole-string equality lookup that fails CLOSED, so pre-fix and post-fix binaries reading each other's rows both no-op rather than misroute, and the change is symmetric and reversible. The id is never on the wire (`x-peer-id` carries `sender_agent_id`), so a mixed-version fleet is a non-event.
  - Pinned by `tests/federation_stable_peer_id_2442.rs`. The load-bearing test is NOT an id comparison — it stands up three live mock peers, queues a DLQ row for B and one for C, decommissions B, and drives a real `replay_once` tick, asserting that no payload queued for B reaches C **and** that C's own row still lands (the positive control, without which a refactor that made `replay_once` bail early would satisfy every other assertion while proving nothing).

### Fixed (the supply-chain build-script gate verified 2 of 90 build scripts; the gate that proves the other gates work was required by nothing)

- **`scripts/check-build-script-vetting.py` now walks `cargo metadata` for EVERY package carrying a `custom-build` target and fails closed on any absent from the ledger** (refs [#2635](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2635); 3x3 adversarial vote, 9 lenses, 6-3). It iterated only its own ledger (`for record in ledger["packages"]`), which held **2** packages while the resolved graph holds **90 with a build script** out of 547 — `cc`-class native builders, `ring`, `libsqlite3-sys`, `aws-lc-sys`, `onig_sys`, `esaxx-rs`, `zstd-sys`, `serde`, `syn`, `libc` and the rest. There was **no reverse direction**, so a new crate carrying a hostile `build.rs` was never examined and the gate printed `PASS (2 records verified)`. A build script executes arbitrary code with the BUILDER's authority at compile time, on every CI runner and every operator machine; this gate is the mechanical enforcement of the operator's firmest standing rule, *"no external code injection. EVER."* — adopted after an external party attempted precisely this vector, including recommending a crate that did not yet exist on crates.io so it could be published later (a cargo-squat trap).
  - **R-203, observed at parent `cc61a899`:** the gate exits **0** while 88 unvetted build-script packages are present, and `--self-test` was not even a recognised argument — it fell through and silently ran the gate, exiting 0 without testing anything. It was the ONLY `check-*` gate in the repo with no self-test, so there had never been evidence it was load-bearing.
  - **The ledger is now an allowlist that must COVER REALITY**, with two honest dispositions. `reviewed` (2) means the source was read and requires a dated `docs/security/build-script-vetting.md` anchor plus a pinned build-dependency closure; `inventoried` (88) means pinned and dated but **NOT source-reviewed**. Stamping 90 `reviewed` records on unread source was rejected by every lens that considered it: it would buy a green check that actively asserts rigor which is not present, which is a net integrity LOSS versus an honest weaker label. The PASS line always prints both counts and states what it does not attest, so it cannot be quoted as "90 build scripts reviewed". Burn-down is by PROMOTION only — the gate refuses a `reviewed` record with no review anchor or date, so a bulk relabel is a large, loud diff rather than a one-word edit.
  - **`inventoried_ceiling` is a monotone ratchet** in the shape this repo already runs green (`hardcoded-literals-baseline.txt`, `required-contexts-joblevel-if-allow.txt`, `dual-trigger-cancel-allow.txt`). Without it, admitting an unvetted build script costs a **one-line append** that rides along unnoticed in a large PR; with it, the same act also requires raising a number that exists for no other purpose. Dependency additions already require operator authorization (`CLAUDE.md` §"Dependencies"), so that red is the policy gate firing where policy already said it must.
  - **Pinning is per source kind, and the vendored branch is not a convenience.** Registry packages are pinned by `Cargo.lock` checksum. `vendor/paste` is the **one** package in the graph with no source and therefore no lockfile checksum — and simultaneously the highest-risk build script present: in-tree, editable in any pull request, no upstream to diff against, and it `Command::new($RUSTC)`s at build time. Treating "no checksum" as "skip it" would have been the same fail-open being closed, so it is pinned by `tree_sha256` over every git-tracked file under `vendor/paste` — covering its `src/` too, which matters because `paste` is a **proc-macro** and therefore also compile-time-executed code. A registry package may never be pinned by a tree digest; that shape is rejected explicitly, so "declare it vendored" cannot become a universal checksum bypass.
  - **`--self-test`** plants an unvetted build-script package against synthetic metadata (no network, no registry, no mutated manifest — the checker's core is a pure function of `(ledger, lockfile, metadata, digest_fn)`) and requires the rejection to NAME that violation and no other. It plants eight sibling defects (stale record, checksum drift, vendored-tree drift, uncomputable digest, registry-pinned-as-vendored, ceiling breach, unsubstantiated review, duplicate record, malformed schema/ceiling, and an EMPTY universe, which must fail closed rather than vacuously pass) and spares six near-miss shapes that must each PASS — a non-custom-build package absent from the ledger, a proc-macro target kind, an all-`inventoried` ledger, a count under the ceiling, a clean vendored digest, a matching closure — so the rule fires on the defect and not its neighbourhood. **The R-203 leg is in-harness:** the FROZEN pre-#2635 ledger-only algorithm is run over the same fixture and must return ZERO violations, so the leg cannot pass tautologically. A grounding leg runs the real algorithm over the real repo, so the suite cannot be a green parser exercise while the shipped configuration is broken.
  - **`--update-checksums`** refreshes the pins of records that already exist and is structurally incapable of adding, removing or re-disposing one — so a routine dependency bump has a sanctioned path that is never the thing which admits a new build script.
  - **The gate is out of the skippable job.** It ran as a STEP inside `Lint (fmt + clippy)`, which carries `if: needs.classify.outputs.docs_only != 'true'` and reports **`skipped`** on a docs-only pull request — and branch protection **counts `skipped` as satisfied**. A supply-chain gate that a classifier verdict about markdown can switch off is not a gate. It is now the dedicated `Build-script custom-build ledger gate (#2635)` job in `ci.yml` with **no job-level `if:` and no `needs:`**, so it always runs and always reports a real success/failure. It is in `ci.yml` rather than `c8-precheck.yml` because it needs a pinned Rust toolchain and a registry fetch, which that deliberately toolchain-free workflow does not carry.

- **Rule (f): every job in a gating workflow must be declared required, or dated-and-tracked as not-required** (refs [#2636](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2636)). Four `c8-precheck.yml` integrity gates ran on every pull request and were required by nothing: `Installer checksum fail-closed gate (#2449)`, `Non-Rust conformance-reader proof gate (#2452)`, `Git-dependency-source supply-chain gate (#2050/#2512)`, and `Required-context + classify-base soundness gate (#2494/#2496/#2508)` — **the last being the gate itself**, the sole mechanical proof that the other required contexts are creatable, reachable, non-skipping, non-cancelled and non-truncated. A pull request that broke the gate proving the gates work could merge. All four are now DECLARED in `scripts/qc-allowlists/required-contexts-release.txt`, alongside the new build-script job, taking the mirror from 24 to **29** declared contexts; live protection stays at 24 until the operator's branch-protection call, which is the ADDITION half of that file's ORDER doctrine (mirror first, protection after — prove, then enforce).
  - **R-203, observed at parent `cc61a899`:** `scripts/check-required-contexts.sh` exits **0** with those four gates unrequired. Rules (a)-(e) all reason mirror -> job, so not one of them can see a job that is simply ABSENT from the mirror. Rule (f) reasons workflows -> inward and closes the direction the other five structurally cannot.
  - **The `KNOWN GAPS` section was itself the gap.** It read *"Two c8-precheck integrity gates run on every PR but are not required"* and named only #2449 and #2452 — **wrong by two**, missing the git-dependency gate and the meta-gate. It has been rewritten from the actual diff. That prose note is exactly why the new ledger is machine-parsed: prose cannot fail CI, so prose rots, and a rotted gap note reads exactly like a closed one.
  - **The ledger `scripts/qc-allowlists/required-contexts-not-required.txt` is EMPTY, and that is the passing state** — every job in every gating workflow is declared required. The teeth are in the rule: a newly-added integrity gate can no longer DEFAULT to unenforced. Entries are `<workflow-file> <job-id> <YYYY-MM-DD> #<issue>`; undated, issue-less and non-ISO-dated entries all fail, so an entry cannot rot into an unexplained suppression. **Stale entries are FATAL here**, unlike the rule (d) pending-fix ledger where a stale line can only suppress a failure that no longer happens: a stale line here pre-absolves whatever job next takes that id, in the workflow where the integrity gates live. Both staleness directions fail — a job that no longer exists, and a job whose context IS in the mirror (required and deliberately-unrequired at once is a contradiction, and the harmful half is the line left behind after a promotion).
  - **PARTIAL matrix coverage fails.** A matrix job with 2 of 3 expansions declared is a silent gap: the undeclared leg can fail and merge while its siblings look green. Rule (a) cannot see it, because it only walks mirror -> job.
  - **Scope is declared, not derived, and is cross-checked in both directions.** `COVERED_WORKFLOWS` is `ci.yml c8-precheck.yml coverage.yml` — the three that carry required contexts. A declared workflow with no parsed jobs FAILS (a stale name would silently shrink the rule's reach) and a mirror context carried by an UNCOVERED workflow FAILS (rule (f) would have a blind spot in a pipeline already trusted with required contexts). Deriving the scope from "workflows carrying a mirror context" was rejected: it would make the scope a function of the mirror, so dropping a workflow's last required context would remove it from rule (f) at the very moment it stopped being covered by rules (a)-(c). It is deliberately NOT repo-wide, unlike rules (d) and (e): those detect static defects that are wrong wherever they appear, whereas (f) encodes a policy judgement that must be authored per workflow, and sweeping in the ~45 jobs of `release.yml` / `publish-sdks.yml` / `yank.yml` — none of which fire on `pull_request` — would build a junk drawer that teaches readers to skim past the ledger.
  - **`--self-test` gained the rule (f) legs**, and the failure is required to NAME rule (f) rather than merely go red. The R-203 leg plants the byte-identical job in an UNCOVERED workflow and requires it to PASS, proving the shape is invisible to every pre-#2636 rule; emptying `COVERED_WORKFLOWS` was considered as the "pre-fix" emulation and deliberately NOT used, because an empty scope correctly trips the SCOPE cross-check — a gate whose scope can be silently zeroed would be the very class of control this rule exists to end. Both legitimate dispositions must PASS, and the ledger-rot, partial-matrix and scope cross-checks each have their own leg.
  - **The mirror was NOT regenerated from live API state**, per that file's standing warning. The canonical demonstration is #2473, where a required context was a name nobody wrote because an unquoted `#` truncated it — and it MATCHED, so the gate was green on a fiction; regenerating would launder the truncation into the declaration.
  - **`scripts/test/test-ci-workflow-invariants.sh` SECTION C now asserts on WHICH RULE fires, not on an exit code.** Its R-203 leg required the frozen pre-fix mirror to exit 0; rule (f) legitimately reds that fixture, because a mirror declaring fewer contexts is exactly what (f) catches. Keying on `RULE (b4)` states the real property — "rule (b4) cannot see this decider until the mirror declares it" — and is strictly stronger than the exit-code form, which one unrelated new rule was able to invalidate.

The drift was one-directional in every instance: **more claimed enforcement than exists.** Four separate published controls were removed or were never wired, and the prose was not updated.

The bench step does exit non-zero on a >10% p95 breach, so the run goes red; branch protection does not act on it. Both triggers also carry `paths-ignore: ['docs/**','**/*.md']`, so "runs on every PR" was false twice over. The HTML said the job "pulls the baseline from the previous release tag" and that "regressions > threshold fail the job and block merge"; `PERFORMANCE.md:164-183` already described the correct posture. `bench.yml:116-147` labels the step "Baseline regression (**advisory**, #1987)", prints "ADVISORY — never fails the build", swallows the CLI exit code, reads a **committed file** (not a tag artifact), and **self-skips the compare entirely** because `performance/baseline.json:4` carries `"bootstrap": true`. The HTML now matches the workflow. Conversely `ROADMAP.md` §9.6 was stale in the OPPOSITE direction — "not yet a CI job — no committed `performance/baseline.json` exists" — and both halves were false at HEAD; corrected, including the bootstrap self-skip.

The sole live control is `coverage.yml`'s `Per-Module Coverage Thresholds` job enforcing `min_line_coverage = 90.0` plus the per-module floors. Practical consequence, now stated: **~2.6pp of coverage regression is undetectable** relative to the advertised ratchet. `.coverage-baseline` is dead config; deleting it is a separate call.

### Docs (security + compliance claim surface: four false or unbacked security claims removed, two stale-in-opposite-directions pages reconciled)

- **The security/compliance document surface now states the controls that exist, in the postures they ship in** (3x7 claims register `docs/audit/3x7-claims-register-2026-08-01.md`, items C-02 / C-04 / C-29 / C-38 / C-47 / C-48 / C-55 + §3.2 C). No code change; every replacement was verified against `release/v1.0.0` HEAD before it was written. The recurring shape being corrected is that **the code states its own limits accurately while a document asserts the opposite**, so the fix is usually to publish what the code already says.
