  - **C-02 — the audit-log tail-truncation mitigation was a marker that does not exist.** `docs/security/audit-trail.md` published "periodic `CHECKPOINT.sig` markers (every `attestation_cadence_minutes`) bound rollback"; `src/audit.rs` says the marker "is **NOT** yet implemented: no emission code exists", and its only runtime effect is a one-shot operator WARN. The mitigation row is deleted and `CHECKPOINT.sig` is marked **RESERVED** in both `audit-trail.md` and `audit-schema.md`, matching the source comment. **Not an over-correction:** tail truncation of the in-DB `signed_events` chain IS detected — by the #1850 off-table forensic watermark high-water (`TruncationCheck`) — and a same-length whole-suffix rewrite by the #1873/#2202 head-hash anchor (`HeadHashCheck`). Both are now published as threat-model rows **with their honest residual bounds** (an interior / mid-suffix rewrite below the anchored row, and the up-to-63 un-anchored rows above the last watermark, are not caught in-DB; `AI_MEMORY_LOG_SINK=syslog` is the residual-closing control). The false control is replaced by the true one rather than left blank.
  - **C-38 — the SOC2 CC7.2 / FedRAMP AU-12 attestation-cadence mapping is withdrawn.** The resolver exists but has no production consumer, so `fedramp.applied = true` produced a 30-minute figure no code acts on — and `audit-trail.md`'s threat model then reused that dead cadence as its truncation defense. The cadence column is gone from both the regulatory mapping and the compliance-preset table; `retention_days` stays, because `AuditConfig::effective_retention_days` is live and consumed. A named control citation that resolves to a no-op is worse than no mapping.
  - **C-04 — the mTLS claim in the procurement pair described the inverse of the code.** Both documents said "the sync daemon refuses to start without mTLS unless an explicit insecure flag is set". It does not: with neither flag set, `tls::select_sync_tls_mode` takes the CA-validated arm and `sync_client_identity` returns `None`, so the daemon starts with no client certificate; server-side `--mtls-allowlist` is an `Option<PathBuf>`, i.e. mTLS is opt-in on both ends, and the empty-allowlist refusal only fires once mTLS has already been chosen. Rewritten to the actual control in `honest-limitations.md` §4 and `nsa-csi-mcp-security-mapping.md` §3.4 — **while preserving what is genuinely strong**: outbound server verification is REQUIRED unless explicitly disabled (`tls::server_verify_required`, unset ⇒ required, pinned by `server_verify_required_default_on_grammar_2448`; accept-any needs four conditions, not one, and `asi-hard` pins the knob), and mTLS Layer 1 is exactly as advertised (`FingerprintAllowlistVerifier`, `client_auth_mandatory() -> true`, constant-time SHA-256(DER), rejection inside the handshake before any Axum layer). Both documents now also state that **federation replicates plaintext memory content** (`src/encryption/mod.rs`, #1968) — the guarantee tenant isolation actually rests on, and these are the documents where it belongs.
  - **C-29 — the two compliance pages contradicted each other about H1, in opposite directions; both moved.** The mapping claimed NSA concern (a) access control flatly `structurally_addressed` while the assessment page on the same landing page listed H1 (High, cross-tenant IDOR via spoofable `X-Agent-Id`) as unremediated post-#2044/#2129/#2154. Verified state: the identity-binding control shipped, and `http_attested_identity_mode` defaults to `advisory` — inert with zero per-agent keys enrolled. Concern (a) is now published as *structurally addressed under `enforce` with per-agent keys enrolled; the shipped default is finding H1*, quoting the CHANGELOG verbatim, and the assessment page gains a **Remediation status** section saying the same thing from the other side. The landing page's "10 of 10 concerns" headline moved with it — a tally must not rest on a corrected row.
  - **C-47 — the published audit `action` vocabulary did not match the wire.** `AuditAction` has **no** `Search`/`List`/`Get` variants (those MCP tools all emit `recall`) and has a 14th, `CaptureLag` (`"capture_lag"`), which a SIEM built to the published 13-value enum meets on the wire and cannot classify. Both documents now publish the shipped 14 with exact wire strings. Two further facts a SIEM integrator needs, found while enumerating: `export` and `import` are declared variants with **no production emitter** at v1.0.0, and read-access events come from the **MCP stdio surface only** — the HTTP read routes emit nothing to this file.
  - **C-48 — the procurement pair's version stamp was stale by 31 schema versions.** Both documents were stamped "v0.7.0 (sqlite + postgres schema v57, lockstep)" and cited "Cargo.lock (~5,479 lines)" — on the stamp a reviewer uses to decide whether the assessment applies at all. Re-stamped to **v1.0.0 / schema v88**, `Cargo.lock` re-measured at **5,747** lines, and §3.9's wire-surface counts corrected from the v0.7.0 figures (89 routes / 74 tools / 82 / 80) to the pinned v1.0.0 SSOT (**94 route registrations over 80 unique paths, 103 MCP entries, 89 CLI subcommands default / 91 under `sal`**).
  - **C-55 — anchors that miss are worse than no anchors.** The pair claimed every claim traced to "a file path + line number ... all verified via codegraph"; sampled anchors missed at HEAD, including one symbol that no longer exists (`decorate_memory` → `decorate_memory_many`) and one pointing at unrelated code. Rather than regenerate coordinates that drift again on the next commit (the #2629 class by construction), **every anchor is converted to a symbol** — module / type / function / test name, each verified to resolve at HEAD, with renamed-or-removed symbols called out at the point of citation. Both `.md` files now carry the currency note that only `index.html` had, disclosing that the underlying v0.7.0 capability inventory has not been re-derived (#1938).

### Fixed (claims audit CERT GATE 2 — federation + enterprise-deployment surfaces)

- **Corrected FALSE and OVERCLAIMED published claims on the federation and enterprise-deployment surfaces**, the two the 3x7 claims register (`docs/audit/3x7-claims-register-2026-08-01.md`) graded DISQUALIFYING. The binding surface for "enterprise ready" is the published claims, not the code; a correct system that overclaims fails that bar. Every correction below was re-verified against code at `0b5662ba`. Docs-only.
  - **The 1,000,000-agent figure is retired** (refs [#2438](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2438)). `docs/federation.md` and `docs/federation-identity.md` both advertised a fleet scaling "1 to ~1,000,000 agents" while `federation.md` itself put the peer-to-peer mesh model at a **~50-peer ceiling** and `enterprise-deployment.md` marked its per-tier agent counts PROVISIONAL. Three orders of magnitude, both numbers public. Replaced with the certified envelope: a **500–1000 agent cluster, composed modularly in 500-agent blocks**, scaled by adding independent clusters rather than growing one mesh. O(1) enrollment removes the key-exchange limit; it does not remove the topology limit, and the topology limit binds first.
  - **`allowed_namespaces` no longer claims to cover "every lane that can reach a write."** It does not: `links[]`, `signals[]`, and the entire pull-accept path are ungated at HEAD — the pull-accept path runs as `CallerContext::for_admin(FEDERATION_CATCHUP)` with `bypass_visibility = true` and never consults `PeerAttestationConfig`. The universal quantifier is replaced by the true enumeration plus an explicit table of the three unscoped lanes and their tracking issues ([#2489](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2489), [#2480](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2480)). Because `contradicts`/`supersedes` edges feed the recall down-weight, the `links[]` gap is a read-path influence primitive against data the peer cannot read — stated plainly, since this is the sentence operators build tenant isolation on. The code fix is tracked separately; the doc must not carry the false version while it lands.
  - **`trust_domain` is no longer labelled "multi-tenant isolation."** It is a **credential-replay scope**: verified only inside `TrustBundle::verify`, consulted nowhere on the receive path, and enforcing nothing between parties inside one domain. New §"What `trust_domain` does and does not bound" states the delivered boundary (separately-administered peers inside one organisation) against the documented one (mutually distrusting tenants) and directs the latter to separate deployments.
  - **`docs/enterprise-deployment.md` §9.4 no longer recommends one cluster per tenant.** That recommendation contradicted §8.8 of the same document ("if subsets of peers should NOT see each other's data, the swarm shape is wrong"). Recommending a topology in one file while disclaiming its safety in another is a trap, not disclosure.
  - **§11.1's 14-cell ops/s capacity table is REMOVED, not annotated.** Eleven of fourteen cells had no producer in `benches/` at all, and the entire Postgres+AGE column came from `benches/age_vs_cte.rs`, which `exit 0`s unless `AI_MEMORY_TEST_AGE_URL` is exported. An unproduced number is not data, and this is the section a Fortune 500 capacity-plans from. Replaced with a per-bench statement of what the seven in-tree benches actually measure, and a pointer to the latency budgets — which are real and mechanically pinned — plus the `ai-memory bench --scale 10000 --json` command to measure throughput on your own hardware.
  - **§11.2 now names the 100k vector-index cap.** `hnsw::DEFAULT_MAX_ENTRIES = 100_000` and the index **evicts oldest** past it, so a deployment sized at 1M–5M memories on SQLite got semantic recall silently truncated to the newest ~100k rows. Neither capacity doc named `AI_MEMORY_VECTOR_INDEX_CAPACITY`; both the knob and the `AI_MEMORY_VECTOR_INDEX_HARD_FAIL` loud-refusal alternative are now documented at the point of sizing.
  - **§14.6 now discloses that at-rest encryption is not end-to-end across federation** (refs [#1968](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/1968)). `federation.md` has always said so; the 1700-line document an architect reads as their compliance gate did not.
  - **§7.4 now states that data residency is enforced in ONE direction.** The serve direction (`/sync/since`) is default-deny before any row crosses the wire; the accept direction is ungated. "What leaves your region is gated; what arrives is not."
  - **§6.6's federation-push-DLQ "not lost" is corrected to "durably queued, replayed by position"** (refs [#2442](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2442)). The DLQ key is a positional index (`peer-{i}`, URL dropped from identity) and replay resolves by `find(|p| p.id == row.peer_id)`, so removing one peer reindexes every id above it and the queued payload is delivered to an unintended host — no counter, no error.
  - **The three-concurrent-auth-layers summary now agrees with `federation.md`.** Under an enforced mTLS posture `/api/v1/sync/*` bypasses the api-key layer by design ([#702](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/702)); the two documents previously contradicted each other within one published surface.
  - **The `curl … /api/v1/health` auth-stack verification runbook is corrected.** `/health` is exempt from the api-key layer and its handler takes no `HeaderMap`, so it never reads `x-peer-id`: a 200 proves TLS + mTLS only. An operator following the old step got a green light for an auth stack that was never exercised.
  - **`?api_key=` is documented as removed, not upcoming.** The query-string credential was rejected at v1.0.0 ([#2032](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2032) L1); `federation.md` still described the removal as slated for v0.8.
  - **Credential revocation is scoped to the credential lane.** "Stop renewing" is true there; the mTLS fingerprint allowlist — the lane the shipped runbooks actually prescribe — has no expiry and no hot-reload, and requires an allowlist edit plus a daemon restart.
  - **Drifted `file:line` code anchors in `federation.md` are converted to symbol-only citations**, and the outbound `/sync/since` gate is corrected: it inlines `namespace_allowed_test_glob`, not the sibling `namespace_allowed` the document named. Line-numbered anchors are the drift class this register documents; symbols survive a refactor, line numbers do not.
  - **`enterprise-deployment.md` is restamped v1.0.0** with an explicit version-currency note, and §14.3 gains the seven v1.0.0 fail-closed federation defaults that post-date its v0.7.0-era checklist, so an operator auditing against it does not conclude they are unset.

### Added (three CI gates + a widened fourth, so the 71 corrected published claims cannot drift back)

- **CERT GATE 2 — the structural fix for the 3x7 claims audit** (closes [#2629](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2629), [#2492](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2492); register `docs/audit/3x7-claims-register-2026-08-01.md` §3.3). A 265-claim audit found **71 FALSE or OVERCLAIMED published claims** while `scripts/check-docs-vs-ssot.sh` was GREEN — README.md alone carried **five stale SSOT values** (94→92/93 routes, 88→78 schema, 30→28 `Memory` fields, 103→101 tools, 91/89→89/87 CLI subcommands). README is, and always was, inside that gate's `DOC_FILES`, so the gap was never the file walk: it was the PATTERN SET. Per the register, *"a gate that greens a page carrying five stale SSOT values is the #2444 'reports success while doing nothing' shape"*, and *"the drift direction is consistently toward MORE CLAIMED ENFORCEMENT THAN EXISTS — that is not random staleness; it is a systematic bias that a gate must be built to counter."* Four closures, all HARD-BLOCK, all wired UNCONDITIONALLY into `c8-precheck.yml` (no `needs: classify`, no job-level `if:`, no `paths:` filter — a gate policing the docs-only short-circuit must not be subject to it), each with a `--self-test` that plants the historical defect and proves the gate rejects it.
  - **#2492 — `check-docs-vs-ssot.sh` now scans NOUN-PHRASE ANCHORS, not hand-written phrasings.** Every original rule was a regex pinned to one exact sentence shape, so a document saying the same thing the seventh way was invisible. Each SSOT const now carries a small anchor set (`HTTP route registrations`, `unique URL paths`, `unique paths`, ``MCP tools at `--profile full` ``, `-entry surface`, `CLI subcommands`, ``-field `Memory` ``, `schema **v`) and ANY adjacent integer in bold / code / plain form is extracted and compared. A re-worded sentence is now caught by the anchor; only a genuinely new NOUN gets past.
  - **The historical guard is load-bearing.** README legitimately carries prior-release narrative paragraphs and ROADMAP §11.3.1 carries a self-correcting frozen v0.7.1 baseline, whose numbers are TRUE statements about a PAST release — re-pointing them would falsify the record, the same reasoning that keeps CHANGELOG.md and the three frozen v0.7 migration guides out of the walk entirely. Lines opening a release-narrative paragraph attributed to a NON-current version, or saying `At the v<x> release` / `release, surface was` / `Ship state at v<x>` / `Frozen v<x> baseline`, are skipped. **Rule N1 closes the hole that would otherwise open:** a paragraph labelled `— current release` MUST attribute the `Cargo.toml` version, which is what catches the single README paragraph carrying four of the five stale shapes.
  - **R-203 is mechanical, and the frozen artefact is the proof.** The pre-fix script is preserved VERBATIM at `scripts/test/fixtures/docs-vs-ssot-prefix-2492.sh` (the `ci-classify-prefix-2496.sh` precedent). The self-test plants the exact pre-fix README phrasings and asserts BOTH directions — the FROZEN gate **ACCEPTS** all five shapes (reproducing the defect) while the live gate **REJECTS** all 11 planted claims. A self-test that only proved the new gate works would be tautological, because the finding was precisely that the old gate greened them.
  - **New gate 9 — `scripts/check-doc-symbol-anchors.sh` (#2629).** The gate pinned VALUES and nothing pinned SYMBOLS. The audit sampled SIX `file:line` / symbol anchors and found **6/6 MISS at HEAD**, including `decorate_memory` — gone since the recall decorator became `decorate_memory_many`. Four rules on PATH-QUALIFIED grammar only: the cited `src/<p>.rs` must exist; a `src/<p>.rs:<N>` anchor must name a line the file has; every identifier in `src/<p>.rs::<sym>` / `::{a, B::c, d}` must be defined IN THAT FILE; and a ``[`sym`](../src/<p>.rs)`` link must resolve. A bare backticked identifier sharing a line with a `src/` path is deliberately NOT checked — measured, that grammar yields 1,827 hits over 879 distinct tokens (tool names, DB columns, env vars), and a gate nobody can leave on is worse than no gate. **No new SSOT** (operator direction): the migration-ladder tip is EXTRACTED and reused from `scripts/check-migration-ladder.sh::read_current_schema_version` rather than derived a third time — which immediately caught `docs/postgres-age-guide.md` naming a ten-versions-stale `migrate_vNN()` as the ladder end, the #2629 title's own example.
  - **New gate 10 — `scripts/check-sdk-route-paths.sh` (register 3.3.2).** Nothing pinned the SDK READMEs or client sources against `src/handlers/routes.rs`. **C-19:** `grant()` / `revoke()` / `cluster()` shipped in BOTH SDKs against three paths with ZERO hits in `routes.rs` — three typed, documented methods that **404 at runtime**. **C-20:** TS `unsubscribe(id)` targets `DELETE /api/v1/subscriptions/:id` while `src/lib.rs` registers delete on the COLLECTION path only and the id rides the query string. The gate NORMALISES path parameters on both sides (`{id}`, `:id`, `${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, `<id>` → `{}`), which is what makes it catch C-20 at all: a raw-string membership test passes it, since the collection path IS registered. **A path is a CLAIM only where it is a CALL** — comments, docstrings and prose are out of scope BY CONSTRUCTION, because the C-19/C-20 correction's own BREAKING-CHANGE notes NAME the dead paths to explain them, and a raw-text rule would fail the FIXED tree and force those migration notes to be deleted. The acceptance criterion is the PAIR: RED on the pre-fix tree, GREEN on the corrected one. The scan set is `sdk/**` by PATTERN, never an enumerated list — `sdk/python/ai_memory/async_client.py` carried all four defects and appears nowhere in the 429-line register.
  - **New gate 11 — `scripts/check-ci-job-claims.sh` (register 3.3.3).** Four claims, one shape — a control was removed and the prose was not. `ci.yml`'s "Code Coverage" job (removed in #1993) still cited as the live coverage gate in README and ROADMAP; the `postgres-age` nightly (deleted in `2b85ba38`) still cited as gating; an AGE bench job cited in `bench.yml`, which has zero `age` hits; and `bench.yml` — which says of ITSELF "Bench is advisory (not in required-status-checks)" — described as gating every PR. EXISTENCE catches the first three. **ENFORCEMENT-TRUTHFULNESS** is the rule that counters the register's systematic bias and the only one that catches the fourth: a doc saying a job *gates* / *blocks merge* / *fails the PR* must resolve to a context actually declared in `required-contexts-release.txt`. Existence alone greens it — the workflow exists, its job exists, and the claim is still false.
  - **Two ledger dispositions, deliberately different.** Gates 4, 10 and 11 carry PENDING-FIX ledgers where a **stale entry is a loud NOTICE, not a failure** (the `dual-trigger-cancel-allow.txt` precedent): five document-correction lanes are correcting these exact claims concurrently, and a stale-fails ledger would red whichever PR lost the race. Gate 9 carries a BURN-DOWN allowlist where a **stale entry FAILS** (the `required-contexts-joblevel-if-allow.txt` discipline), because nothing is concurrently correcting those anchors. In all four a MALFORMED entry HARD-FAILS, so no ledger can rot into prose.
  - **`cargo test` twin `tests/doc_claims_integrity.rs`** (the `tests/migration_ladder_integrity.rs` precedent). All four gates live in ONE workflow, so a deleted job or a renamed script would make every one of them stop running while the branch stayed green. The twin re-asserts SDK path membership and named-CI-job existence, that every ledger parses, and that each gate is wired into `c8-precheck.yml` **with its `--self-test` step** and stays unconditional. It does not duplicate the pattern sets: two definitions that can disagree teach reviewers to ignore both.
  - **Every gate fails CLOSED on an empty scan set** — zero SDK files, zero workflows, zero `.rs` files under `src/` are each a hard failure rather than an unearned pass, because a control that reports success while doing nothing is worse than a missing control.
### Removed — BREAKING (SDK methods that called routes the daemon has never registered)

- **`grant()`, `revoke()` and `cluster()` are deleted from the Python SDK (sync + async) and the TypeScript SDK, and from both SDK READMEs** (refs the 3x7 claims register, `docs/audit/3x7-claims-register-2026-08-01.md` C-19). They posted to `/api/v1/memories/{id}/grant`, `/api/v1/memories/{id}/revoke` and `/api/v1/cluster`. `grep -oE '"/[^"]*"' src/handlers/routes.rs` returns 80 paths and **none of those three is among them** — the routes were never registered, in any release that shipped the methods, so every call 404'd. There is no server-side plan for them, which is why this is a deletion rather than a caveat: a shipped method against a nonexistent route is a claim, not a feature.
  - **Replacements, both of which already exist.** Per-memory access control is `metadata.scope` (`"private"` | `"collective"`) on the write plus a namespace governance standard (`docs/governance.md`). Peer management is out-of-band configuration (`--quorum-peers`, the peer-attestation allowlist, `AI_MEMORY_FED_INVENTORY_PATH`) with `POST /api/v1/sync/push` + `GET /api/v1/sync/since` as the HTTP federation surface (`docs/federation.md`).
  - The now-orphaned `GrantRequest` / `RevokeRequest` / `ClusterRequest` / `ClusterResponse` type aliases in `sdk/typescript/src/types.ts` are left exported for one release so a `tsc` consumer importing them does not break at the same moment its call sites do.

### Fixed (SDK webhook teardown targeted an unregistered path, so decommissioned endpoints kept receiving signed deliveries)

- **`unsubscribe(id)` now issues `DELETE /api/v1/subscriptions?id=<id>` on all three SDK clients** — TypeScript, Python sync, and Python async (refs the 3x7 claims register C-20). The daemon registers `delete` on the COLLECTION path only (`src/lib.rs`, `handlers::routes::SUBSCRIPTIONS`) and reads the id from the query string (`UnsubscribeQuery`, `src/handlers/subscriptions.rs`). The SDKs sent `DELETE /api/v1/subscriptions/{id}`, which matches no route.
  - **Why this outranks the other three SDK path defects.** `grant`/`revoke`/`cluster` fail loudly at the call site — an integrator sees a 404 the first time. This one fails in the direction that *looks* safe: teardown appears to have been attempted, the caller moves on, and the decommissioned endpoint keeps receiving HMAC-signed deliveries indefinitely with no error anywhere in the operator's logs. A webhook that cannot be turned off is a disclosure surface for as long as the URL resolves.
  - **The register named only the TypeScript client. Both Python clients had the identical defect** and are fixed here; `sdk/python/ai_memory/async_client.py` is not referenced anywhere in the register.
  - **R-203 regression pins, offline, on both harnesses.** `sdk/typescript/__tests__/client.test.ts` injects a capturing `fetch` (the client's second constructor argument) and asserts `url.pathname === "/api/v1/subscriptions"` with `?id=`; `sdk/python/tests/test_client.py` does the same through an `httpx.MockTransport`, plus a `hasattr` guard that the three removed methods are gone from both client classes. Verified FAILING at parent `0b5662ba` — jest: `Expected: "/api/v1/subscriptions" / Received: "/api/v1/subscriptions/sub-abc-123"`; pytest: the same path assertion plus `AssertionError: AiMemoryClient.grant must not exist`.
  - The Python `unsubscribe` signature is unchanged; callers should check the returned `deleted` flag, which the TS README example now does.

### Fixed (`docs/API_REFERENCE.md` — eleven published claims that the daemon contradicts)

- **The HTTP API contract document is re-derived against the code at HEAD.** This is a certification-gate correction: the published claims are the binding surface, and these eleven were adjudicated FALSE or OVERCLAIMED in `docs/audit/3x7-claims-register-2026-08-01.md`. Each replacement was verified against the cited source before it was written.
  - **`?api_key=` is documented as a BREAKING CHANGE with a migration note, not as a future plan** (C-16). The doc said "Still accepted at v0.7.0 for back-compat … slated for rejection at v0.8." The query-string credential was REMOVED at v1.0.0 (#2032 L1): `api_key_auth` reads the header and nothing else (`src/handlers/transport.rs`), so every integrator on the documented path gets a silent 401 identical to presenting no credential at all. The section now carries the before/after `curl`, names the once-per-process `http::auth` WARN as the only diagnostic channel, and tells operators to rotate the key they had been putting in URLs.
  - **HTTP admission control is documented as ON by default and CPU-scaled** (C-17). The doc said "opt-in … compiled default `0` = disabled … byte-identical to a build without admission control". Since #2032 M3 an unset knob resolves to `clamp(available_parallelism × 64, 256, 4096)` (`config::resolve_default_max_inflight_requests`) and only an EXPLICIT `0` disables it (`compose_admission_control`, `src/lib.rs`). The tri-state table, the typed 503 + `Retry-After: 1`, and the `/health` `/metrics` exemptions are now published — this is the safer posture and it is stated as such.
  - **`GET /api/v1/links/{id}` documents its ACTUAL eight-column projection** (C-18). The doc promised `signature`, `attest_level` and `signed_at`. `db::get_links` (`src/storage/mod.rs`) selects `source_id, target_id, relation, created_at, valid_from, valid_until, observed_by, attest_level`; `signature` is withheld BY DESIGN as "the verification surface owned by the `memory_verify` tool", and **`signed_at` is not a column on `memory_links` at all**. Integrators building link attestation are now pointed at `POST /api/v1/links/verify`.
  - **`POST /api/v1/memories/bulk` carries an explicit warning that HTTP 200 does not imply any row was created** (C-39). The terminal response is a bare `Json(json!({"created": …, "errors": […]}))` with no `StatusCode` (`src/handlers/memories_query.rs`), so a batch in which EVERY row was rejected by the per-agent quota answers **200 with `created: 0`**. Callers MUST key their retry on `created`/`errors`, not on `response.ok`. The code fix (207 Multi-Status / 400 on total rejection) is still required and is tracked as [#2588](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2588); this documents the contract as it actually is so a retrying client is not misled in the meantime.
  - **The HTTP↔MCP coverage table stops claiming `format` is MCP-only** (C-41), and the document stops contradicting itself. `src/handlers/recall.rs` (GET and POST) and `src/handlers/memories_query.rs` (search) all call `toon::WireFormat::parse_http`, and the document's own recall/search sections said so 500 lines earlier. TOON **is** supported on HTTP recall and search; `toon_compact` is ~79% smaller than the JSON envelope and integrators should be taking it. Only `GET /api/v1/memories` (list) genuinely lacks `format` — `ListQuery` has no such field — and that row is preserved as the one true `✗`.
  - **Two further coverage-table rows were false and are corrected** — neither is in the register. `memory_recall`/`context_tokens` was published as MCP-only; both `RecallQuery` (CSV, #1622) and `RecallBody` (array) carry it, and the parity note under the search section asserted the same falsehood. The `memory_store`/`ttl_secs` note claimed "the MCP tool exposes `expires_at`"; MCP `StoreRequest` (`src/mcp/tools/store/mod.rs`) exposes neither — `expires_at` lives on `memory_update`.
  - **The route and tool counts agree with the SSOT and with each other** (C-50, C-51). One paragraph asserted 80 unique paths in prose, 78 as its own self-labelled "authoritative" command output, and cited a const holding 80; another said the full profile "returns 101" fourteen lines after the same page said 103. Re-run at HEAD: `grep -oE '"/[^"]*"' src/handlers/routes.rs | sort -u | wc -l` = **80**, `grep -oE 'crate::mcp::[a-z_]+::[A-Za-z]+Tool' src/mcp/registry.rs | sort -u | wc -l` = **103**, matching `EXPECTED_PRODUCTION_UNIQUE_PATHS_COUNT = 80`, `EXPECTED_PRODUCTION_ROUTES_COUNT = 94` (`src/lib.rs`) and `Profile::full().expected_tool_count()`. The prose, the command, and the const now agree. The 7-vs-8 core-profile ambiguity is resolved in place rather than picked: 7 family tools, 8 wire entries once the always-on `memory_capabilities` is appended.
  - **`GET /api/v1/health` documents its full body and, critically, THE ONLY WAY IT FAILS** (C-64). The published response was `{status, service}` with no status-code contract at all. The body also carries `version`, `embedder_ready`, `federation_enabled`, `checks{connection, fts_index}` and `fts_integrity{status, checked_at, interval_secs}`, and the endpoint returns **503** whenever `!live || verdict.is_unhealthy()` (`health_status_code`, `src/handlers/transport.rs`). Orchestrator probe configs are written against this. The FTS5 verdict is **cached** (default 6 h, `AI_MEMORY_FTS_INTEGRITY_INTERVAL_SECS`) and can read `pending`/`stale`/`disabled` — none of which 503, so a 200 does NOT mean the index was just verified, and `stale`/`disabled` need their own alert.
  - **429 is in the status table with its actual triggers, and "No per-client rate limiting at the HTTP layer" is deleted** (C-65). 429 is emitted at nine production sites including both primary write surfaces (`src/handlers/create.rs`, `src/handlers/links.rs`) plus update-growth, consolidate, signals, federation receive, and the Postgres `StoreError::QuotaExceeded` mapping. The Python SDK's own error table already listed `RateLimitError | 429` — the SDK knew what the reference did not. The replacement states what is actually true and is more useful than the sentence it removes: per-agent quotas return 429, global admission control returns 503, there is no requests-per-second throttle, and bulk folds quota rejections into `errors[]` rather than answering 429.
  - **Recall is documented as PURE** (C-40). The doc said recall "**Mutates the database** (touches, auto-promotes)". Recall has been unconditionally pure since #1953 — `touch_after_recall` has no production caller on the recall path — and the access ladders are applied out of band by the fold job. That is a STRONGER property (safe to retry, safe on a read replica) and it is now stated as one, together with the honest caveat that on an MCP-stdio or CLI-only topology with no `serve` daemon nothing folds until a GC chokepoint. The same stale claim is corrected in `sdk/typescript/README.md`.
  - **C-11 was checked and is a no-op for this file.** The auth-stack verification runbook (`curl --cert … -H "x-peer-id: …" …/api/v1/health`, claimed to prove "TLS + mTLS + API key all aligned") does NOT appear in `docs/API_REFERENCE.md`; it lives in `docs/federation.md:397`. The underlying fact is nonetheless now published here: `/api/v1/health` is exempt from the api-key middleware and `pub async fn health(State(app): State<AppState>)` takes no `HeaderMap`, so it reads no request headers and a 200 proves transport reachability only.

### Fixed (recall read path: an unbounded outbound embed call, and a cross-encoder loaded where it can never fire)

- **The query-embedding call on the recall path is now bounded and cached, and the neural cross-encoder is no longer constructed on deployments where the rerank stage is structurally unreachable** (refs [#2577](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2577), [#2576](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2576); AVAILABILITY + DEGRADE-never-corrupt; 5-agent adversarial vote `4d3ea1c5`). Both issues were independently re-measured before any code was written, and **the headline diagnosis in #2576 is REFUTED** — see below.
  - **#2577 — an unbounded outbound call on a READ path is an availability defect.** The remote embed client is built with `GENERATE_TIMEOUT` (30 s), a *generation* budget sized for chat completions, applied to a *read*. Measured in-tree against a loopback endpoint that accepts the connection and then never answers (the exact shape a connect-timeout does not catch): **30,002 ms unbounded** vs **703 ms** with the new budget — the same call, the same endpoint, 43x. The issue's "NO TIMEOUT" claim is therefore partially refuted (a 30 s bound existed); what did not exist was a *read-appropriate* budget or any degrade-on-SLOW path — #1593 degrades only on embedder CONSTRUCTION failure, so a provider that is up but slow degraded nothing and just blocked.
  - **Blast radius, which is why this outranks the latency.** On **MCP stdio** the loop is single-threaded by JSON-RPC protocol design (the #965 audit), so a stalled embed blocks EVERY subsequent tool call on that server — including `memory_store`. That is a plausible mechanism for an MCP client dropping its connection mid-session, which is the #1388 lost-directive failure mode the L1-L4 capture architecture exists to defend against. On the **HTTP daemon** each stalled recall holds an admission permit for its whole duration (#2032 M3, default-on), so sustained provider latency saturates the in-flight cap and sheds HEALTHY traffic — including durable-truth WRITES — with 503s. A third-party read dependency must not be able to shed the write path.
  - **`AI_MEMORY_RECALL_EMBED_BUDGET_MS`** (env #152, default **2000**, tri-state: explicit `0` disables). On expiry the recall degrades to keyword and reports `mode:keyword` honestly. This is a DEGRADE — fewer, FTS-ranked results — never a wrong result: the durable text is untouched, recall is pure (#1869/#1953), and the response tells the caller which ranking it got. 2000 ms is ~4x the observed p99 (492 ms) and ~13x the p50 (156 ms) for a healthy round trip, so under the measured distribution it fires on approximately nothing; it also equals the substrate's own `READ_CLASS_DEADLINE_MS`, so the codebase does not now hold two answers to "how long may a read spend out-of-process". The expiry calls `note_failure`, so repeated stalls trip the EXISTING circuit breaker and fast-fail instead of each paying the full budget.
  - **`AI_MEMORY_QUERY_EMBED_CACHE_ENTRIES`** (env #153, default **512**, `0` disables) — the only lever that removes the ~156 ms round-trip FLOOR rather than merely bounding its tail. Key = `(SHA-256(exact query bytes), embedding_space fingerprint)`. The exactness is a correctness property, not tidiness: a lossy fold (case, whitespace, unicode) is the ONLY way this cache could return a WRONG vector, by colliding two different queries onto one entry. The #2167 fingerprint in the key makes a model swap a KEY CHANGE — a miss — rather than an invalidation event some funnel could forget to fire, so a foreign-space vector can never be served. Bounded LRU + a 900 s TTL (the one hazard the key cannot express: a remote provider silently re-pointing a model behind a stable id). Query text is digested, never held in cleartext, because this is a long-lived process-global holding caller-supplied free text.
  - **Caching is opt-IN per embedder, and the fail-safe default is "do not cache".** `Embed::space_fingerprint`'s own DEFAULT returns a single constant sentinel for every implementor that does not override it, so it cannot serve as a cache key — two unrelated embedders collide under it. Keying on it was caught by CI on this feature's first run: a deliberately FAILING embedder was served a previous caller's cached vector, was never invoked at all, and the recall reported `mode:hybrid` when it should have degraded to `mode:keyword`. **A cache that masks an embedder failure and then claims a semantic ranking it never performed is a WRONG RESULT on the wire, not a slow one** — the precise data-integrity violation this design was supposed to be immune to. Caching is now gated on a new `Embed::query_cache_space() -> Option<String>` that defaults to `None`; only the production `Embedder` overrides it, because only its fingerprint is derived from the resolved model id + prefix scheme. An implementor that has not reasoned about it pays a round trip and stays correct. Pinned by `an_undeclared_space_is_never_cached_so_a_failure_cannot_be_masked_2577`.
  - **One funnel, pinned mechanically.** Every read-path query embedding now crosses `embeddings::recall_query_embedding` (HTTP ×2, MCP, CLI, and both `load_family` intent-match sites); `tests/embed_budget_funnel_ceiling_2577.rs` fails if any production site calls `embed_query` directly. This is the #2445 lesson applied: `db::open` was the funnel every interface BOOT crossed but NOT the funnel every WRITE crossed, and four paths bypassed it. A behavioural test proves the funnel bounds the call it exercises; it cannot prove a future call site went through the funnel at all.
  - **#2576 — the reported cause is REFUTED, on measurement.** The issue attributes the 701 ms rerank to a mis-tuned `AI_MEMORY_RERANK_MAX_SEQ` (256) that "pads far beyond the actual content length", and proposes 256 -> 64 for a measured ~30% win. `neural_score_pairs` already sets `PaddingStrategy::BatchLongest`: the batch is padded to the longest sequence IN THAT BATCH, never to `max_seq`. `max_seq` is a **TRUNCATION** bound. Tokenizing all 7,855 Atlas rows with the real ms-marco tokenizer: at `max_seq=256` **0.0%** of (query, doc) pairs truncate and the batch pads to ~135 tokens — **the 256 default costs nothing on this corpus**; at 64, **91.8%** truncate and the median document loses ~28% of its tokens. The 30% win is bought by deleting the document. **The default stays 256** (5/5), pinned by `tests/rerank_cross_encoder_gate_2576.rs`. The env #76 rationale, which asserted both the pad-to-512 behaviour and an O(n^2) attention scaling (it is ~linear in L at these lengths — 2.2x shorter measured 2.0x faster, not 4.8x), is corrected in place.
  - **#2576 — what the rerank actually buys, measured.** With the default `limit=10` the pipeline assembles a blended pool of up to ~80 candidates (`fts_limit = max(limit*3,30)`, `ann_limit = max(limit*5,50)`), truncates to `limit` (`storage/mod.rs`), and only THEN reranks. So the cross-encoder re-orders exactly the rows it returns and cannot promote anything from outside the page. Measured on the live pipeline over 20 queries: top-10 set overlap hybrid vs hybrid+rerank **10.00/10**, rank-1 identical **20/20**, Kendall tau **+0.884**. The stage is positioned AFTER the truncation that would give it power. This is filed as its own issue rather than "fixed" here, because the fix is to over-fetch and rerank down — which makes recall SLOWER while making it better, a product decision, not a performance patch.
  - **#2576 — what is actually fixed.** (a) The cross-encoder is no longer constructed when no embedder is available: rerank only runs when recall reached `mode == "hybrid"`, which requires a query embedding, so on any `AI_MEMORY_INFERENCE_EGRESS=deny` (env #131) or #1593-degraded deployment the model load and its resident memory were paid for a stage that could never fire. Gated on the RESOLVED embedder, never on the tier — the tier still reads "autonomous" when the embedder failed, which is the bug. (b) The padding/truncation-configured tokenizer is built at most ONCE per encoder instead of deep-cloning the 30k-entry WordPiece vocabulary on EVERY rerank call; it is initialised at first use, not at construction, so a boot seed landing after encoder construction is still honoured (the #2233 defaults-lie class). (c) A synthetic warm-up forward runs on a detached background thread at load, so the cold first-forward cost (weight paging + gemm kernel selection) is no longer paid by whichever user arrives first — never inline, and never gating a readiness signal, because seconds of dead air before `initialize` answers would be strictly worse than one slow recall.
  - **Honest scope.** The steady-state cross-encoder forward (~40 GFLOP for a `[10, ~135]` batch on CPU) is NOT reduced by this change and cannot be without either truncating content (refused, above) or not reranking. A wall-clock rerank budget was voted DOWN 3-2 and filed separately: an in-flight candle forward has no cancellation point, so a "budget" could only abandon a thread that keeps burning CPU, and it would make result ORDER a function of machine load — non-deterministic ordering for every downstream test and every user.
  - **Two operator-facing CLI stderr strings changed** (`ai-memory recall`). `embedding query failed: {e}, falling back to keyword` -> `embedding query unavailable within budget, falling back to keyword`, and `context_tokens embed failed: {e}, using primary only` -> `context_tokens embed unavailable, using primary only`. The error text moved to the structured `recall.embed.degraded` WARN (which every surface now emits identically instead of each call site inventing its own message), and the new wording names the BUDGET because that is the cause an operator has to act on. Flagged explicitly because anything scraping those lines will need updating; the exit status and the `mode:keyword` JSON field are unchanged.
  - **Observability.** `ai_memory_recall_embed_degraded_total` and `ai_memory_query_embed_cache_hits_total`, plus a structured `recall.embed.degraded` WARN. Note MCP stdio serves no `/metrics` endpoint, so on the surface most damaged by the stall the WARN is the only channel — an operator alerting on the degrade RATE needs the HTTP surface.
### Fixed (every process start re-read the whole day's forensic audit log)

- **`governance::audit::init` now resolves the forensic chain tail from a bounded 256 KiB suffix instead of JSON-parsing every line of the newest `forensic-<date>.jsonl`** (refs [#2584](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2584)). `src/main.rs::init_forensic_audit` runs on EVERY process start — every CLI invocation, every `ai-memory mcp` stdio boot, every `serve`/`curator` boot, and every firing of the `governance check-action` PreToolUse hook — and `read_chain_tail` streamed the ENTIRE newest file through `serde_json::from_str::<ForensicDecision>` just to keep the last row's hash.
  - **Measured end-to-end** (release vs release, same host, interleaved, n=40, empty database so the corpus is not a variable): `ai-memory list --limit 10` p50 **184.87 ms -> 23.14 ms (8.0x)**, `ai-memory stats` p50 **343.04 ms -> 23.59 ms (14.5x)**; `read` syscalls **2,087 -> 30** while the `futex` call count is UNCHANGED at 57, which is the direct refutation of the thread-synchronisation hypothesis. Chain-tail equivalence was also proved on the REAL production log: given byte-identical 39,660-line copies, the pre-fix and fixed binaries appended rows carrying the IDENTICAL `prev_hash` (`2b6f1c09…`), so the hash chain links continuously across an upgrade.
  - **Measured on this node against a 16,556,309-byte same-day forensic log** (`strace -f -tt -T`, installed v1.0.0 release binary): **2,021 of the process's 2,052 `read` syscalls**, and a **254 ms contiguous window of the 305 ms straced run**, were this one function — bracketed exactly by `openat(".../forensic-2026-07-31.jsonl", O_RDONLY)` and the `statx(".../recorder-keys")` that follows it inside `init`. Controlled A/B with `AI_MEMORY_AUDIT_DIR` pointed at an empty directory: **173.97 ms → 10.84 ms p50** for `ai-memory list --limit 10` on an empty database (`--version` floor 4.41 ms, n=25) and **2,052 → 28 `read` syscalls**. So ~94% of the reported per-invocation overhead was this scan.
  - **The cost was never a constant.** It is O(TODAY'S LOG SIZE), so it grows all day and resets at UTC midnight; #2584 reported it as a fixed ~130 ms because that was its size at measurement time. The accompanying `futex`-dominated `strace -c` profile ("79% of syscall time, 15 threads") was an ARTEFACT: the 14 `clone3` calls are the tokio multi-thread runtime's workers (`available_parallelism()` on a 14-core host) and `strace -c` attributes their PARKED time to `futex`. Thread-synchronisation was not the cost, and the timeline shows the runtime is not even constructed until after the scan completes.
  - **The optimisation cannot change an answer.** The old scan returned `self_hash()` of the last line that PARSED; every line after it is by definition unparseable, so a backward walk from EOF meets those same lines first and returns the very same row. When the 256 KiB window is exhausted without a parse (a tail damaged beyond the window, e.g. after a SIGKILL mid-append) the code FALLS BACK to the original full forward scan, retained verbatim — so the returned value is identical for every input, and the worst case is the pre-fix behaviour rather than a guess. Blank-line skipping, `\r\n` trimming, and invalid-UTF-8 tolerance mirror `BufReader::lines()` line for line.
  - Pinned by three in-`src` regressions in `src/governance/audit.rs`: an equivalence matrix over ten tail shapes (empty file, no trailing newline, blank lines, CRLF, truncated last row, trailing garbage, all-garbage, invalid-UTF-8 tail) asserting the bounded read equals the full scan on each; an R-203 guard asserting the BOUNDED path alone resolves the tail of a file three windows long (reverting to a full scan reds it); and a fail-safe asserting an all-garbage window declines (`None`) while the exact fallback still recovers the true tail.

### Fixed (`memory_load_family` fetched 1000 full rows on Postgres to return 0)

- **The `metadata.family` predicate is pushed into SQL through a new SAL `Filter::metadata_eq` axis honoured by BOTH adapters, instead of materialising a 1000-row superset and filtering it in Rust** (refs [#2580](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2580); 5-agent adversarial vote `4d3ea1c5`). `memory_load_family` is an always-on **core-profile** tool (also reached through `memory_smart_load`), so every default Postgres deployment paid this on every call: `MAX_BULK_SIZE` (=1000) FULL rows regardless of the requested `k`, ~982 kB of content+metadata, 54.3 ms p50 on the 8k-row Atlas corpus — to return **zero** rows, because no row in that corpus carries `metadata.family` at all.
  - **Postgres** binds `metadata @> jsonb_build_object($9::text, $10::text)`, which the pre-existing `memories_metadata_gin` index answers with a Bitmap Index Scan. Measured with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the live corpus: **3.807 ms execution / 321 buffers / 1000 rows** for the pre-fix `LIMIT 1000` shape versus **0.286 ms / 11 buffers / 0 rows** for the containment shape. The non-indexable alternative `metadata->>'family' = $v` was measured too and REJECTED: 17.759 ms, `Rows Removed by Filter: 10724`.
  - **SQLite** binds the twin `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(memories.metadata) WHERE json_each.key = ? AND json_each.value = ? AND json_each.type = 'text')`, mirroring the sibling `tags_any` fragment. Both bind the KEY as a query parameter rather than interpolating it into a JSON path, so no key value can alter the predicate's shape.
  - **Semantics are preserved exactly, and the axis rides the SHARED `list` query on both backends** rather than a bespoke one — deliberately, so the #1948 fail-closed lifecycle allow-list, the expiry guard, the scope=private visibility clause, the #1834 claim-bitemporal AS-OF window and the #2383 undecryptable-row skip all keep applying unchanged. `json_each.type = 'text'` and jsonb containment both restrict to JSON STRING values, making the SQL byte-exact with the Rust predicate it replaces (`metadata.get(k).and_then(Value::as_str) == Some(v)`). A twelve-shape matrix — string/other/prefix/case/empty, number, null, bool, array, nested object, key-elsewhere, absent — is asserted IDENTICAL on sqlite and on live Postgres, so jsonb `@>`'s documented array/nesting special cases are pinned against the live planner rather than against the docs.
  - **Fail-closed by construction.** The handler RETAINS the in-process `metadata.family` re-check (`MetadataEq::matches`), mirroring the belt-and-suspenders `is_visible_to_caller` re-apply inside `PostgresStore::list`. The pushdown is therefore strictly NARROWING: an adapter that ignored the axis could only DEGRADE to fewer results, never widen the set with rows the caller did not ask for.
  - **A pre-existing correctness defect is fixed, not merely a slow path — and it fired on ordinary deployments, not just huge namespaces.** Because the old code applied `LIMIT 1000` BEFORE the family filter, family-tagged rows sorting below global rank 1000 were SILENTLY DROPPED, so Postgres returned fewer rows than SQLite for identical data (SQLite's `handle_load_family` always pushed the predicate down). The trigger is not an exotic 1000-row namespace: **calling `memory_load_family` / `memory_smart_load` WITHOUT a `namespace` spans the whole table**, so any deployment holding more than 1000 memories in total was affected — on an always-on core-profile tool. Demonstrated end-to-end over HTTP against the live 8,724-row corpus: a 74-shape request matrix (8 families x 3 namespaces x 3 `k` values plus the namespace-omitted variants, over a seeded fixture carrying duplicate `(priority, updated_at)` pairs, wrong-typed `family` values, a nested-`family` decoy, expired + tombstoned rows, and `scope=collective`/foreign-private rows) returns **byte-identical responses on 72 of 74 shapes**; the 2 that differ are exactly the namespace-omitted ones, where the pre-fix daemon returned 5 and 4 rows against the fixed daemon's 9 and 8. In both cases the pre-fix list is an **exact ORDERED PREFIX** of the fixed list — every row the old code returned is still returned, in the same position, with the silently-dropped rows appended in correct rank order. The change is a strict SUPERSET (restricting the ordering to family-tagged rows can only move a family row UP in rank); **no row is ever lost**. Also pinned by a live-Postgres regression that seeds 1050 untagged high-priority rows plus 3 low-priority family rows and asserts the legacy pipeline finds ZERO while the pushdown finds all three.
  - **Measured end-to-end** (two `--release --features sal-postgres` daemons, same host, same live PG 18.4 instance, interleaved to bracket drift, HTTP keep-alive, n=300): `memory_load_family` p50 **53.84 ms -> 2.59 ms (20.8x)**, p99 78.26 -> 4.17 ms. The pre-fix figure independently reproduces the 54.27 ms p50 recorded in #2580.
  - **The `k` bound is honoured without risking an under-return.** The fast path asks for exactly `k` rows; because the SAL `list` applies the strictly-narrower Rust `is_visible_to_caller` (the #1921 team/unit/org subtree gate has no twin in the SQL `$6` clause) AFTER the SQL `LIMIT`, a bare `LIMIT k` could return fewer rows than the old 1000-row window did. When the narrowed set is short of `k` the handler therefore re-asks once at the historical `MAX_BULK_SIZE` window — at most two round trips, the second carrying only family-tagged rows.
### Fixed (postgres read path — a missing index, an O(limit) round-trip ledger, a dead AGE branch, and 43-column reads that used 31)

- **Four postgres read-path defects, each reproduced by EXECUTION against the live certified tier before any code was written** (refs [#2578](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2578), [#2581](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2581), [#2582](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2582), [#2585](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2585); schema **v87 -> v88**; 5-agent adversarial vote `4d3ea1c5`). Two of the four issues' own framings are corrected below, and one proposed index is deliberately NOT shipped because measuring it showed a regression. **Evidence discipline:** the box these were developed on ran six concurrent audit lanes at load ~20 on 14 cores, so every headline claim below is anchored to a LOAD-INDEPENDENT signal — `EXPLAIN` plan shape, buffer counts, rows read, statement counts, wire bytes — and wall-clock figures are quoted as indicative only.

  - **#2578 — the v56 composite list indexes never landed on postgres (schema v88).** v56 (#1579 A2 + B6d) shipped `idx_memories_ns_list_order` / `idx_memories_list_order` / `idx_archived_ns_archived_at` to SQLite and left `migrate_v56()` a postgres version-stamp no-op, so for the whole v56..v87 range a namespace-scoped `list` on postgres read EVERY row in the namespace and sorted it — O(namespace size) where SQLite is O(limit). Confirmed on the live tier (8,724 rows, 7,855 in one namespace) against the exact statement `MemoryStore::list` issues: **buffers 1,880 -> 8, rows read 7,855 -> 10, the top-N heapsort node eliminated entirely** (~9.7 -> ~0.07 ms). `LIMIT 1000` (the `memory_load_family` shape): buffers 2,079 -> 321. **Scope stated honestly:** the win is proportional to namespace size — a 10-row namespace measures no win and no loss — and it is contingent on postgres keeping a CUSTOM plan; forced to a generic plan the composite is not chosen and the win is zero. Extra filters (`tier` / `agent_id` / `since` / `until` / `valid_at`) do NOT regress: the planner declines the composite and both index sets converge on the same plan.
  - **#2578 — the UNSCOPED `idx_memories_list_order` is deliberately NOT shipped, against the issue's own proposal and against SQLite parity.** It was in the first draft; an adversarial re-measurement removed it. In a namespace whose rows are expired-but-not-yet-GC'd, its presence makes the planner ABANDON the namespace-scoped composite and walk the unscoped index ACROSS EVERY NAMESPACE — an O(namespace) scan becomes O(table). Measured on an isolated copy with 7,000 of `atlas-corpus`'s 7,855 rows expired, namespace-scoped `LIMIT 10`: **before (no composites) 1,989 buffers / 7,000 rows filtered in-namespace; ns-scoped composite ONLY 1,854 buffers / 6,882 in-namespace; BOTH composites 3,041 buffers / 9,621 filtered across ALL namespaces.** Its only benefit is the rarer unscoped `list` (0.58 ms absolute) against permanent write amplification. Shipping it would have made a real scenario measurably worse to speed up a rarer one; it is filed separately with the evidence rather than smuggled in on parity grounds.
  - **#2578 — a plain in-transaction `CREATE INDEX` here would have been a fleet-wide BOOT BRICK, and it is not a large-table hazard.** Every pooled connection carries `statement_timeout = 30s` + `lock_timeout = 5s` from the `after_connect` hook, and `connect_*` clears them ONLY on the dedicated advisory-lock connection — never on the connection a migrate arm's `pool.begin()` hands out. `CREATE INDEX` wants a SHARE lock. Reproduced against the live tier with ONE ordinary uncommitted `INSERT` open: `ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout` at **5.002 s** — the arm's tx rolls back, the version is not stamped, `migrate_locked` returns `Err`, `connect()` returns `Err`, and the daemon cannot boot, identically on every retry while any writer is active. That is concurrency-driven, not size-driven: it fires on an 8k-row table as readily as a 3-billion-row one. So `migrate_v88` builds `CONCURRENTLY`, on a dedicated connection, outside any transaction, with `lock_timeout` cleared (CIC must be able to wait a writer out) and `statement_timeout` BOUNDED rather than cleared (an unbounded wait would hang `connect()` past a supervisor's start deadline and turn a clean wait into a crash-loop). Same probe with CONCURRENTLY succeeded, leaving `indisvalid = t`.
  - **#2578 — the arm is FAIL-OPEN and self-healing.** These indexes are derived, disposable, non-UNIQUE artifacts regenerable from the durable memory TEXT; nothing about correctness rests on them and a build failure DEGRADES to exactly today's query plan. Refusing to boot a fleet over a missing performance index would trade total availability for zero integrity, so the arm WARNs and stamps. Because the stamp means the arm never re-runs, the same idempotent helper runs on EVERY connect (three catalog probes and a no-op once valid), so a node that lost one build self-heals instead of staying silently un-indexed forever. The probe is on `pg_index.indisvalid`, never mere existence: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS` silently no-ops over a leftover INVALID index, which the planner ignores for reads while postgres still maintains it on every write — pure cost, permanently; an invalid leftover is dropped and rebuilt.
  - **#2578 — `list_archived` also needed the #1473 sargable split, or the new archive index would have been unusable.** The OR-NULL idiom `($1 IS NULL OR namespace = $1)` is non-sargable, so under the GENERIC plan sqlx's prepared statements settle into, the planner never chooses the composite. Measured on a 200k-row archive with realistic multi-tenant skew, forced generic plan, namespace-scoped `LIMIT 20`: **47.912 ms / 180,000 rows filtered -> 0.062 ms / Index Cond on `namespace`**. Without this the index would have been pure write amplification for zero read benefit.
  - **#2581 — the recall ledger issued one INSERT round trip per returned candidate.** `recall_observation_insert` was `BEGIN` + one INSERT PER CANDIDATE + `COMMIT`, so recall — otherwise pure since #1869/P0-1 — was **O(limit) in round trips**, and the ledger is the only write a recall performs. It is now ONE `INSERT … SELECT … FROM UNNEST(…) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`: **`2 + limit` statements -> 1**, a structural, load-independent fact. Measured over the extended/prepared protocol (what sqlx actually uses) inside one transaction: **limit=10 8.04 -> 3.89 ms (-52%), limit=50 21.75 -> 5.40 ms (-75%)**, marginal cost 0.36-0.45 ms/row — consistent with the **0.19 ms/row** the issue measured against a real daemon at `log_min_duration_statement=0`. **An earlier draft of this entry claimed 4.8x/16.4x; that was wrong** and is corrected here: those figures came from a `psql` harness whose simple-protocol autocommit made each statement its own WAL fsync (3.5 ms/row), measuring N fsyncs where the daemon pays one per recall.
  - **#2581 — this is a LATENCY fix only; the ledger rows are byte-identical.** Same eight columns, same values, same `folded = FALSE`, same `observed_at`, same `ON CONFLICT (recall_id, memory_id) DO NOTHING` disposition, same all-or-nothing atomicity, same returned count of rows ACTUALLY inserted. Verified on the live tier that an intra-batch duplicate `memory_id` behaves identically in both forms (first entry inserts, second is a silent conflict no-op). `UNNEST` over four arrays rather than a multi-row `VALUES` list, because `candidates` is bounded by `LIST_MAX_LIMIT`: a VALUES form would emit ~5k bind parameters and a DIFFERENT SQL string per candidate count, thrashing sqlx's statement cache one order of magnitude below the protocol's hard 65535-parameter ceiling; UNNEST is eight parameters for any N. The explicit transaction is gone because a single statement already carries identical atomicity. A code comment and a regression test pin that this must NOT become `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, which would raise `21000` on the very input the loop accepted — a hard failure on an append-only AUDIT surface.
  - **#2582 — `find_paths`'s AGE branch has never once succeeded on the pinned AGE version.** `build_find_paths_current_view_cypher` emits an `ALL(e IN relationships(p) WHERE …)` guard, and **AGE 1.7.0 rejects it at parse time** (`syntax error at or near "("`) — reproduced against both a scratch graph and the LIVE `memory_graph`; `ALL`/`ANY`/`NONE` are grammar keywords there, not callable functions, and AGE 1.7 implements no list predicates. So every call paid `BEGIN` + `LOAD 'age'` + `SET LOCAL search_path` + a failing parse + a rollback + a per-call WARN, then ran the CTE anyway. `find_paths` now routes to the relational recursive CTE unconditionally: **zero answers change** (100% of production AGE results already came from the CTE), the wasted round trips go, and a WARN that fired on every single call — burying the real `age_substrate_unreachable` signal it looks like — stops. **Fixing the Cypher would have been the wrong repair:** on a purpose-built 20,003-vertex / 60,000-edge graph a PARSEABLE depth-4 AGE traversal returning 120 rows takes **987.8 ms**, and its plan is a Nested Loop whose outer side is a `Seq Scan` over ALL 20,003 vertices with 2,400,240 rows removed by `age_match_vle_terminal_edge` — the cost scales with |V|, not depth, so no depth K favours AGE and the crossover only recedes as a corpus grows. A vertex-property GIN index does not rescue it (987.8 -> 979 ms; it fixes the O(V) START lookup, not the walk). Consistency strictly improves: `memory_links` is the durable relational truth and the AGE projection is a derived artifact that can lag it (#1735 already routed `deferred` mode here for that reason; `sync` now gets the same guarantee). `find_paths_cypher` and its builder are RETAINED — they still back the #2032 L4 Cypher-injection guard tests and the live-AGE equivalence suites.
  - **#2582 — honest comparison.** An earlier draft quoted 877x against a simplified DIRECTED CTE that production does not run. Like-for-like against the ACTUAL `find_paths_cte` (undirected, visited-path array) on the same graph at depth 4: AGE **987.8 ms** vs **462.99 ms** — **2.1x**. The AGE path being dead code means it was never a live latency cost, only wasted round trips; and the production CTE's own 463 ms at depth 4 is a separate, larger problem, filed separately.
  - **#2585 — every `memories` read that maps into a `Memory` used `SELECT *`, fetching 43 columns to use 31.** Eight read shapes (`get` by id, `list`, `list_by_namespace_prefix`, `list_by_source_uri`, `list_memories_updated_since`, `search`, and BOTH recall pools) now project the single `MEMORY_READ_COLUMNS` SSOT — the postgres twin of the 31-column list #2384 already shipped on SQLite, so the two adapters project identically. Real wire bytes (`COPY … BINARY`, n=500): **4,527 -> 1,016 B/row (-77.6%)** with 768-dim embeddings present, **2,008 -> 1,269 B/row (-36%)** on a corpus with none. Isolated 30-row fetch: **2.86 -> 0.53 ms (5.4x)** embedded, **0.86 -> 0.63 ms (-27%)** unembedded.
  - **#2585 — the issue's "latent, zero measured impact" framing is REFUTED.** The waste is paid today on an unembedded corpus, because the `tsv` `GENERATED ALWAYS … STORED` tsvector is transferred at **459 B/row on the wire — larger than `content`** — and is consumed entirely server-side (`tsv @@ …`, `ts_rank(tsv, …)`). The issue also missed the worse of the two recall pools: the SEMANTIC pool's `SELECT *` fetched the `embedding` column for `5 x limit` rows that ALL carry embeddings by construction, purely to discard them (it scores via `embedding <=> $1`, computed server-side). `encrypted_envelope` is deliberately KEPT in the projection despite not being a `Memory` field — it is the #2303 at-rest decrypt input, and without it every sealed row would map to the empty-content sentinel and `list_memories_updated_since` would RELAY that sentinel to federation peers, who would re-seal an empty string under their own key.
  - **Cross-backend parity.** #2578 is postgres-only (SQLite has had the indexes since v56; its v88 is a no-op and the ladder's unconditional tail stamp carries it, the v69 precedent). #2582 is postgres+AGE-only (SQLite has no graph backend). #2585 is postgres-only in effect: SQLite's `memories` also carries an `embedding` BLOB the mapper never reads, but rusqlite decodes lazily and there is no socket, so the cost is near-zero — and #2384 already narrowed the one SQLite shape where it mattered. #2581's per-row loop exists on SQLite too but has no network round trip to amortise; the tail the issue observed there is a separate finding, filed separately.
  - **Tests (R-203).** `tests/pg_projection_column_fidelity_2585.rs` — five OFFLINE guards (no database, no network) that parse the shipped DDL and census every `memories` column as projected-or-documented-derived, pin the projection as a subset of the real schema, pin `Memory::FIELD_COUNT`, and assert `encrypted_envelope` stays in while `embedding`/`tsv` stay out. Proven load-bearing by execution: dropping `cid` from the projection and re-adding `embedding` each turn it red. `tests/pg_read_path_perf_shapes_2578_2581_2582.rs` — six live-postgres pins asserting SHAPE, never wall-clock (a latency threshold in CI is a flake generator that proves nothing about the mechanism): index presence AND `indisvalid`, the ABSENCE of the withheld unscoped index, the planner actually choosing the composite with no sort node (read out of `EXPLAIN`), ledger first-wins on an intra-batch duplicate plus cross-call idempotence, and `find_paths` still returning correct paths now that the AGE attempt is gone.


### Fixed (two observability endpoints did O(corpus) work per request — a liveness probe that kills healthy pods, and a permanent scrape tax)

- **`GET /api/v1/health` is now O(1) and `GET /metrics` does ZERO database work at steady state; the FTS-integrity signal moves to a paced background check whose CACHED verdict `/health` renders, and to `ai-memory doctor`** (refs [#2579](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2579) + its independent re-measurement [#2586](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2586), and [#2583](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2583); MANAGEABLE-AT-SCALE + the [#2444](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2444)/[#2445](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2445) honest-control class; 5-agent adversarial vote `4d3ea1c5`, 4-1 on both decisions). Both issues were REPRODUCED by execution at five corpus sizes before any code was written, and one of the audit's framings is corrected below.
  - **#2579 root cause, and the authoritative curve.** `db::health_check` ran `INSERT INTO memories_fts(memories_fts) VALUES('integrity-check')` on every request. `memories_fts` is an **external-content** FTS5 table (`content=memories`), so that command does not walk an index — it re-tokenizes every row's `title`/`content`/`tags` out of `memories` and compares the derived doclists. The authoritative measurement is the independent re-measurement filed as **#2586**: **13.4 ms at 1k rows → 850 ms at 128k**, i.e. **~6.5 us/row → ~6.5 s at 1M**, with `COUNT(*)` a flat **0.01 ms** so **100%** of the cost is the FTS check. This lane REPRODUCED the same class independently on a SECOND, larger-document corpus grown by doubling (best-of-3 warm, at the SQL layer): **0 rows 0.000 s · 2,036 rows 0.299 s · 8,144 rows 0.243 s · 32,576 rows 0.766 s · 130,304 rows 2.844 s**, linear at **21.8-29.8 us/row**. The two curves agree on the SHAPE and differ only in the constant, which is the substantive finding: the cost tracks TOKENS, so document size sets the slope and no single us/row figure is portable. Against the Kubernetes default `timeoutSeconds: 1` the probe blows its budget at ~154k rows on #2586's corpus and ~48k on this one. The original issue's ~8.8 s-at-1M extrapolation was therefore the right order of magnitude but is superseded by #2586's measured curve.
  - **#2586 also CORRECTED a wrong inference in the original framing:** daemon boot is **O(1)** (~44 ms at 128k rows). What looked like boot scaling was the FIRST `/health` call. That is worth stating because it changes what the fix must do — and this one does it: the background checker's first pass is deliberately deferred behind a random `[0, 5 min]` offset, so boot never pays the deep check at all.
  - **Two aggravations, both load-independent and both structural.** (1) SQLite prepares that `INSERT` as a **non-readonly** statement — verified by execution: it fails with `attempt to write a readonly database` on a `mode=ro` connection — so it takes the single WAL **writer lock** for its whole multi-second duration while ALSO holding the daemon's shared `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`, i.e. the probe blocks every WRITE as well as every read; and a sustained probe stream keeps a write transaction perpetually open, which blocks WAL checkpointing and lets the `-wal` file grow unbounded on exactly the largest nodes. (2) `/health` is EXEMPT from admission control (env #79), so it can neither be shed under overload nor rate-limited — the cost is reachable at an unauthenticated caller's chosen rate. A probe that blocks writers and cannot be shed is worse than a merely slow probe.
  - **#2583 root cause, measured.** `prometheus_metrics` called `db::stats` per scrape and used exactly ONE of its ten fields (`total`). `db::stats` issues eight statements; timed at the parent commit: at 8,144 rows the set costs ~15 ms of which `dim_violations` (which walks every row's `embedding` BLOB) is 11 ms; at 130,304 rows the set costs ~130 ms of which `dim_violations` is 98 ms. Two full `GROUP BY` aggregations (tier, namespace) were computed and discarded on every scrape. It ran holding the daemon's single `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`, and `/metrics` is likewise admission-exempt.
  - **The posture decision, and what `/health` no longer proves.** Liveness-only-plus-`doctor` was the strongest competing option and lost 4-1: `db::health_check` was the **only** FTS-integrity check anywhere in the codebase (`doctor` did not have one), so making the probe cheap without relocating the control would have deleted the signal — and this repository has SHIPPED that corruption class (v63 dropped the `memory_links` sync triggers; v65 restored them). `/health` now proves (a) the connection answers SQL and (b) the FTS5 index is REACHABLE — a bounded `MATCH` for an absent term, which is one segment-index lookup and genuinely exercises the `fts5` module and its `_data`/`_idx`/`_config` shadow tables. It no longer proves per-request that the index AGREES with `memories`. The response says so: an additive `checks` block names what was verified, and an additive `fts_integrity` block carries `{status, checked_at, interval_secs}` so the verdict's AGE is visible rather than implied.
  - **The fail-closed contract is preserved, not dropped.** A cached `failed` verdict still answers **503**, exactly as the per-probe check did. What changed is FRESHNESS: a corruption is detected within one interval instead of on the next probe. That window is bought consciously and is rendered.
  - **A stale pass expires on its own.** An `ok` verdict older than 3 intervals degrades to `stale`, so a checker that dies cannot re-present its last PASS forever — the #2444 shape re-entering through the checker's own liveness, which three of the five adversarial lenses raised independently. `pending` (no check completed yet) and `disabled` (cadence set to `0`) are distinct values and neither is `ok`.
  - **`pending` / `stale` / `disabled` do NOT 503.** Only a CONFIRMED corruption does. 503-ing a node that merely has not finished its first check would deadlock a rolling fleet restart, and 503-ing on staleness would convert a monitoring gap into an outage.
  - **The checker runs on its OWN connection, and that is load-bearing.** Because the deep check is a writer, running it under the daemon's single mutex would block every reader — `/health` included — for its whole duration, i.e. the probe-timeout kill would return as a 1-in-N event, which is a strictly worse failure mode than a deterministic one. On a separate connection (`db::open_unmigrated`) it takes only SQLite's write lock: WAL readers are unaffected and writers queue behind `busy_timeout`.
  - **An operational error does not flip the verdict.** Moving to a separate connection makes `SQLITE_BUSY` reachable where it was not before, so only a genuine corruption code (`SQLITE_CORRUPT` / `SQLITE_CORRUPT_VTAB`) records a failure; anything else retains the previous verdict and logs a WARN. Without that split this change would have introduced a NEW false-503 class.
  - **Paced and jittered, never a synchronized blast.** First check at a random offset in `[0, 5 min]` (so a fleet restart spreads immediately without leaving any node verdict-less for a whole interval), then every `AI_MEMORY_FTS_INTEGRITY_INTERVAL_SECS` (default 6 h) +/- 20%.
  - **The corpus gauge is pre-computed, and its freshness is published.** `ai_memory_memories` is refreshed by a paced background loop issuing ONE `COUNT` (`AI_MEMORY_METRICS_GAUGE_REFRESH_SECS`, default 60 s); the scrape path renders. Cost is now independent of corpus size AND of scrape rate. The new `ai_memory_memories_refreshed_at_seconds` gauge is NOT optional decoration: without it a dead refresher would freeze a plausible-looking count forever — straight through a mass deletion — while Prometheus `up` stayed 1. A cold process (a router with no loop, or a disabled cadence) pays ONE count on its first scrape rather than serving a `0` indistinguishable from an empty corpus.
  - **An incrementally-maintained counter was REJECTED.** Other OS processes write the same SQLite file (MCP stdio, `curator`, every CLI invocation), so an in-process delta would DRIFT and publish a confidently wrong number. SQLite has no `pg_class.reltuples` equivalent — `COUNT(*)` scans the narrowest index end to end, and `sqlite_stat1` holds only a stale post-`ANALYZE` estimate — so a cheap exact count does not exist and a cheap estimate would be a wrong number sold as truth.
  - **`?deep=1` was REJECTED** even though the issue proposes it: `/health` is unauthenticated AND admission-exempt, so a query parameter would hand any remote party a documented trigger for the single most expensive statement in the system while it holds the write lock. "Probes do not set it" is a convention, not a control. Sampling (1-in-N) was rejected for the same reason plus a nondeterministic p99.
  - **`doctor` gains the deep check it never had.** `ai-memory doctor` now runs the full FTS5 integrity check in its `Index` section, reports `verified` or a CRITICAL `FAILED`, and names the rebuild remedy. The index is DERIVED and regenerable from the durable memory TEXT, so a failure is a degrade-class event, not data loss — the note says that too, so nobody reaches for a restore.
  - **Postgres, checked and NOT silently assumed clean** (the [#2488](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2488) opposite-directions lesson). Both issues are sqlite-flagged, and `/metrics` genuinely is (its gauge path is sqlite-only). `/health` is NOT: `PostgresStore::health_check` runs `SELECT COUNT(*)::BIGINT FROM memories`, and `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` against the live 10,724-row certified stack shows an `Index Only Scan` over ALL rows (1.6 ms) — the same O(corpus) shape on the same endpoint, two orders of magnitude cheaper per row. `src/store/postgres.rs` is owned by a concurrent lane this release, so the four-line change is filed as [#2617](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2617) rather than conflicted into this PR.
  - **Measured after, interleaved A/B on the same box in the same window.** `/api/v1/health` p50: **0.198 -> 0.169 ms** at 0 rows, **110.796 -> 0.278** at 2,036, **215.575 -> 0.168** at 8,144, **679.636 -> 0.217** at 32,576, **2,576.256 -> 0.306** at 130,304 (**8,419x**). `/metrics` p50: **0.421 -> 0.163**, **3.614 -> 0.136**, **8.320 -> 0.133**, **34.785 -> 0.135**, **221.661 -> 0.157** (**1,412x**). The untouched `/api/v1/inbox` CONTROL stays at 0.13-0.22 ms in BOTH variants at every size, which is what makes the two columns attributable to the endpoints rather than to the host. The SHAPE is the claim: BEFORE is linear (54.4 / 26.5 / 20.9 / 19.8 us/row, converging on ~19.8), AFTER is CONSTANT — both endpoints stay inside the noise of the empty-corpus case across a 130,304-row growth. CPU fraction at 130k BEFORE is **1.00**: pure in-process burn.
  - **This does NOT make `/health` liveness safe on its own — it removes ONE of two contributors.** Lens C measured, on a quiet box, that the recall-access fold loop stalls writes for **24.3 s at 128k distinct memories** (seconds 10-32 complete ZERO writes; ~190 us per distinct memory, extrapolating to ~190 s at 1M). It holds the SAME writer mutex the FTS integrity check was on. So pre-fix, `/api/v1/health` was blowing its probe budget during **every fold pass**, not only on its own cost — two independent sources of the same orchestrator-kills-healthy-pods outcome. This change removes the per-probe source; the fold-loop stall is [#2599](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2599) and is NOT closed here. A reader seeing `/health` land at 0.306 ms should not conclude liveness is safe at scale until #2599 lands too.
  - **The measurement harness's own failure is the sharpest evidence.** The first interleaved run logged `FAILED TO START before/c130k` — but the daemon HAD started (`ai-memory listening on http://127.0.0.1:9293`); what failed was the harness's readiness probe, `curl -m 2` against a `/health` that takes 2.576 s. The pre-fix daemon at 130k rows failed a **2-second** health check 180 consecutive times while being perfectly healthy. Kubernetes' default `timeoutSeconds` is **1**, i.e. half of what this harness allowed. #2579 is therefore not a projection about a hypothetical 1M-row future: at a corpus size this substrate already carries, the pre-fix daemon is DEFINITIONALLY unhealthy to its orchestrator, whose correct response is to kill it and restart it into the same condition. The fixed binary answers the same probe on the same corpus in 0.306 ms — ~3,200x of margin against that 1 s budget.
  - **The first draft of this fix MANUFACTURED the defect class it exists to remove, and that is left in the record deliberately.** Both background loops take the local sqlite handle (`db_path` / `db_state`). On a `--store-url postgres://…` daemon that file is a near-empty SIDECAR, not the corpus being served — so the draft would have run the integrity check against a database nobody reads and rendered `fts_integrity: ok` at `/health` on the strength of it. That is EXACTLY the #2444 shape (a control reporting success while measuring nothing), re-created by the change whose entire purpose is to remove it, and it would have been strictly worse than the O(corpus) probe it replaced: the slow probe was at least telling the truth. Caught in self-review before push, not by a reviewer and not in CI — which is the lesson: relocating a control off the request path silently changes WHAT the control is pointed at, and "is this still measuring the thing it claims to measure?" has to be asked explicitly at the new call site. Both loops are therefore gated to the SQLITE backend, and that gate is a CORRECTNESS gate, not an optimisation. A postgres daemon therefore renders `fts_integrity: disabled` beside `checks.fts_index: not_applicable` (postgres has no FTS5 index; it uses a stored `tsvector` + GIN). The same reasoning surfaced a PRE-EXISTING defect that is filed rather than entrenched: `prometheus_metrics` has ALWAYS read the sqlite `Db` regardless of backend, so `ai_memory_memories` reports `0` on a populated postgres corpus ([#2621](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2621)).
