Pacing a wrong number would have made it look more authoritative, so the refresher is gated off there and the defect is named in the code comment.
  - **Residuals filed, not deferred:** [#2617](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2617) (the postgres `/health` twin), [#2618](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2618) (`doctor` can now DETECT a corrupt FTS index but not repair it; a daemon-side auto-heal is deliberately NOT proposed, because auto-rebuilding on detection would turn a loud operator-visible degrade into a silent multi-second write-lock hold at an unpredictable time), and [#2621](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2621) (the postgres gauge above).
  - **Tests (R-203).** `tests/health_metrics_constant_cost_2579_2583.rs` — cells A-E reference NO symbol introduced here, so the file compiles unchanged at the parent commit and FAILS there: A traces the statements `db::health_check` actually executes and finds the integrity-check command; B times it at 5,000 rows against a 20 ms budget (~110 ms at parent, <1 ms after — a 20x margin over the fixed cost and a 5x margin under the parent cost, so the cell is neither flaky nor vacuous); C finds no `checks`/`fts_integrity` block; D finds no freshness gauge; E cannot hold a refresh stamp still across 14 back-to-back scrapes. Cells F-G pin what `/health` STILL guarantees (a `failed` verdict is 503 and never decays into silence; an `ok` verdict ages out on its own). Cell H is the CONTROL — a real daemon on a real 37-row corpus serves `/health` 200 and reports the REAL count — so the refusal cells cannot pass because nothing ever ran (the [#2449](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2449) harness lesson).

### Fixed (`export` / `export --full` / `import` reported success over operations that did not happen)

- **The three sibling verbs in `src/cli/io.rs` now fail closed on a Postgres store, refuse to conjure a database, account for every row the export boundary withheld or mutated, and stop swallowing link failures on import** (refs [#2490](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2490); DATA-INTEGRITY, the [#2444](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2444) false-success class; 5-agent adversarial vote `4d3ea1c5`, decision memory `10132d0e`). Every defect below was reproduced by EXECUTION against `release/v1.0.0` @ `89e21191` before any code was written, and the issue text was not adopted as premise — two of its implied claims are refuted at the bottom of this entry.
  - **Postgres false-success, all three verbs (CONFIRMED).** With `AI_MEMORY_STORE_URL=postgres://…` and no `--db` file present: `export` exited 0, CREATED an 802,816-byte SQLite database, and emitted `{"count":0,"memories":[],"links":[]}`. `export --full` was worse — the conjured file bootstraps real default governance rules, so the v2 envelope carried `db_schema_version: 87`, four `governance_rules` and a `trust_anchor` wrapped around `memories: []`, and printed NOTHING on stderr. `import` exited 0 reporting `{"imported":1}` into the same conjured file. All three now route through the shared `cli::backup::resolve_sqlite_store` gate #2444 already shipped (Postgres refused naming `pg_dump` with the DSN password redacted, unrecognised scheme refused, argv/env disagreement refused, empty `sqlite://` path refused), so no artifact and no database are produced.
  - **`import` REFUSES a disagreeing `sqlite://` store URL rather than redirecting — the biggest risk the review found.** `resolve_sqlite_source` does not merely refuse: for a `sqlite://` URL that disagrees with `--db` it silently REDIRECTS the operation to the env-named path behind a one-line `note:`. Defensible on a read-only `backup`; applied verbatim to `import` it would make `AI_MEMORY_STORE_URL=sqlite:///var/lib/ai-memory/prod.db ai-memory --db ./scratch.db import < bundle.json` write the bundle into prod.db — and `docs/postgres-age-guide.md` + `docs/production-deployment.md` both instruct operators to export that variable at shell/cron scope. The disposition is now a typed parameter: read verbs redirect-with-note (unchanged), the WRITE verb refuses. Reading the wrong file wastes time; writing the wrong file destroys data.
  - **`export` refuses a non-existent database.** `db::open` creates the file and runs the whole migration ladder on it, so a conjured database is indistinguishable from a real one by any schema probe — non-existence is the only honest discriminator and the first invocation destroyed it. `import` deliberately keeps creating (importing into a fresh database IS the documented restore path).
  - **Silent partial export (CONFIRMED).** A database holding three live memories — one carrying a PEM private key, one carrying an AWS key + a GitHub token, one clean — exported `count: 2`, exit 0, with the PEM row DROPPED by the fail-closed forbidden-class gate ([#1838](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/1838)/G28) and the credential row's content silently MUTATED to `aws key [REDACTED:secret] token [REDACTED:secret]`. Neither appeared on stderr. Because `count == memories.len()` always, the artifact is fully SELF-CONSISTENT: the loss is unfalsifiable from the bundle, and the signed `export.forbidden_class_refused` row lands in the SOURCE database — the one artefact a DR operator no longer has. `export` now emits an additive in-band `withheld` marker (counts + a class histogram) plus ONE structured stderr line keyed `export_report` carrying the ids, and a PARTIAL export exits **3**.
  - **Exit `3`, not `1`, and the artifact is still written.** The universal backup idiom `ai-memory export > out.tmp && mv out.tmp out` deletes the partial artifact on ANY non-zero status, and plain `1` collapses "your backup is incomplete but valid and on disk" into the same bucket as "the process crashed". A distinct code lets an orchestrator branch. `--expect-withheld <N>` is a RATCHET, not a mute: exit stays 0 while `withheld <= N` and goes non-zero the moment it EXCEEDS the acknowledged number, so a NEW withholding still alarms — an unbounded acknowledgement would be forever-green, the same signal death as the forever-red it prevents.
  - **The withheld IDs are NOT written into the artifact.** The forbidden-class gate is an EXPORT-boundary control — no read surface consults it — so publishing "these ids carry private key material" into the portable bundle would hand whoever holds it a precise index into the source corpus's key material. Counts and a class histogram in-band; ids on the operator channel only.
  - **The withheld count would itself have under-reported.** `storage::export_all` applies the fail-closed lifecycle allow-list IN SQL, so `Quarantined` and `Tombstoned` rows never reach the screen; a count derived from the screen alone would report `0` on a node running `AI_MEMORY_FED_QUARANTINE_UNATTRIBUTED=1` ([#1948](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/1948)) — the same false-success relocated one layer down. `storage::export_excluded_counts` accounts for the SQL-level exclusions separately: quarantined counts as partial (real data withheld), tombstoned/expired are reported but not (erasure and retention are intended).
  - **`portability_complete` becomes an AND.** On `--full` it was computed SOLELY from the audit-chain re-verify + operator anchor, so an envelope could assert completeness over a corpus whose withheld rows it provably did not carry. It is now `L3 && nothing withheld`. This is a VALUE correction to an EXISTING field: the envelope is parsed with `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` under `spec_version = "2"`, so ADDING a field would make every already-shipped binary refuse new bundles.
  - **TOTAL silent link loss on import (CONFIRMED, three separate paths).** (1) `let _ = db::create_link(..)` discarded every insert error; (2) `if validate_link(..).is_err() { continue; }` skipped invalid edges silently; and (3) — found by this change's own regression test, not by the issue — `serde_json::from_value::<Vec<MemoryLink>>(..).unwrap_or_default()` meant ONE unparseable edge collapsed the WHOLE array to empty, taking every other edge with it. Links were never counted in the report at all. Executed: a bundle with a dangling endpoint imported as `{"imported":1,"errors":[]}`, exit 0, EMPTY stderr, zero links landed; same for an unrecognised relation. The parse is now per-element, every disposition is counted (`links_imported` / `links_refused` / `links_skipped_by_covenant`), and a refusal exits 3.
  - **Covenant-honoured skips are counted SEPARATELY and never fail the command.** A destination forget tombstone and a dest-archived id are the substrate doing its job, and [#1725](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/1725) puts every in-place-edited row into `archived_memories` — so counting them as failures would pin a repeat restore forever-red and the alarm would be `|| true`-ed away.
  - **Import REFUSES to overwrite a live unmasked row with a redacted one.** This is what makes "report redaction, exit 0" safe on the export side: export-time masking only becomes destruction of the source of truth at RESTORE time, and executed evidence confirmed re-importing a redacted artifact persisted `[REDACTED:secret]` as the durable content. A masked row is still admitted where the destination has nothing (nothing is destroyed) or is itself already masked (nothing is lost). The alternative — making redaction a non-zero export exit — was rejected 4-1 because `AI_MEMORY_SECRET_SCREEN_MODE` is global, so pressure to disable it would also disable the pre-WRITE credential screen on every surface.
  - **`archived_memories` + `namespace_meta` join the `excludes` marker.** Neither export mode has ever read those tables; the marker simply did not say so, so the artifact asserted a scope it did not have. Truthfulness fix using the mechanism that already ships — no behaviour change.
  - **REFUTED, and deliberately NOT "fixed".** (a) The round trip does not restore `version`: that is CORRECT — executed evidence shows the merge path INCREMENTS the destination-local CAS counter and never reads the payload's, so carrying the source value would inject a foreign counter into the destination's optimistic-concurrency lineage. (b) The round trip re-mints `cid`: also correct where `agent_id` is restamped, because `cid` COMMITS to `agent_id` — preserving the payload cid beside a restamped id would persist a row that fails `verify_cid` against its own `cid_genesis`, manufacturing the exact partial-corruption signal cid exists to detect. The genuine residue is narrow (`--trust-source` on an already-EDITED row mints an address over CURRENT content while keeping the GENESIS `created_at`) and belongs to [#2385](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2385); it is cross-referenced, not folded in. All 28 other `Memory` fields round-trip exactly, asserted field-by-field.
  - **Scope, stated plainly.** This closes the DR-artifact verbs. It does NOT make the CLI Postgres-safe in general: every other CLI write verb (`store`, `link`, `mine`, `forget`, …) still calls `db::open` and will conjure the same phantom SQLite database under a Postgres deployment. The HTTP admin export sibling is likewise unchanged. Both are filed separately.
  - **Tests (R-203).** `tests/export_import_false_success_2490.rs` — 11 subprocess cells driving the real binary, referencing no new struct field so the identical source compiles and runs at the parent commit, where the store-guard, exit-code and link-accounting cells fail. Two CONTROL cells (a genuine SQLite export, a clean import) pin that the refusals are not passing for a trivial reason — the [#2449](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2449) harness lesson that exit-127 and early-abort "fail" too. Round-trip fidelity is asserted FIELD-BY-FIELD, never by row count: a count-only assertion is precisely how this class hides.

### Removed (CI cost — nightly native AGE stack build)

- **The `postgres-age` nightly job is deleted, not repaired** (operator directive 2026-07-31: *"there is zero need to do nightly AGE testing with native postgresql"*; *"stop doing nightly AGE testing that wastes time"*). The job (#2012) apt-installed and built the SSOT-pinned certified stack — PostgreSQL 18.4 + Apache AGE 1.7.0 + pgvector 0.8.5 — **natively on the runner every night**, asserted the live extension versions against the pins, then ran the `AI_MEMORY_TEST_AGE_URL`-gated Cypher/KG suites. That is a from-source rebuild per night to reproduce a stack that already exists continuously as the `ai-memory-pg:18.4-age1.7.0-vec0.8.5` container on the validation host, so it was removed rather than fixed. **AGE / Cypher / KG work is validated against that local certified stack** — where the #2511 AGE-read seam (seven dead-path defects) and the postgres arms of #2478 / #2479 / #2503 / #2537 were each actually proven, including fail-at-parent evidence. The `postgres-parity` job in the same workflow is UNTOUCHED: it uses a `pgvector/pgvector:pg16` service container, needs no AGE, and still runs the three `#[ignore]`-gated parity binaries the workflow was originally created for (#1855). Whether any IN-PR AGE coverage is wanted is left open on [#2548](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2548), to be justified on its own merits and with a container image rather than a native build if it ever is; the CI-vs-SSOT AGE version drift ([#2512](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2512) defect 2) is deferred behind that same question.
### Fixed (there was NO downgrade guard — an older binary silently opened and WROTE a newer database, while the deployment doc promised a refusal twice)

- **`observed > CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` now REFUSES on both backends, before either adapter replays its bootstrap DDL, and `docs/production-deployment.md` stops lying** (refs [#2445](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2445); DATA-INTEGRITY; both backends; 5-agent adversarial vote `4d3ea1c5`, decision memory `4c4789ac`, 5/5 APPROVE-WITH-CHANGES). Both migrate entrypoints treated "database newer than binary" as "nothing to do" (`if version >= CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION { return Ok(()) }` in `src/storage/migrations.rs` and `PostgresStore::migrate_locked`), so an OLDER binary opened a NEWER database silently and then WROTE it. `docs/production-deployment.md` promised a downgrade refusal that did not exist — twice, once INSIDE the rollback runbook, at the precise moment an operator is performing the rollback that would trigger it. Rollback is the second half of every canary deployment.
  - **Executed evidence at the parent commit (`89e21191`), both backends, before any code was written.** sqlite: `PARENT PROBE: binary tip=v87; db stamp=v92; db::open=Ok; rows written=1`. postgres (live PG 18.4 + AGE 1.7.0 + pgvector 0.8.6): `PARENT PG PROBE: binary tip=v87; db stamp=v92; connect_ok=true`, `observed=92`.
  - **The predicate.** `>` refuses; `==` keeps the historical no-op fast path byte-for-byte; `<` still runs the ladder. Only the strictly-greater case is new.
  - **The placement is the fix, not a detail.** sqlite gates in `db::open` AFTER the pragma block (so `busy_timeout` is in force and ordinary write-lock contention is retried rather than misread as damage) and BEFORE `execute_batch(SCHEMA)`; postgres gates inside the `connect_*` bootstrap block (so it holds `MIGRATION_ADVISORY_LOCK_KEY` and two racing daemons cannot both pass) and BEFORE `raw_sql(INIT_SCHEMA)`. Refusing only inside `migrate` — the issue's literal suggestion — would leave an older binary's `CREATE … IF NOT EXISTS` set replaying over a newer database first, which can resurrect a table or index the newer ladder deliberately removed ([#2424](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2424) proved that class is live here). A refused open is asserted to leave the database BYTE-IDENTICAL — `sqlite_master` name+sql, the stamp, and `PRAGMA integrity_check` on sqlite; the full `information_schema.columns` fingerprint on postgres. Without that assertion the change would silently reduce to the weaker variant. The `migrate` / `migrate_locked` refusals are kept as defense-in-depth for future callers; today each has exactly one production caller, so they close nothing on their own and are not presented as if they did.
  - **The probe is TRI-STATE, and that is a SECOND data-loss defect fixed here.** `migrate` read the stamp with `.unwrap_or(0)`, collapsing a READ ERROR into "fresh" — and because the pre-migration safety snapshot is gated on `version > 0`, an unreadable stamp replayed the ENTIRE v1→tip ladder over a POPULATED database WITH THE SNAPSHOT SUPPRESSED, including the `reversible: false` arms. An absent `schema_version` relation is still 0 (genuinely fresh); a relation that is present but unreadable now refuses. postgres was already correct here and is unchanged in that respect.
  - **Disposition — refuse WRITES, preserve EGRESS.** The first draft refused the OPEN, and three of the five adversarial lenses independently killed it: `db::open` is also the funnel for `backup`, `boot`, `doctor`, `export` and every `verify-*` verb, so a guard whose observable effect is "you may not back up your durable text, and you may not find out why" INVERTS the North Star it serves — the memory TEXT is the source of truth and the schema shape is a derived property of it. So: every write funnel refuses with the typed `StoreError::SchemaAheadOfBinary` / `storage::schema_guard::SchemaAheadOfBinary` (slug `SCHEMA_AHEAD_OF_BINARY`, HTTP **503** — not 500, because it is a deliberate refusal an orchestrator should park a node on, not a fault); `ai-memory backup` falls back to the new `db::open_unmigrated` funnel and still produces a snapshot; `boot` downcasts the typed error into the EXISTING `WarnSchemaUnsupported` manifest (without which that status became structurally dead code, since below-MIN is documented unreachable) and `doctor` names the observed and supported versions instead of flattening to "could not open database". **`open_read_only` cannot serve `backup`** — `PRAGMA query_only = ON` refuses `VACUUM INTO`; verified by execution, not assumed, which is why a dedicated funnel exists.
  - **The escape hatch takes the EXACT observed version, never a boolean.** `AI_MEMORY_ALLOW_SCHEMA_AHEAD=<observed>`: a boolean gets pasted into a systemd unit during one incident and then silently permits every future downgrade forever, whereas an exact-version hatch stops applying the moment the database moves again and is greppable in a fleet audit. Unset / malformed / mismatched all fail CLOSED (the #131 FBL-14 rule); a mismatch gets a distinct message so a stale unit file is diagnosable. Under the hatch the bootstrap DDL AND the ladder are BOTH skipped — a hatch that replayed an old bootstrap over a newer schema would re-open the exact window the guard closes, which was an adversarial finding against the first draft. Registered in `security_profile::KNOBS` as the FIRST permissive knob in that SSOT (hard floor: unset), so an `asi-hard` deployment refuses to boot with it set — without that entry the hardened PROCUREMENT posture would have been silently weaker than its no-disable contract advertises ([#2448](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2448)'s defect shape).
  - **`db::open` is the funnel every interface BOOT crosses — it is NOT the funnel every WRITE crosses**, and the comment in `src/storage/connection.rs` claiming otherwise has been false for two releases. FOUR production CLI paths opened a raw `rusqlite::Connection` and wrote through it: `governance check-action` (both arms — one of them the `--from-pretool-stdin` PreToolUse hook, the highest-frequency write surface in the product, appending to the `signed_events` audit spine), `governance install-defaults` (`UPDATE governance_rules SET enabled = 1`) and `calibrate confidence` (`UPDATE confidence_shadow_observations`). All four now call `storage::assert_schema_not_ahead` directly; the hook arm is deliberately NOT re-routed through `db::open`, which would put the bootstrap + ladder on the agent's critical path. **[#1946](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/1946)'s open-time rollback-evidence check was absent on the same four surfaces and remains so** — that is stated, not silently fixed.
  - **The funnel inventory is MECHANICAL, because an audit true for one merge rots.** `tests/db_open_funnel_ceiling_2445.rs` pins every production raw-sqlite-open site in `src/` with its disposition and fails on an ADDED one *and* a REMOVED one. It immediately found a site the manual sweep missed (`src/vectorlite.rs` — an in-memory ANN index, benign) which is the argument for the gate in one line. The six raw opens in `src/subscriptions.rs` are recorded as ORDERING-covered, not structurally covered: they hold only because the webhook dispatcher is spawned from a `serve` whose `bootstrap_serve` already crossed `db::open`, so the day a standalone dispatcher exists the pin moves and the test fails.
  - **`restore --skip-verify` no longer bypasses the forward-schema refusal.** [#2444](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2444)'s check reads `manifest.schema_version` from INSIDE the `if !args.skip_verify` block — and `--skip-verify` is the only way to restore the manifest-less pre-migration snapshot the rollback runbook recommends, so the documented recovery path was also the path that disabled the guard. The refusal is now re-derived from the snapshot FILE off the already-open read-only probe connection: manifest-independent, un-skippable, one extra query.
  - **`store_err_to_response`'s `_` wildcard is replaced by explicit terminal arms.** A new `StoreError` variant previously landed silently in a generic 500; naming `StoreError::Backend(_)` makes the next one a compile error instead. This surfaced that `StoreError::QuotaExceeded` was in that wildcard — unreachable in practice (an `if let` returns the full 429 envelope first), now named so the two cannot drift apart. `arch_9_store_error_slug_round_trip` gains a length assertion, because its `zip` TRUNCATES and would otherwise silently skip a variant added to only one of its two arrays.
  - **Tests (R-203), both backends, failing at the parent commit.** `tests/schema_downgrade_guard_parent_probe_2445.rs` is written against the PRE-#2445 public API only so it COMPILES AND RUNS at `89e21191`, where it fails: *"an older binary (ladder tip v87) must REFUSE a database stamped v92"*. It is kept permanently as the black-box assertion. `tests/schema_downgrade_guard_2445.rs` (8 cells) and `tests/postgres_schema_downgrade_guard_2445.rs` (3 cells, validated against the live 5433 tier) cover the refusal, the byte-identical-after-refusal proof, the unreadable-stamp refusal, the hatch's admit/fail-closed/no-replay behaviour, egress survival, and cross-backend message parity modulo the backend token. The R-203 CONTROLS pin that `==` is a pure no-op, that `<` still migrates forward to the tip, and that a fresh database is unaffected.
  - **Interaction with the migration-ladder gates: NONE, verified.** `scripts/check-migration-ladder.sh` scans strictly `<`-anchored arms (`if version < CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION {`), so the new `>` and `==` arms are invisible to its const-arm count pins and it passes unchanged. `tests/postgres_ladder_replay.rs` stamps v67 / v73 / v83 — all strictly below the tip — so the new arm never fires, and its greenfield leg lands on `==`; it passes unchanged against the live tier.
  - **Deliberately NOT closed, filed instead.** The guard is OPEN-TIME only: a process already running when another node migrates the shared schema keeps writing until it restarts, so it prevents the RECOVERY, not the damage, in that window ([#2553](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2553)). `observed > tip` is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT — a crashed ladder can leave a structurally-newer sqlite database at an EQUAL stamp, and the guard does not detect it ([#2554](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2554)). `schema_version` has no PK/CHECK on sqlite and is writable by anything with DB access, so a poisoned row is a fleet kill-switch with no in-product repair verb ([#2555](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2555)); zeroing the stamp is the strictly better attack and is undefended ([#2564](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2564)). The pre-migration snapshot has no manifest, so it is only restorable via `--skip-verify` ([#2565](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2565)), and `MIGRATION_LADDER` metadata has been stale since v54 so the `reversible: false` inventory the runbook leans on is unrecorded for 33 migrations ([#2566](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2566)).


### Fixed (a namespace standard bound cross-namespace was served verbatim into every recall with NO visibility filter, and silently dropped from the results)

- **`mcp::inject_namespace_standard` / `mcp::lookup_namespace_standard` now gate the injected standard through the canonical `visibility::is_visible_to_caller` predicate, and no longer `retain`-drop the bound row from `memories`** (refs [#2537](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2537); SECURITY / DATA-HONESTY; 5-agent adversarial vote `4d3ea1c5`, decision memory `e071ec17`). Found while closing [#2479](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2479). Both halves were reproduced with executed evidence against `release/v1.0.0` @ `0825dabc` before any code was written.
  - **HALF 1 — cross-tenant read amplification (CONFIRMED).** `storage::set_namespace_standard` deliberately permits binding a standard memory that lives in a DIFFERENT namespace — the documented shared-policy feature ("one policy, many projects"), comment verbatim: `// Verify the memory exists (but allow cross-namespace — shared policy)`. The READ path turned that into a cross-namespace read primitive: `lookup_namespace_standard` did a raw `db::get` with **no visibility filter and no namespace predicate**, and `inject_namespace_standard` injected the FULL serialized `Memory` — title, content, tags, metadata, owning namespace — into the response for EVERY level of `build_namespace_chain`. Executed repro: bob (`caller=ai:bob`, `X-Agent-Id: bob`) recalling `t2537-tenant` received `standard.content = "needle CLASSIFIED-ALICE-PAYLOAD"`, `standard.namespace = "t2537-victim"`, `standard.metadata.agent_id = "ai:alice"` — alice's **default-private** row in a namespace bob never queried. Reproduced on MCP `memory_recall` (all three retrieval branches), MCP `memory_session_start`, and HTTP `POST /api/v1/session/start`. The adjacent `memories` array in the SAME response object was already caller-filtered by the same predicate (#1468 / #1420), so the response simultaneously said "you may not see row X" and shipped row X's full body.
  - **HALF 1 scope correction against the issue text.** The issue said "every recall". HTTP `POST /api/v1/recall` (`src/handlers/recall.rs`) and the CLI recall path do **not** inject and were never affected; the postgres HTTP `session/start` branch returns before the injector, so postgres-backed daemons never injected a standard at all. The affected surfaces are the sqlite MCP recall + session_start paths and the HTTP `session/start` route that delegates to them.
  - **HALF 2 — retrieval suppression (CONFIRMED, narrower than filed).** `memories.retain(|m| !standard_ids.contains(m.id))` + `response["count"] = memories.len()` ejected any bound id from the results array. Executed repro: two matching rows, one bound as the namespace's standard → the caller received `count: 1`. The filed claim that the response "lies about what matched" holds for `count` and the array; the claim of data loss does **not** — the body relocated to `response["standard"]`. What the relocation DID lose is the `decorate_memory_many` trust decoration (`score`, `provenance_tier`, `confidence_tier`, `freshness_state`, #1709 §2.5 T2), so the single row promoted to *governing authority* over the namespace was the one row delivered with its provenance and staleness signals stripped. Combined with the binding being an attacker-influenceable input, this is a retrieval-suppression primitive over what every caller of that namespace sees.
  - **The fix is the canonical predicate, not a bespoke carve-out.** `caller: Option<&str>` is threaded into both helpers from entry points that ALREADY held it for #1468/#1720; `None` (single-tenant MCP stdio with no `AI_MEMORY_AGENT_ID`) preserves the documented trust-all read posture byte-for-byte. The "admit the standard when its namespace is a link in the recalled chain" alternative was ranked LAST by 4 of the 5 adversarial lenses and is recorded here so it is not re-proposed: `"*"` is a link in EVERY chain (so it legitimises a fleet-wide broadcast exemption); the recall `namespace` argument is caller-supplied and unauthenticated (so the attacker simply recalls the victim's namespace directly); `namespace_meta.parent_namespace` is caller-supplied via `set_standard(parent=…)` and `auto_detect_parent` resolves parents by `-`-prefix truncation (so a chain is graftable, and a string-prefix collision becomes a visibility grant — the #1921 failure mode); and a chain predicate is not derivable at the non-inherit `get_standard` site at all. A second, weaker visibility predicate is itself the defect class #951 exists to prevent.
  - **`memory_namespace_get_standard` is fixed in the same change**, because it is the SAME body read: both its `inherit=true` chain walk and its non-inherit branch now route through the one `lookup_namespace_standard` chokepoint and therefore the one predicate. Fixing only the injection would have left an equivalent tool call open. The MCP dispatch resolves the caller via `identity::resolve_read_visibility_caller` (mirroring `dispatch_memory_recall`).
  - **Withholding is DISCLOSED, as a bare count.** A standard that resolves but fails the predicate contributes `standards_withheld: <n>` and nothing else — deliberately no id, no owner, no namespace, no reason, because the resolved ancestor chain is information the caller never supplied and a per-entry marker would make the honesty field a cross-tenant existence oracle. Precedent shape: the `confidence_filtered_out` count emitted two lines above the injection call. Enforcement is unaffected: governance gates read the standard from storage themselves (`resolve_governance_policy`), so a caller who does not receive the body is still fully bound by it — withholding creates no fail-open governance hole.
  - **WIRE-SHAPE CHANGE (`count` / `memories`), stated plainly.** The `retain` is removed: a matched row stays in `memories` and `count` is the true match count. This inverts the previously documented "Deduplicated from results. Count excludes standard." contract — carried 3-2 in the sub-decision vote on the grounds that a response silently shrinking itself under attacker influence is the North Star's forbidden failure mode, and that a withheld standard must never be able to remove a row the caller WAS entitled to see. Cost: when the caller's own query matched the policy, that one row now appears both in `memories` and under `standard`. Three tests pinned the old behaviour and are rewritten in this change (`test_inject_namespace_standard_top_of_recall_response`, `test_inject_namespace_standard_dedup_keeps_originals_order`, `tests/integration.rs::test_mcp_namespace_standard_auto_prepend`). When the standard IS among the results its already-decorated value is reused as the `standard` payload, so the governing row never ships with weaker trust signals than the rows it governs.
  - **KNOWN AVAILABILITY IMPACT — read this before upgrading a multi-agent fleet.** Standards provisioned over HTTP carry `scope: "shared"` (stamped by both the auto-seed and the unowned-ownership-claim branches, precisely "so the SAL #910 filter still surfaces the standard to every reader") and keep publishing to every caller unchanged. A standard bound via the MCP path from a caller's OWN pre-existing memory is **default-private** and will now be injected only for its owner; a legacy standard whose `metadata.agent_id` is empty becomes invisible to every caller (the canonical owner-keyed semantic, already true on every other read path since #1720). This is a DEGRADE, not corruption — nothing is deleted, the binding is untouched, and `standards_withheld` makes it visible in the first response rather than weeks later as unexplained agent behaviour. Remediation is one `memory_update` setting `metadata.scope` to `shared` / `collective` on the standard memory, or `ai-memory namespace get-standard` (deliberately unfiltered — operator-as-actor) to inspect it. **No legacy-permissive env flag is provided:** a compatibility escape hatch defaulting to a cross-tenant read is not a fix.
  - **Deliberately NOT changed, and filed instead.** The HTTP `GET /api/v1/namespaces?namespace=…` standard-fetch route keeps its no-caller-gate posture: that is a pre-existing, in-tree, documented product decision with its own filed follow-up (the `#945-sibling` note and the postgres arm's `CallerContext::for_admin` — "namespace standards are governance POLICY — readable by any caller that can query the namespace itself", [#959](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/959)), and gating only the sqlite arm would fork sqlite/postgres behaviour on one route. The `ai-memory namespace get-standard` CLI passes `None` for the same operator-as-actor reason the CLI is exempt from quotas and the L1-6 governance hook — a caller with shell access to the DB file is not a security boundary, and this verb is the operator's remediation path.

### Fixed (a CORRECTLY-AUTHORIZED delete stripped the governance binding of namespaces it had no authority over, then resolution failed OPEN)

- **The unqualified `DELETE FROM namespace_meta WHERE standard_id = ?1` on every reap funnel becomes an audited SEVER, and a namespace whose standard was reaped now resolves to a fail-CLOSED floor instead of allow-on-silence** (refs [#2503](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2503); SECURITY / data-integrity, CWE-284; both backends). `set_namespace_standard` deliberately permits CROSS-NAMESPACE binding ("allow cross-namespace — shared policy") and `build_namespace_chain` prepends the global `*` standard to EVERY namespace's chain, so deleting one in-scope memory destroyed the `namespace_meta` binding ROW of namespaces anywhere in the tree — including namespaces the deleting principal is explicitly denied — and `resolve_governance_policy` then returned `None`, i.e. allow-on-silence ([#1569](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/1569)). A federated `deletions[]` push that the [#2447](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2447)/[#2488](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2488) namespace gate CORRECTLY ALLOWS could therefore disarm policy resolution for the whole node via a single `*`-bound standard. Reachable at DEFAULT config; present at the parent commit, so introduced by none of #2488/#2497/#2528/#2539.
  - **What is achievable here, stated before what was done.** The victim's POLICY is genuinely unrecoverable — it lived in the deleted memory's `metadata.governance`, and no metadata bookkeeping resurrects it. What IS achievable, and what this change delivers, is that the deletion can no longer silently WIDEN the victim's authority, and can no longer destroy configuration it had no authority over. Any summary claiming the policy is preserved would be false.
  - **SEVER, not DELETE.** A `namespace_meta` row carries TWO independent operator configurations: `standard_id` (which memory holds the policy) and `parent_namespace` (the explicit inheritance link `build_namespace_chain` walks). Only the first has anything to do with the reaped memory; the second was collateral. All FOUR sqlite reap funnels (`delete`, `archive_memory_no_tx`, `archive_memory_for_caller`, and `size_gc`'s non-archive branch — the last is easy to miss, since the const name is uppercase and a `namespace_meta` grep does not find it) plus `PostgresStore::delete` now route through `storage::sever_namespace_standards`, which sets `standard_id = NULL`, keeps the row and its parent link, and emits a WARN naming the severed namespaces plus a signed `substrate.namespace_standard_severed` audit event over canonical bytes with a SORTED namespace list. When the reaped memory is nobody's standard — the overwhelmingly common case — it performs no UPDATE, no WARN and no event, so an ordinary delete is byte-identical to before.
  - **The #1642 dangling-pointer invariant is preserved, not traded away.** The unqualified DELETE existed as the [#1642](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/1642) fix: a reap must not leave a `standard_id` pointing at a memory that is gone. Severing satisfies that LITERALLY — the pointer is NULL, so no row names a nonexistent memory — and the observable #1642's own regression test pins (`get_namespace_standard` returns `None` after the standard memory is deleted) is byte-identical, because both adapters map a NULL `standard_id` to "no standard bound". `live_delete_cleans_namespace_meta_pg_1642` passes UNCHANGED. What #1642's remedy never fixed is its own STATED harm ("protection silently lapses"): a dangling row and an absent row were INDISTINGUISHABLE to the resolver, so both fell through to allow-on-silence. Severing is what makes them distinguishable; the floor is what closes the fail-open.
  - **The severed FLOOR — a fail-open → fail-closed posture flip.** A chain level whose `namespace_meta` row EXISTS but whose standard is unresolvable (severed, or a legacy dangling pointer) no longer contributes nothing. It is remembered, the walk CONTINUES, and the resolved policy is returned with `write`/`promote`/`delete` raised to at least `Owner`. Three properties are deliberate: it can only TIGHTEN (an intact ancestor `write: Approve` survives — a severed CHILD must never downgrade a governed ANCESTOR, or the fix inverts itself and breaks the feature `parent_namespace` exists for); it costs nothing on a corpus with no severed rows; and the floor is `Owner` rather than `Approve` because `Approve` QUEUES a `pending_actions` row per attempt (a severed `*` standard would flood the queue node-wide) and a floored `delete: Approve` would block erasure/`forget` on rows nobody can approve. A namespace that was NEVER governed keeps allow-on-silence — the floor fires only where an operator actually configured a standard. Applied in all THREE governance walks: sqlite `resolve_governance_policy`, postgres `resolve_governance_policy`, and the separate in-tx walk inside `PostgresStore::enforce_governance_action`.
  - **gc no longer erases the confinement on a timer.** Both backends' dangling-reference sweeps DELETED the row, which made them the back door onto the reap-path fix: a severance the delete path deliberately preserved would be destroyed on the next gc tick (~30 min) and allow-on-silence silently restored. They now perform the SAME sever, so a dangle always becomes SEVERED, never ABSENT. The `standard_id IS NOT NULL` guard is load-bearing on sqlite in a way it is not on postgres — `NOT EXISTS (… id = NULL)` is TRUE, so the sqlite predicate matched ALREADY-SEVERED rows and would have deleted every one on the next tick, while postgres' `NOT IN` form evaluates to NULL on a NULL left side and never matched them. **The two backends already disagreed about NULL here before this issue.** The guard also makes the heal MONOTONE: each dangling row heals once and leaves the set, so no per-tick `updated_at` churn or federation-fanout storm.
  - **Cross-backend arms that were broken in OPPOSITE directions** (the #2488 lesson; each verified live). `PostgresStore::apply_remote_deletion` — the ATTACKER-REACHABLE federated `deletions[]` arm — performed NO `namespace_meta` maintenance at all, so the identical push CLEARED the binding on sqlite and left it DANGLING on postgres; it now severs, closing that arm of [#2493](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2493). `PostgresStore::archive_by_ids` likewise omitted what BOTH sqlite archive funnels have done since #1642; it now severs inside the per-batch tx. `get_namespace_standard` decoded `standard_id` as a NON-NULLABLE `String` on BOTH adapters, so a severed row was a hard decode error — a 5xx on the HTTP surface for a state the substrate now creates deliberately; both now decode `Option` and collapse NULL to "no standard bound".
  - **One divergence discovered while proving the floor on live postgres, and fixed because the fix depends on it.** An `Owner`-level policy with NO resolvable owner has always been `Deny` on sqlite ("owner-level action has no resolvable owner") and `Allow` on postgres — opposite directions on the same state. It is fixed here rather than deferred because the severed floor makes the arm materially more reachable: a severed namespace resolves `write: Owner`, but its owner is read from the very standard memory that was reaped, so `ns_owner` is `None` and a `Store` would sail through — the postgres half of the floor would have been security theatre while the sqlite half worked. Aligned to the sqlite precedent verbatim, message included.
  - **Tests (R-203), both backends, failing at the parent commit on ROW STATE *and* on RESOLVED POLICY.** `tests/delete_governance_strip_2503.rs` (sqlite, 10 cells) — `test result: FAILED. 4 passed; 5 failed` with `src/` reverted to the parent and the tests unchanged; `tests/delete_governance_strip_2503_pg.rs` (postgres, 8 cells, live-validated) — `test result: FAILED. 2 passed; 6 failed`, with the two #2493 arms failing on a literal dangling UUID. Row state is asserted via RAW SQL, never through `get_namespace_standard`, which deliberately collapses NULL to `None` and so cannot distinguish "row deleted" from "row severed" — an assertion routed through it would pass at the parent. A dedicated cell asserts ONLY the resolved policy, so the security half fails at parent independently of the row layout. Controls pin that the legitimate same-namespace cleanup still prevents the #1642 dangle, that an ordinary delete of a non-standard memory is byte-identical INCLUDING `updated_at`, that a severed child does not downgrade a governed ancestor, that gc heals monotonically, and that a never-governed namespace keeps allow-on-silence.
  - **NOT closed by this change, and tracked separately.** The `#1777` owner gate on `clear_namespace_standard` short-circuits when the standard is unresolvable (`src/mcp/tools/namespace.rs`, `PostgresStore::clear_namespace_standard`), so a LOCAL caller can clear a severed row and return to allow-on-silence — the federated `namespace_meta_clears[]` lane is already scope-gated by [#2539](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/pull/2539), so this bounds the local threat model only. `namespace_meta` rows severed by a reap are not counted in the `/sync/push` response envelope (`namespace_meta_cleared` still counts only the clears lane), which needs a `storage::delete` signature change across every funnel. Filed as [#2545](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2545) and [#2546](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2546). Also still open and unaffected: [#2480](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2480), [#2489](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2489), [#2498](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2498), [#2536](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2536).
  - Design resolved by a 5-agent adversarial vote (`4d3ea1c5`): first choices A=3, B=2; Borda A=4, B=5 — decided as the SYNTHESIS (A's substrate + B's resolver change), because the two lenses ranking A first both stated it leaves the escalation live, and the two ranking B first both stated the same. Objections that changed the design: the ancestor-downgrade finding (→ floor instead of replacement), the promote-still-`Any` finding (→ a dedicated floor, not `default_for_managed_namespace`), the `Approve`-floods-pending finding (→ `Owner`), the gc-erases-it-on-a-timer finding (→ the heal), the fourth sqlite site a `namespace_meta` grep misses, and the clear-gate disarm (→ filed, and the PR states the limitation rather than implying the floor is unconditional).


### Fixed (a committed "SOURCE-OF-TRUTH" policy file that nothing reads asserted a required-check set that cannot report)

- **`.github/branch-protection.yml` no longer declares any required-status-check set; it now states plainly that it is documentation, that nothing applies it, and that the declaration lives in `scripts/qc-allowlists/required-contexts-release.txt`** (refs [#2443](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2443); DOCS/CONTROL-INTEGRITY, no runtime or workflow behaviour change). The file opened with "This file is the SOURCE-OF-TRUTH manifest for the branch-protection rules" and listed five `required_checks` per branch for `main`, `release/**` and `develop`. Its declaration was wrong in both directions simultaneously.
  - **Over-declared, and unrequireable twice over.** Three of the five per branch were written as `Batman Mode acceptance gate / <job>`. A GitHub Actions job's check-run name is the JOB name alone (`Rust integration (issue_800_batman_mode)`), never `<workflow> / <job>`, so the prefixed string names no context that exists — pinning it would leave `Expected — waiting` forever, and `enforce_admins: true` means no admin merge clears it. Independently, the carrying workflow's `pull_request` trigger is `paths:`-filtered, so on any PR outside that path list the job emits no check-run at all — rule (c) of `scripts/check-required-contexts.sh`. Both halves are the class [#2494](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2494) closed on the release branch.
  - **Under-declared.** It named two contexts that do exist and are live-required (`C8 caller-context allowlist check`, `Vendor-monoculture + SECS_PER_* lint-gate (#1174 PR10)`) while omitting the other twenty-two `release/v1.0.0` requires.
  - **What the file IS, established mechanically before editing it.** Documentation only. `grep -rn 'branch-protection' .` over the tree returns exactly two references to the path and both are prose — this file's own header and a comment in `batman-mode-acceptance.yml` pointing at its `nightly_schedule` block. No workflow step, no script, and no `gh api …/protection` write reads or applies it, and GitHub never reads a checked-in file. So editing it cannot mutate live protection, and it could never have been an attestation of anything. That is what made it worse than absent: an enterprise reviewer reads the committed file, not the API, so a file asserting `enforce_admins: true` over checks that cannot report MANUFACTURES assurance.
  - **The fix is not a better list.** A second hand-maintained list is how this happened. There is now exactly ONE required-context declaration in the repository — `scripts/qc-allowlists/required-contexts-release.txt`, verified against the workflows on every PR by the `Required-context + classify-base soundness gate (#2494/#2496/#2508)` job — and this file points at it, records only the two contracts documented nowhere else (the Batman nightly-schedule contract and the CODEOWNERS cross-link), and carries per-branch policy INTENT labelled as intent rather than as a claim about live state. No branch-protection API call is made by this change; every protection edit remains operator-gated.
  - **Two adjacent statements corrected while they were provably false.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` told contributors the required set on `main` was the manifest's Batman/C8/Vendor list and that "none of the per-OS `Check (...)` matrix legs are themselves pinned as required" — the exact inverse of the live posture, where those three legs are the whole set. The release mirror's `KNOWN GAPS` still carried an `IN FLIGHT (#2473)` note saying live protection required the TRUNCATED L3 context; both halves of that swap have since landed, so the note is rewritten as CLOSED and explicitly marked a narrative record rather than a control — the gate has no API access by design, so no dated live-state line in a comment re-checks itself.

### Fixed (a CI job name silently truncated by YAML, so the required status check pinned a string nobody wrote)

- **`c8-precheck.yml`'s `l3-boundary-gate` name is now QUOTED, the hand-authored mirror declares the FULL string, and a new HARD-BLOCK rule (e) makes the class un-relandable** ([#2473](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2473); INTEGRITY). The job declared `name: L3-boundary perma-ban gate (§25.3 S5 / RQ-10 #1853)` UNQUOTED. In YAML a `#` **preceded by whitespace** opens a comment, so the parsed job name — and therefore the check-run GitHub emitted — was 44 characters ending at `RQ-10`, with ` #1853)` silently discarded. Because the live required-status-check set was selected by observing which check-runs *reported* on real PR heads, the truncation was copied verbatim into branch protection on `release/v1.0.0`: a required context that no one had authored. Sibling names survive (`(#1174 PR10)`, `(#2146)`, `(#1989)`) because there the `#` is preceded by `(`, which YAML does not treat as a comment start — the boundary is one character wide.
  - **Why this could not be fixed in isolation.** Quoting the name RENAMES the check-run. With `strict: true` and `enforce_admins: true`, an absent required context is `pending` forever and no admin merge clears it, so the rename and the protection edit are one coupled change whose halves pull in OPPOSITE directions: the TRUNCATED context must leave protection **before** the rename merges (after it lands, no PR ever reports that name again — including the PR that renamed it), and the FULL context must enter protection **after** (before it lands, no PR reports the new name either). The mirror's `HOW TO CHANGE THIS FILE` section now carries that sequence explicitly, alongside the general ORDER doctrine it specialises (additions: mirror first; removals: protection first). The intermediate state — the L3 gate running and visible on every PR but not required for one merge window — is the deliberate cost, and it is strictly cheaper than any ordering that wedges the branch.
  - **New rule (e) in `scripts/check-required-contexts.sh` — HARD-FAIL, never allowlistable, applied to EVERY job in EVERY workflow.** A job `name:` written as an unquoted scalar whose raw value contains whitespace-then-`#` is rejected. Scope is repo-wide by the same argument as rule (d): a truncated name is a declared≠actual lie in every UI today and becomes a branch wedge the moment someone adds that context to `required_status_checks.contexts` — which is precisely the mechanism that put the malformed string there. There is no ratchet and no allowlist because the remedy is one character of quoting; a deliberate trailing YAML comment stays expressible by quoting the scalar first (`name: "Foo"  # note`). The risk flag is computed on the RAW scalar tail **before** the comment is stripped, since after stripping the evidence is gone.
  - **Also fixed, and it is why rule (e) works at all: a latent field-split defect in the gate's own record reader.** `read` treats space/tab/newline in `IFS` as *IFS whitespace* and collapses runs of them into ONE delimiter, so with a tab `IFS` an EMPTY MIDDLE field silently shifts every later field left. The `JOB` record's `needs` field is empty for every job with no `needs:` — which is **every c8-precheck gate**, including the one this issue is about — so the newly appended truncation flag landed in the `needs` slot and rule (e) read empty: **blind on exactly the jobs it exists for.** The first version of the (e) self-test leg passed anyway, because a bare unquoting also makes the mirror entry unmatchable and rule (a) fired instead. Both are fixed: the reader splits on `0x1f` (not IFS whitespace, so empty fields are preserved positionally) while the record stream stays TAB-delimited for `--dump` and its `awk -F'\t'` consumers, and the same fix is applied to the rule (b3) STEP loop, where a `run:` step's empty `uses` field was sliding the step NAME into the `uses` slot. Proven on the REAL pre-fix `c8-precheck.yml` replayed from `origin/release/v1.0.0`: rule (e) now names `c8-precheck.yml|l3-boundary-gate` and prints the truncated parse.
  - **Load-bearing evidence.** The `--self-test` (e) leg now makes THREE assertions, and the third is the one that matters: it proves through the gate's own `--dump` that the planted unquoted name really parses TRUNCATED at the `#`; it rewinds the fixture mirror to the TRUNCATED string so **every other rule is satisfied and rule (e) is the only thing left that can fail**; and it requires the failure output to NAME rule (e) and to NOT contain rule (a). "The gate went red" is not the claim being made. The clean control keeps the quoted `#` name and the unquoted `(#` name side by side, so both YAML outcomes stay exercised on the PASS side. The awk parser was re-cross-checked against PyYAML across all 59 jobs in all 17 workflows: zero mismatches.
  - **Frozen-fixture scope, stated rather than discovered later.** `scripts/test/fixtures/required-contexts-prefix-2494.txt` also carried the truncated entry, and the R-203 regression leg runs the REAL gate with that mirror against the REAL workflows requiring exit 0 — so the rename would have broken it. The FROZEN property is the DECIDER ABSENCE (asserted mechanically, and still asserted); the rest of the fixture necessarily tracks live job names or the leg becomes unrunnable. Both the fixture header and the harness now say which is which, so the next rename is not mistaken for a repaired baseline. Harness: 29/29 PASS.

### Added (supply-chain: no git-source cargo dependencies — CI gate)

- **New HARD-BLOCK gate `scripts/check-git-dependency-sources.sh`** (wired as the `c8-precheck.yml` job `Git-dependency-source supply-chain gate (#2050/#2512)`): no cargo dependency in this repo may resolve from a `git` source. Registry (crates.io) or in-tree `path = "vendor/<crate>"` only. Scans every `Cargo.toml` for a `git = "…"` key (inline-table AND `[dependencies.x]` section form) and every `Cargo.lock` for `source = "git+…"`, including under `vendor/`. Ratchet allowlist at `scripts/qc-allowlists/git-dependency-sources-allow.txt`, currently EMPTY by design; `--self-test` proves the gate is load-bearing against three violation shapes plus a clean control ([#2050](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2050), [#2512](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2512) defect 1).
  - **The class.** `Cargo.toml` pinned `paste = { git = "https://github.com/alphaonedev/paste", rev = "6a30252" }` as the RUSTSEC-2024-0436 workaround. On 2026-07-15 the fork REPOSITORY was deleted out-of-band — `git ls-remote https://github.com/alphaonedev/paste` returns "Repository not found" and `GET /repos/alphaonedev/paste` returns 404 — so every cold `cargo` resolve in this repo began failing permanently. Nothing in this repo had changed. GitHub does not preserve a deleted repository's objects, and cargo has no fallback source for a git dependency the way it does for a yanked registry crate: **`rev` pinning buys immutability of CONTENT, never of EXISTENCE.**
  - **Why a static ban and not a reachability probe.** Probing remotes at PR time would make this repo's CI depend on third-party availability, go red for network reasons, and teach reviewers to ignore it. The ban is offline and deterministic, and states the actual rule: third-party source we depend on lives in-tree under `vendor/` where it is reviewable, diffable, and rebuildable with no network — the posture [#2051](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/pull/2051) already adopted for `paste`, now structural instead of a convention recorded in a manifest comment.
  - **Two properties that made it hard to see, both of which the gate removes.** (1) It presented as flake: jobs with a warm `~/.cargo/git` cache kept passing and only cold resolves failed, so #2050 was first filed against two unrelated PRs; developer machines stayed green indefinitely. A gate that only fires on a cold runner is a gate that does not fire — this one fires on every PR, warm or cold. (2) It survived its own fix for 15 days: #2051 landed the vendoring on `release/v1.0.0` and was verified by PR-time CI there, but `main` — the DEFAULT branch, and therefore the only branch GitHub runs `schedule:` workflows from — never received it, so `postgres-parity-nightly` stayed hard-red on the identical error every night from 2026-07-15 and was rediscovered from scratch as #2512.
  - **DATA-INTEGRITY posture (North Star: DEGRADE, never corrupt).** The failure prevented is not a wrong answer, it is a build that cannot be reproduced — which erases the ability to rebuild, audit, or bisect any artifact this repo has ever shipped. Refusing the un-vendorable edge up front is the fail-closed choice; discovering it on a cold runner months later is not.
  - **Provenance of the recovered code, for the record.** Rev `6a302522990cbfd9de4e0c61d91854622f7b2999` is `dtolnay/paste` `master`/HEAD — commit "Add unmaintained note", authored and committed by David Tolnay, 2024-10-07 — so the deleted fork was an unmodified mirror and remains fetchable from upstream. `vendor/paste/` is byte-identical to that tree apart from the omitted `.github/` CI directory: the #2051 vendoring introduced NO new or unknown code. A fork carrying real local modifications would have been unrecoverable.

### Fixed (Apache AGE graph reads never executed — `kg_query` / `kg_timeline` / `lineage` / `kg_invalidate` silently served by the relational CTE)

- **Every AGE-routed graph READ was rejected by AGE at parse time and silently re-served from the relational recursive CTE, while `Capabilities.kg_backend` kept reporting `Age`** ([#2511](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2511), HIGH / data-honesty). A control reported one engine while a different engine answered — the campaign's core defect class. Verified live against BOTH certified AGE builds (1.6.0, the CI image; 1.7.0, the SSOT-pinned version). FIVE INDEPENDENT causes, each sufficient on its own; fixing only the one the issue named would have left the headline true:
  - **The `cypher()` third argument was an inlined `'{…}'::agtype` literal** (`age_params_literal`, five production sites: `kg_query_cypher`, `kg_timeline_cypher`, both `kg_invalidate_cypher` statements, `lineage_cypher`). AGE's `convert_cypher_to_subquery` analyzer requires a bare, `agtype`-TYPED `Param` node there and rejects a literal with `ERROR: third argument of cypher function must be a parameter`. The v0.7.0 comment that introduced the literal blamed the CAST in `$1::agtype`; the real cause is the bind's DECLARED TYPE — `PREPARE q(agtype) … cypher(…, $1)` is accepted, `PREPARE q(text) … cypher(…, $1::agtype)` is rejected, both confirmed live. Every site now binds through the existing `Agtype` sqlx wrapper (which declares `ag_catalog.agtype` by name, so sqlx resolves the real type OID and sends it in `Parse` — the wire equivalent of `PREPARE q(agtype)`) and writes a bare `$1`. This is the shape the AGE *write* path (`project_link_into_age`) has used successfully since v0.7.0.1 G2; only the read paths were left on the rejected form. `age_params_literal` is DELETED rather than deprecated so the shape cannot be reintroduced. `.persistent(false)` (#1482, per-call-unique cypher text) is preserved — sqlx resolves declared parameter type OIDs before `Parse` for the unnamed statement too.
  - **`kg_query`'s Cypher body used two constructs AGE's parser does not implement.** `ALL(e IN relationships(p) WHERE …)` — the #1689 temporal-validity guard — raises `ERROR: syntax error at or near "("` (as do `ANY` / `NONE` / `filter(…)` / list comprehensions), and `reduce(s = a.id, n IN nodes(p)[1..] | s + '->' + n.id)` — the path-string builder — raises `ERROR: syntax error at or near "|"`. A prior session hit the same `reduce` wall on `find_paths_cypher` and fixed it THERE, leaving the `kg_query` twin. `length(r)` over a variable-length pattern's relationship list also fails (`length() argument must resolve to a scalar`).
  - **The body is now reduced to the smallest AGE surface that can carry the contract** — a plain variable-length `MATCH`, one scalar (`b.id`), plus `nodes(p)` / `relationships(p)` (which AGE returns as full vertex / edge payloads). Everything derived is computed Rust-side from those payloads, so the AGE branch stays row-for-row equivalent to `kg_query_cte_filtered` (the #648 parity contract) now that it actually executes: the #1689 per-edge `valid_until` guard (`age_path_edges_all_current`, fail-CLOSED on a malformed stamp), the CTE's node-uniqueness / cycle arm, `relation` (the `last(r).relation` twin, property-then-label), `depth`, and the `->`-joined path string (byte-identical to the CTE's `array_to_string(nodes, '->')`).
  - **`lineage_cypher` was unusable for two FURTHER reasons.** Its pattern was a relationship-type ALTERNATION (`-[r:derived_from|reflects_on|derives_from*1..N]->`) — AGE's parser does not implement `|` alternation AT ALL, with or without a variable-length quantifier — and it projected `length(r)`. The pattern is now UNTYPED and the provenance-subset (`P`) filter is applied Rust-side per edge (`age_edge_is_lineage_relation`, reading the same `MemoryLinkRelation::LINEAGE` SSOT `lineage_cte`'s `relation IN (...)` list is built from, and failing CLOSED on an edge whose relation cannot be read). The filter requires EVERY edge on the path to be in `P`, mirroring the CTE's predicate on both the seed and the recursive step — an untyped traversal would otherwise surface a path that hops through a `related_to` edge, which the CTE can never return: a WRONG result, not merely a different one.
  - **The agtype RESULT decode was broken too, and could only surface once the statements executed.** Every AGE read branch read its scalar cells with `try_get::<String, _>` on an `agtype` column. sqlx receives results in PostgreSQL's BINARY format and AGE's binary wire form is a `version` byte (`0x01`) followed by the text payload, so a `String` decode either fails the type check or glues `0x01` onto the value. The bug sat latent from v0.7.0 because the statements were rejected at parse analysis, `rows` was always empty, and the decode loops never ran — the only reason `find_paths_cypher` avoided it is that it already used the `Agtype` wrapper explicitly. Fixing the statements made the decode reachable for the first time, and it errored → `is_age_runtime_failure` → straight back to the CTE. All fifteen agtype cells across `kg_query_cypher` / `kg_timeline_cypher` / `kg_invalidate_cypher` / `lineage_cypher` now read through one `age_cell_text` helper.
  - **The #1948 R19/A3 fail-closed lifecycle allow-list is now applied on the AGE branch too.** The AGE projection carries no lifecycle state and the CTE enforced the allow-list in its `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM memories … lifecycle_visible_clause)` tail. Pre-fix this divergence was unobservable (the AGE branch never returned a row); making the branch execute WITHOUT it would have widened KG visibility to tombstoned / erased / quarantined targets on every AGE deployment. `kg_query_cypher` re-derives it from the relational source of truth in one round-trip.
- **Fallback honesty: an AGE→CTE fallback caused by a statement THIS ADAPTER built wrong is no longer laundered as a transient substrate outage** (#2511). `warn_age_fallback` / `warn_age_fallback_pair` already emitted a WARN, but with the message "AGE backend unreachable" and no cause discrimination — so a PERMANENT adapter defect affecting every AGE deployment on every request read as a transient degradation an operator should wait out. AGE's own parser/analyzer rejections are now classified (`is_age_adapter_statement_defect`, a deliberately narrow signature list that can only ever UNDER-report, never mislabel a real outage as a code bug) and emitted on a dedicated tracing target `store::postgres::kg::adapter_defect` with `reason = adapter_statement_rejected`, naming it a developer-actionable defect. Genuine outages keep the existing target + message with `reason = age_substrate_unreachable`. Both still fall back to the CTE — degrade, never hard-fail a live KG surface. `docs/kg-backend-fallback.md` documents the third cause class + both targets.
- **R-203 regression coverage** — `tests/age_cypher_param_binding_2511.rs`. The live tests assert through DIRECT Cypher, never through `kg_query` (which falls back, so a `kg_query`-only assertion cannot tell the two engines apart — the #2397 executed-evidence trap): they drive AGE and the relational mirror into deliberate DISAGREEMENT (an edge present ONLY in AGE with no `memory_links` row; the mirror case with the row surviving and the AGE edge deleted) and assert `kg_query` reports the AGE-side truth. Both FAIL at the parent commit. A third live test pins the substrate premise itself (the inlined literal must be REJECTED, the typed-Param form ACCEPTED) so a future AGE version that changes the contract surfaces here rather than as another silent degradation. A DB-free source-inspection pin (the `qual_pg_write_funnel_parity_2393_2397` pattern) structurally scans every `cypher('memory_graph', $$ … $$` statement in the adapter and fails if its third argument is anything but a bare `$1`, so the rejected shape cannot come back on a host that never sees AGE. Wired into the `postgres-age` job of `postgres-parity-nightly.yml` (`-- --include-ignored`, the #1799 live-PG lane convention).
- **KNOWN RESIDUAL, same class, deliberately not fixed here:** `build_find_paths_current_view_cypher` still carries `ALL(e IN relationships(p) …)`, so EVERY AGE-routed `find_paths` is also parse-rejected and CTE-served. It reaches the defect through a different door (the 2-arg `cypher()` form, untouched by the third-argument fix) and porting the Rust-side guard needs two decisions that warrant their own review (`LIMIT {cap}` currently applies BEFORE the guard; whether `find_paths_cte`'s visibility semantics need the same explicit re-derivation). Documented in the builder's rustdoc and tracked on #2511. `Capabilities.kg_backend` reporting is also unchanged in this PR (a separate contract question).

### Fixed (federated `deletions[]` funnel namespace confinement, both backends)

- **The federated `deletions[]` lane was broken in OPPOSITE directions on the two backends; neither was correct and they disagreed, so a mixed-backend mesh could not converge on what exists** ([#2488](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2488) CWE-284 / GA-blocker, [#2491](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2491) data-integrity). Fixed together because they are the same two lines on the two funnels, and fixing either alone leaves them disagreeing. Design decided by a Fable 5 1x7 adversarial vote (`4d3ea1c5`), 7/7 unanimous.
  - **postgres — fail-OPEN (#2488).** The `#2447` delete gate wrapped itself in `receive_auth::inbound_write_needs_existing_namespace`, which is documented in that module as a hot-path READ-ELISION optimisation and returns `false` for an enrolled peer whose `allowed_namespaces` is empty/absent. That is a legal shape — `PeerScope::allowed_namespaces` is `#[serde(default)]`, so an operator who enrols a peer purely for `allowed_sender_agent_ids` silently gets `[]` — and it is exactly the shape `#2447` Layer 2 was voted in to refuse. In the WRITE lane a `false` verdict still falls through to Layer 2; in the DELETE lane it skipped ALL checking, so `apply_remote_deletion` ran unguarded. Net: a peer refused every write could still hard-delete any row in any namespace by id. **An optimization predicate used as an authorization predicate** — the elision predicate is now used only for the job it was written for.
  - **sqlite — silently LOSSY (#2491).** The `#1934` gate called `peer_attestation::namespace_allowed` unconditionally, with no enrolled-posture wrapper. Its `scope_for(peer) == None` arm falls through to `sync_trust_peer_bypass()` (`AI_MEMORY_FED_SYNC_TRUST_PEER`, default **false**), so in the ZERO-CONFIG posture — and on any header-absent push that reached the loop — EVERY federated deletion was refused and counted `skipped` inside an **HTTP 200**. Not DLQ'd, so never retried. Since [#2341](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2341) a `skipped > 0` receiver report is a non-ack (`sync.rs` `success_report_non_ack_reason`), so the origin's quorum tracker does NOT count the refusal as replicated — but `broadcast_delete_quorum` handles that `Fail` with a **warn-only log and no retry, no DLQ enqueue** ([#2498](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2498)), `/sync/since` carries no tombstones, and `QuorumPolicy::majority` can still let the local commit plus one healthy peer satisfy `W` — so the operator's DELETE returns 200 while a replica keeps the row forever. Replicas diverge permanently and silently. On a GDPR-erasure or credential-rotation path that is a **wrong result surfaced as success**, which the North Star ranks above the confidentiality direction. `receive_auth.rs` had documented this exact trap for the write lane since `#2447`; the delete lane never got the `has_allowlist()` guard.
  - **The fix.** Both funnels are now guarded on the ENROLLED posture (`PeerAttestationConfig::has_allowlist()`) and route through the shared `receive_auth::inbound_by_id_namespace_authorized`, so every lane that reaches the verdict returns the same answer for the same peer shape (zero-config, enrolled-scoped, enrolled-unscoped, header-absent, not-in-a-non-empty-allowlist), and the empty-scope disposition honours `AI_MEMORY_FED_REQUIRE_PUSH_NAMESPACE_SCOPE` (env row 147) instead of hard-coding it. Precisely: `memories[]` + `deletions[]` on BOTH backends, and `archives[]` + `restores[]` on sqlite — on postgres those two subcollections never reach the verdict at all because the funnel reports them `unsupported_on_postgres` (fail-closed, so no hole, but "all four lanes on both backends" would be false as written). The stored-namespace probe stays ELIDED on the Layer-2-only shapes, where the stored namespace provably cannot change the verdict — so the fix costs **zero extra reads** versus the broken code.
- **`inbound_by_id_namespace_authorized` now takes `stored_namespace: Option<&str>`** so "unread on the Layer-2 path" is compiler-enforced rather than conventional: no caller can fabricate an empty string into a Layer-1 glob match, and an absent value arriving while Layer 1 IS armed fails CLOSED instead of being waved through.
- **The federated-delete namespace gate is no longer a permanent erasure-denial primitive** (in-PR rider, [#2488](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2488)). Both delete funnels probed the target row through a FULL-ROW read (`db::get` on sqlite, `MemoryStore::get` → `SELECT * FROM memories WHERE id = $1` on postgres) to learn one TEXT column. Two consequences, the second severe: the postgres shape shipped the `embedding vector(N)` (~12 KB at 3072-d), the stored generated `tsv`, the full `content` and the `encrypted_envelope` per probed id, un-pipelined, up to `max_page_size` ids per request — and, because both full-row mappers are pinned to `DecryptFailurePolicy::FailClosed`, a row whose at-rest envelope will not open on this node returned `Err`, landing in the gate's fail-closed arm and making that row **permanently un-deletable by federation, with no operator escape hatch** (`AI_MEMORY_STRICT_DECRYPT_READS` only hardens, never relaxes). A row whose content this node cannot even read is the row an operator most urgently wants gone, and it was the one row the gate made immortal — behind an HTTP 200. Both lanes now use a SCALAR namespace projection, which cannot fail for the decrypt reason at all: sqlite reuses `db::namespace_by_id` (whose doc comment has warned about routing a namespace gate through `get` since `#2447` — the delete lanes were the only lanes ignoring it) and postgres gets a new `MemoryStore::namespace_by_id` trait method (default impl composes `get` so third-party impls keep compiling; both shipped adapters override it with a single-column projection). The postgres override reuses `SQL_SELECT_NS_VERSION_BY_ID`, the same shape `apply_remote_deletion` already used internally.
- **An unresolvable-row delete refusal is now distinguishable from a scope refusal.** Both increment the same `skipped` counter in a 200 response, so an operator could not tell "your peer lacks scope" (fix the config) from "this node cannot resolve that row" (an un-erasable row — investigate the storage). The refusal WARN now carries `cause = namespace_probe_unresolvable`, a new closed-set token in `receive_auth` that `push_dlq::classify_quarantine_cause` maps (following the `unenrolled_author_strict` precedent).
- **The Layer-2 refusal WARN is lane-conditional.** For `lane == "deletions"` the shared prose read *"its read + delete scope are already empty — refusing this deletions entry"*, i.e. "your delete scope is already empty, therefore I refuse your delete" — circular, unactionable, and no longer even true now that the delete disposition is governed by env row 147 rather than hard-coded. Layer 2 is also factored into ONE site so the prose cannot fork per lane.
- **Docs / infra:** env-table rows **147** (delete-lane claims were false at HEAD; the row already named DELETE as one of its "three lanes") and **25** (`AI_MEMORY_FED_SYNC_TRUST_PEER` becomes structurally unreachable on the delete lane) carry truth-fixes; no new env row was added, because no new knob was voted. `src/handlers/federation_receive.rs`, `src/handlers/federation_signing_check.rs` and `src/federation/receive_auth.rs` join the foundational `__ALL__` list in `scripts/ci-test-impact.sh` so a future PR that re-breaks the gate cannot ship without re-running the proof. A doc comment on `MemoryStore::apply_remote_deletion` now explains WHY both adapters discard `_ctx` (per-row ownership is the wrong control for a replication lane — restoring it would refuse multi-hop relays of third-party deletions and make unstamped legacy rows permanently un-deletable; refuted by the same vote) so the next auditor does not re-file it.
- **Scope of this fix, stated narrowly — the destructive-capability class is NOT retired.** What shipped is the `deletions[]` funnel confined on both backends. `apply_remote_deletion` is only one of several receive-side funnels that can reach a hard `delete`, and an adversarial review of this PR probed two others end-to-end to a destroyed row under **default config** with a correctly-enrolled, correctly-scoped, TOFU-passing peer: `pending_decisions[]` reaches `storage::delete` on an attacker-chosen `memory_id` with **no namespace check** (`pending_author_authorized` inspects only `requested_by` and the payload's `metadata.agent_id` — never `pa.namespace`, and it never resolves `pa.memory_id`), and `namespace_meta[]` has **no scope gate at all**, which lets a peer rebind a foreign namespace's governance standard to an approver it controls and then self-approve (`set_namespace_standard` permits cross-namespace binding; `ApproverType::Agent` compares ids and never calls `is_registered_agent`). Both are tracked as [#2478](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2478) and [#2479](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2479), both are sqlite-reachable, and **neither increments the `deleted` counter**, so such a delete is invisible in the 200 response, in the refusal WARN, and in the DLQ cause set this entry extends. And a third, filed from the same review as [#2503](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2503), runs straight THROUGH the confined funnel: `storage::delete` unconditionally executes `DELETE FROM namespace_meta WHERE standard_id = ?1` with no namespace predicate (the #1642 dangling-pointer fix), and `set_namespace_standard` permits cross-namespace binding — so an in-scope delete the gate CORRECTLY allows strips the governance policy of a namespace the peer is denied, and via a global `*` standard the whole namespace tree at once, with `resolve_governance_policy` failing OPEN and the envelope reporting `deleted: 1, namespace_meta_cleared: 0`. Stated precisely, then: **namespace scope is the control on WHICH ROW the `deletions[]` funnel erases; it is not the control on WHAT THAT ERASURE DESTROYS**, and it is not yet the control on the destructive capability as a whole.
- **The rollout knob governs ONE peer shape; the other two are refused unconditionally** ([#2497](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2497), in-PR regression fix). The first revision of this fix routed three distinct peer shapes through one fall-through arm, so with `AI_MEMORY_FED_REQUIRE_PUSH_NAMESPACE_SCOPE=0` an **anonymous** push (no `X-Peer-Id`) hard-deleted a row on a node whose only enrolled peer was scoped elsewhere — turning a documented per-shape rollout hatch into an anonymous-delete grant, and falsifying that knob's own doc claim that its "entire blast radius is ONE config shape". A new `receive_auth::peer_enrolled_in_allowlist` predicate now refuses **header-absent** (including a whitespace-only header, which `extract_peer_id` collapses to `None`) and **not-in-a-non-empty-allowlist** BEFORE the knob is read, so the knob is once again true to its documentation rather than re-scoped to match the code. **Availability note for the staged-rollout posture:** because the refusal lives in the SHARED Layer 2, this also changes `memories[]` / `archives[]` / `restores[]` for the (allowlist configured + header-less legacy peer + knob `=0`) combination — those writes were applied before and are refused now. That is the correct direction, but it means `=0` is **not** a general rollout hatch: an operator on that posture loses writes as well as deletes on upgrade, silently, inside an HTTP 200 with no DLQ enqueue ([#2498](https://github.com/alphaonedev/ai-memory-mcp/issues/2498)). Identify the peer (enrol it, with `["**"]` for a deliberate per-peer allow-all) or remove the allowlist entirely for the zero-config posture — a per-peer scope cannot be applied to a peer that cannot be identified, so for a header-less push "enrol the peer" is not an actionable remedy.
- **Tests:** `tests/federation_delete_ns_scope_2488.rs` (sqlite) + `tests/federation_delete_ns_scope_2488_pg.rs` (postgres) fill coverage cells that were **all empty**: pg x enrolled-unscoped (the #2488 exploit), sqlite x zero-config (the #2491 outage), header-absent disposition, knob-reachability under `=0`, enrolled-scoped controls both directions, zero-config availability guards, and — the cell that proves the scalar probe removed the trap — an UNDECRYPTABLE-ENVELOPE row in the deletions lane on both backends, asserting it DELETES rather than `skipped`. Both files build their OWN router: `tests/l07_3_chunk_d_http_surface.rs` already asserted `deleted >= 1` on a zero-config sqlite push and was GREEN over the broken lane, because `build_router_fixture` pre-sets `AI_MEMORY_FED_SYNC_TRUST_PEER=1` and masks the refusal (`install_federation_legacy_bypass_pg` does the same on pg) — a new test written against either fixture would have passed BEFORE the fix and proved nothing. Every assertion is on DB ROW STATE with the counter as secondary (refusal counters increment for several unrelated reasons), and posture teardown is an RAII drop guard so a panicking assertion cannot leak an enrolled allowlist into the next test in the binary.
